explanation.summary: Baseline SGA monitoring per RANZCP is anthropometry (weight, BMI, waist), BP, fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipids, and 12-lead ECG. Prolactin is symptom-driven or agent-driven (risperidone, amisulpride). Clozapine adds baseline echocardiogram, troponin and CRP.
key_points: Baseline panel: anthropometry, BP, fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipids, ECG
Repeat at 6 weeks, 12 weeks, then annually
Prolactin only when agent-driven or symptomatic
Clozapine adds echo, troponin, CRP at baseline
explanation.pearls: The 10 to 20 year mortality gap in schizophrenia is largely cardiometabolic and preventable with a structured schedule.

options.rationale: The RANZCP-endorsed Lambert schedule requires anthropometry (weight, BMI, waist), blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c, and a fasting lipid profile at baseline, plus a 12-lead ECG to establish a QTc reference before any antipsychotic (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Medication Monitoring).

Prolactin is not part of the routine baseline metabolic screen for every SGA and is measured only if a prolactin-raising agent is chosen or if the patient develops symptoms; anthropometry and ECG are also required at baseline (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Medication Monitoring).

OGTT, fasting insulin and HOMA-IR are research-tier measures and not part of the routine schedule; baseline echocardiogram is required for clozapine, not for a first SGA choice (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

UEC and TFTs are appropriate for lithium initiation, not for baseline SGA metabolic screening; fasting glucose or HbA1c and fasting lipids are the required metabolic bloods (Source: AMH: antipsychotic monitoring).

Deferring baseline bloods leaves no reference point when adverse metabolic changes appear in the first 12 weeks and is inconsistent with the RANZCP schedule (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Medication Monitoring).

explanation.summary: Risperidone and amisulpride cross the blood brain barrier poorly at the tuberoinfundibular tract and raise prolactin more than other SGAs. Menstrual disturbance, galactorrhoea, sexual dysfunction or new gynaecomastia on these agents should prompt a fasting serum prolactin, with pregnancy and thyroid disease excluded first.
key_points: Risperidone and amisulpride are the SGA prolactin offenders
Aripiprazole is prolactin-sparing and often the switch target
Values under 3000 mIU/L usually drug-related; higher values warrant pituitary MRI
Sustained hypogonadism risks bone loss over years
explanation.pearls: Menstrual change on risperidone is not just an inconvenience - it flags hypogonadism and future osteoporosis risk.

options.rationale: Amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea on a known dopamine antagonist are most likely medication-mediated hyperprolactinaemia; pelvic imaging without checking prolactin first puts the cart before the horse (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Medication Monitoring).

Imaging is indicated only after prolactin is measured and only if the value is disproportionately high (typically over 3000 mIU/L) or does not fall with dose reduction or switch (Source: AMH: risperidone).

TSH is already normal today and hypothyroidism is not causing the picture; broad endocrine screening does not change the immediate step, which is to check the pituitary hormone most likely elevated by this drug (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Risperidone is a strongly prolactin-elevating antipsychotic; amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea with pregnancy and thyroid disease excluded should trigger a fasting serum prolactin before any imaging or endocrine referral (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
DEXA becomes relevant later if sustained hyperprolactinaemia and hypogonadism are confirmed; it is not the first test at symptom onset (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Medication Monitoring).

explanation.summary: For first-episode schizophrenia the SGA choice should be individualised to baseline cardiometabolic risk. Aripiprazole and lurasidone have the lowest weight, glucose and lipid signal; olanzapine and clozapine the highest; risperidone and quetiapine sit intermediate.
key_points: Lowest metabolic burden: aripiprazole, lurasidone
Highest metabolic burden: olanzapine, clozapine
Match the drug profile to the patient's baseline risk
All SGAs still need scheduled metabolic monitoring
explanation.pearls: In diabetes plus central obesity, aripiprazole is the pragmatic first-line SGA - not because it is stronger, but because you are not adding a second chronic disease to an existing one.

options.rationale: Olanzapine has the highest weight gain, dyslipidaemia and dysglycaemia signal of the SGAs and would compound established type 2 diabetes and central obesity (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia).

Quetiapine carries an intermediate to high metabolic burden with meaningful weight gain and dyslipidaemia, and is not the preferred first choice when cardiometabolic risk is already established (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Aripiprazole and lurasidone have the lowest weight gain and metabolic burden among the SGAs and are the preferred first choice when baseline cardiometabolic risk is high; efficacy for positive symptoms is comparable in first-episode schizophrenia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Risperidone has intermediate weight gain and dysglycaemia risk and raises prolactin; when a metabolically friendlier alternative is equally effective, it is not the preferred first choice here (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia).
Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after two adequate trials of other antipsychotics and carries the highest metabolic burden of all agents (Source: AMH: clozapine).

explanation.summary: The RANZCP schedule is baseline, 6 weeks, 12 weeks, then annually. A rising HbA1c into pre-diabetes range within 12 weeks is a trigger to tighten cadence rather than defer to annual, and to intensify lifestyle input, consider metformin, or switch to a lower-burden SGA.
key_points: Baseline, 6 wk, 12 wk, then annual is the default schedule
Tighten to 3-monthly if HbA1c is rising or over 42 mmol/mol
Metformin has the best evidence for antipsychotic-induced weight gain
Switch to aripiprazole or lurasidone if lifestyle plus adjuncts fail
explanation.pearls: Any HbA1c that crosses into pre-diabetes on an SGA earns a three-month re-check, not a twelve-month wait.

options.rationale: Annual review is the baseline schedule for a stable patient without a rising trajectory; a rise in HbA1c into the impaired-glucose-regulation range within 12 weeks warrants tighter follow-up (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Medication Monitoring).

A jump into the pre-diabetes range with concurrent weight gain and central obesity on the most metabolically active SGA requires early re-testing within three months, coupled with intensified lifestyle input, to catch progression to diabetes and inform the switch or metformin discussion (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

OGTT is not the standard first-line screen; HbA1c and fasting glucose per the RANZCP schedule are sufficient, and OGTT is reserved for discordant results or specific clinical uncertainty (Source: RACGP Red Book).

HbA1c is more informative than fasting glucose alone for tracking trajectory on an SGA and is part of the RANZCP schedule; dropping it loses the earliest signal (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Medication Monitoring).

SGA-associated dysglycaemia is often silent until well established; symptom-triggered screening misses the intervention window that structured monitoring is designed to catch (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: The Australian CVD Risk Guideline 2023 recognises serious mental illness as a risk-enhancer that pushes intermediate-risk patients into pharmacological therapy. A five-year absolute risk of 5 to under 10 percent plus SMI warrants a moderate-intensity statin alongside lifestyle change.
key_points: AU CVD risk under 5% low; 5 to under 10% intermediate; 10% or over high
SMI, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander heritage, family history and CKD are risk-enhancers
Moderate-intensity statin is first-line lipid therapy
Fibrates for severe hypertriglyceridaemia only
explanation.pearls: Serious mental illness deserves the same primary prevention aggression as diabetes at the intermediate-risk band.

options.rationale: Absolute CVD risk of 9% over five years combined with a chronic serious mental illness reclassifies her into the higher-risk group where statin therapy is recommended alongside lifestyle change (Source: NVDPA Absolute CVD Risk Guidelines).
Fibrates are not first-line for LDL-driven risk reduction; they are reserved for severe hypertriglyceridaemia, which is not the picture here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
Ezetimibe monotherapy has weaker outcome data than statins and is used as add-on when statins are insufficient or not tolerated; it is not first-line (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

A switch may lower future metabolic burden but does not correct her current five-year risk; deferring statin therapy in an intermediate-risk patient with a risk-enhancer misses the primary prevention window (Source: Australian CVD Risk Guideline 2023).

Australian absolute CVD risk of 5 to under 10 percent is intermediate risk, and serious mental illness plus antipsychotic therapy is a risk-enhancer that shifts intermediate-risk patients into treatment; a moderate-intensity statin is first-line (Source: Australian CVD Risk Guideline 2023).

explanation.summary: When lifestyle measures fail to control antipsychotic-induced weight gain in a patient responding to their current agent, metformin is the first pharmacological adjunct in Australian practice. It attenuates weight, HbA1c and lipid worsening and is safe in patients with normal renal function.
key_points: Metformin is first-line adjunct for antipsychotic weight gain
Dose-halving risks relapse in known responders with prior failures
Orlistat and topiramate have weaker evidence in this setting
Switch remains an option if adjunct plus lifestyle still fails
explanation.pearls: In a known responder with prior failures, protect the antipsychotic first and treat the metabolic syndrome with an evidence-based adjunct.

options.rationale: Halving an effective dose risks psychiatric relapse when he has already failed two alternatives; dose reduction is not the recommended first pharmacological step for antipsychotic-induced weight gain (Source: AMH: olanzapine).

Orlistat has a smaller evidence base than metformin for antipsychotic-induced weight gain and gastrointestinal tolerability limits use; it is not first-line in this setting (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Metformin has the strongest evidence base and is the recommended first pharmacological adjunct for antipsychotic-induced weight gain and dysglycaemia when lifestyle measures have not achieved control, with renal function safely permitting use (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

His BMI of 29 is below the accepted bariatric surgery threshold and pharmacological and lifestyle steps have not been exhausted; bariatric surgery is not the next step (Source: NHMRC Obesity Guidelines).

Topiramate has cognitive side effects and a weaker evidence base than metformin in this context, and is not the recommended first pharmacological adjunct in Australian psychiatric practice (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Amisulpride and risperidone are the strongest prolactin-elevating antipsychotics. Symptomatic values under about 3000 mIU/L are almost always drug-related and the first move is to switch to a prolactin-sparing agent such as aripiprazole, then re-check prolactin. Values above about 3000 mIU/L or non-resolving after switch warrant pituitary imaging.
key_points: Under 3000 mIU/L on offending agent: switch first, image later
Aripiprazole is the prolactin-sparing switch target
Cabergoline risks worsening psychosis and is not first-line
Address hypogonadism, not just the withdrawal bleed
explanation.pearls: Prolactin under 3000 on amisulpride is drug guilt until proven otherwise; MRI is not the first move.

options.rationale: Values under about 3000 mIU/L on a strongly prolactin-elevating antipsychotic like amisulpride are almost always drug-related; imaging is reserved for higher values, discordant clinical features or failure of prolactin to fall after switching or reducing the offending drug (Source: AMH: amisulpride).

Dopamine agonists risk aggravating psychosis in patients on antipsychotics and are not first-line for drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia; addressing the offending agent is preferred (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Aripiprazole is prolactin-sparing (partial dopamine agonism) and is the recommended switch target for symptomatic drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia when the primary agent is prolactin-elevating; a cross-titrated switch with prolactin re-check in 6 to 8 weeks is the pragmatic step here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Restoring withdrawal bleeds masks the underlying hypogonadism, does not address bone loss risk over years, and leaves a modifiable prolactin driver untreated (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Medication Monitoring).

A moderately elevated prolactin on a known prolactin-elevating antipsychotic with a clear management pathway does not require endocrinology gatekeeping; refer only if prolactin does not fall after switch or if the value is disproportionately high (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: In a clear clozapine responder with new pre-diabetes and atherogenic dyslipidaemia at 12 weeks, protect the antipsychotic and treat the metabolic syndrome: intensified lifestyle input, metformin, and a repeat panel in 4 to 6 weeks. Cessation is reserved for life-threatening adverse events; dose reduction risks loss of response after failed trials of alternatives.
key_points: Trigger for action: over 7% weight gain, new IFG, new dyslipidaemia
Metformin has the best evidence for clozapine weight gain
Repeat panel at 4 to 6 weeks to track response
Cessation only for life-threatening adverse events
explanation.pearls: In a clozapine responder, treat the metabolic syndrome around the antipsychotic, not by walking away from it.

options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of clozapine in a clear responder without a life-threatening adverse event risks rapid rebound psychosis, which for clozapine can be severe; the metabolic changes are significant but do not justify walking away from the only effective agent (Source: AMH: clozapine).

Weight gain over 7% and new impaired fasting glucose with atherogenic dyslipidaemia in a clear clozapine responder meets the RANZCP threshold for intensified intervention rather than cessation; metformin has the best evidence for clozapine-associated weight gain and the metabolic panel should be repeated to track response (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

A 12-week jump into pre-diabetes plus dyslipidaemia is exactly the trigger for tightening the schedule, not deferring it; the annual interval assumes stable metabolic parameters (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Medication Monitoring).

Halving an effective dose risks loss of response and is not the recommended first step for clozapine-associated metabolic adverse effects when lifestyle plus adjunctive pharmacotherapy have not been trialled (Source: AMH: clozapine).

Adding a second antipsychotic to allow clozapine dose reduction is not the recommended first step for metabolic adverse effects and does not address the primary metabolic driver, which is clozapine itself (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis under DSM-5 requires five or more persistent inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms, several present before age 12, evident across two or more settings, causing functional impairment, and not better explained by another disorder. Cross-setting impairment is essential to distinguish ADHD from a context-specific issue (workplace mismatch, relationship stress) and is the most under-documented criterion in adult first-presentations.
key_points: Adult DSM-5 threshold is 5 symptoms (paediatric threshold is 6)
Symptoms and impairment must be evident in 2 or more settings
Several symptoms must be documented before age 12
Neuropsych testing and neuroimaging are not diagnostic
explanation.pearls: AADPA 2022 endorses collateral information from a partner, parent, or workplace as the strongest evidence for the cross-setting criterion in adult first-presentations, and school reports are the highest-yield corroboration for the age-of-onset criterion.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

options.rationale: Adults require at least five (not six) inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms under DSM-5. Six is the paediatric threshold. Self-report scales support but do not replace clinician-verified symptom count and cross-setting evidence. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022))
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

options.rationale: Symptomatic response to stimulants is not diagnostic; healthy individuals also show attentional improvement. The AADPA guideline treats medication response as a treatment marker, not a diagnostic test. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022))
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

options.rationale: Childhood onset is required, but the more central issue in her case is documenting cross-setting impairment. Age of onset is necessary but insufficient without demonstrated functional impairment in more than one domain. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022))
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

options.rationale: DSM-5 adult ADHD requires several symptoms before age 12, five or more current symptoms, AND clear evidence of impairment in two or more settings (e.g. work AND home). Her history documents workplace impact but not home/social functioning; cross-setting evidence is the most commonly missed criterion in adult first-presentation and the strongest safeguard against over-diagnosis. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022))
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

options.rationale: Neuroimaging and QEEG are not recommended for ADHD diagnosis in Australian practice. Findings overlap with healthy controls and other disorders. AADPA explicitly recommends against these investigations for diagnostic purposes. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022))
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

explanation.summary: Pre-stimulant cardiovascular screening in adults consists of a focused personal and family cardiac history, examination, and baseline pulse and blood pressure. Further investigations are targeted to positive findings on this screen. This risk-based approach is endorsed by AADPA, RANZCP, and AMH, and mirrors overseas paediatric-adult concordance since routine ECG in low-risk populations shows a high false-positive rate.
key_points: Routine baseline ECG is not required in asymptomatic adults
Trigger ECG or cardiology on personal symptoms, examination signs, or premature sudden death under 50
Ongoing HR and BP monitoring at each dose titration is required
Paternal CAD at age 62 is not premature disease
explanation.pearls: Ongoing surveillance for stimulants means measuring HR and BP at each dose change and at least every 6 months; sustained resting HR above 100 or BP above 140/90 warrants dose review before continuing.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

options.rationale: Biomarkers and ambulatory monitoring have no role in pre-stimulant screening in asymptomatic adults. Neither AADPA nor AMH endorses this workup. (Source: AMH)

Routine ECG is not recommended for all adults; it does not improve outcomes and generates false-positive referrals. ECG is indicated only where the history, examination, or family screen identifies cardiac risk. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022))
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

options.rationale: Paternal coronary stenting at age 62 is not premature cardiac disease and does not trigger structural imaging or stress testing. The AADPA screen targets premature (<50 years) sudden cardiac death or inherited arrhythmia syndromes. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022))
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

options.rationale: Cardiology referral is reserved for patients with red-flag symptoms, abnormal examination (e.g. dynamic murmur), or family history of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or sudden cardiac death under 50. Routine referral introduces delay without benefit. (Source: RANZCP Professional Practice Guideline)

AADPA and RANZCP guidance recommends routine cardiovascular history, examination, pulse and blood pressure measurement before stimulants. Baseline ECG is reserved for those with personal cardiac symptoms, examination findings, or family history of premature sudden death or inherited arrhythmia. This patient has none of these features. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022))
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

explanation.summary: ADHD with a co-occurring substance use disorder is common and worsens outcomes for both. AADPA recommends integrated treatment rather than sequential abstinence-first approaches. Non-stimulants (atomoxetine, guanfacine) are preferred initially where active substance misuse exists because they lack misuse liability. Long-acting stimulants may be introduced once substance use is stable and monitored under Schedule 8 arrangements.
key_points: Do not withhold ADHD treatment pending abstinence
Atomoxetine is first-line where active substance misuse coexists
If a stimulant is used, choose long-acting to minimise diversion
Concurrent substance use treatment is essential
explanation.pearls: Lisdexamfetamine, a prodrug requiring gastrointestinal enzymatic conversion, has lower intranasal and IV misuse potential than dexamfetamine and is often preferred if a stimulant is later commenced in this population.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

options.rationale: Short-acting formulations have higher diversion and misuse risk in patients with active substance use disorders and are avoided as first-line in this context. Long-acting stimulants would be preferred if a stimulant is chosen. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022))
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

options.rationale: Immediate-release methylphenidate carries greater misuse and diversion risk than long-acting formulations. In active substance use, guidelines steer away from short-acting stimulants as the initial choice. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022))
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

options.rationale: In adult ADHD with active substance use disorder, non-stimulant treatment with atomoxetine is preferred first-line because it has no misuse or diversion potential and treats ADHD symptoms; guidelines recommend it while concurrent substance use is being addressed. Long-acting stimulants may be considered later once substance use stabilises. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022))
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

options.rationale: Bupropion is not TGA-approved for ADHD and has weaker evidence than atomoxetine. It also lowers the seizure threshold, which is relevant given heavy alcohol use and potential withdrawal. (Source: AMH)

Withholding treatment until abstinence is achieved is not supported by AADPA guidance. Treating ADHD in parallel with substance use intervention improves both outcomes; non-stimulants allow this without diversion risk. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022))
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD pharmacotherapy follows a sequential ladder: adequate trial of one stimulant class at target dose, switch to the alternative stimulant class if response is inadequate, then non-stimulants if both stimulant classes fail. Methylphenidate and amphetamine-class stimulants have distinct pharmacology and non-response to one does not predict non-response to the other.
key_points: Methylphenidate and dexamfetamine-class stimulants are the two first-line classes
Switch class before switching to non-stimulant if response is inadequate at target dose
Osmotic-release methylphenidate usual adult maximum is 54 mg per AMH
About one-third of methylphenidate non-responders respond to dexamfetamine class
explanation.pearls: Lisdexamfetamine is the prodrug form of dexamfetamine and requires gut peptidase activation, giving a smoother onset over roughly 60 to 90 minutes and a duration of 10 to 14 hours, useful for adults with long working days.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

options.rationale: Augmentation with alpha-2 agonists is not the recommended next step in adults with inadequate response to one stimulant class. AADPA advises switching to the alternative stimulant class first. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022))
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

options.rationale: CBT is a useful adjunct but does not address inadequate pharmacological response. When one stimulant class fails, the guideline directs a switch of stimulant class before adding non-pharmacological augmentation as the sole change. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022))
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

options.rationale: Approximately 30 percent of adults do not respond adequately to methylphenidate but do respond to a dexamfetamine-class stimulant. AADPA recommends switching to the alternative stimulant class when the first has been adequately trialled at target dose with poor response before considering non-stimulants. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022))
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

options.rationale: The AMH lists 54 mg as the usual adult maximum for osmotic-release methylphenidate; exceeding this is not first-line. Continuing to push dose without response is unlikely to yield benefit and increases side-effect burden. (Source: AMH)

Atomoxetine is generally reserved for after both stimulant classes have failed, or where stimulants are contraindicated or misused. It would be premature before trialling the alternative stimulant class. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022))
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of psychomotor dysregulation that occurs in mood disorders (most common), psychotic disorders, and general medical conditions. The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale identifies core features including mutism, negativism, waxy flexibility, posturing, echopraxia, and stereotypy. A lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IM or IV with reassessment within 10 to 15 minutes) is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Antipsychotics should be withheld in untreated catatonia because they can precipitate malignant catatonia or NMS.
key_points: DSM-5 catatonia requires 3 or more of 12 features
Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IM or IV is first-line diagnostic and therapeutic step
Withhold antipsychotics until catatonia resolves
Consider ECT if benzodiazepine response is inadequate or catatonia is malignant
explanation.pearls: A positive lorazepam challenge is a partial or complete reduction in Bush-Francis score at 10 to 15 minutes; responders proceed to scheduled lorazepam typically 2 mg every 4 to 8 hours titrated upward as needed.

options.rationale: Passive rehydration alone delays specific treatment. Lorazepam challenge is diagnostic and often produces rapid symptomatic improvement enabling oral intake to resume. (Source: RANZCP Professional Practice Guideline)

Antipsychotic use in untreated catatonia risks precipitating neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Antipsychotics should be withheld until catatonia is treated and resolved with benzodiazepine or ECT. (Source: eTG: Psychotropic)

ECT is second-line for catatonia after lorazepam trial, or first-line where catatonia is life-threatening (e.g. malignant catatonia with autonomic instability). Vital signs here are stable and a lorazepam challenge should be attempted first. (Source: RANZCP Professional Practice Guideline)

The clinical picture (mutism, negativism, waxy flexibility, posturing) meets Bush-Francis criteria for catatonia. A parenteral lorazepam challenge, 1 to 2 mg IM or IV with reassessment within 10 to 15 minutes, is both diagnostic and therapeutic and is the recommended first step. (Source: RANZCP Professional Practice Guideline)
NMS requires antipsychotic exposure, rigidity, hyperthermia, and elevated CK. She has none of these features and no antipsychotic exposure. Dantrolene is not appropriate here. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: NMS and malignant catatonia share features (mutism, hyperthermia, autonomic instability) and lie on a shared spectrum. NMS is distinguished by clear antipsychotic exposure, lead-pipe rigidity, and markedly elevated CK, whereas catatonia is characterised by waxy flexibility, negativism, and posturing without necessary antipsychotic exposure. NMS management is stopping the offending drug, aggressive supportive care, and directed pharmacotherapy (dantrolene, bromocriptine); ECT is reserved for refractory cases.
key_points: NMS: antipsychotic exposure + lead-pipe rigidity + hyperthermia + CK rise
Catatonia: waxy flexibility, negativism, posturing, mutism; often without CK rise
First-line NMS management: cease drug, cool, hydrate, dantrolene
Depot antipsychotics prolong recovery and are relevant to prognosis
explanation.pearls: Dantrolene 1 to 2.5 mg/kg IV can be repeated up to 10 mg/kg per 24 hours in severe NMS; bromocriptine 2.5 mg 6- to 8-hourly is the oral alternative, and depot antipsychotic depletion may take weeks to months, prolonging the course.

options.rationale: The clinical picture (recent antipsychotic exposure, hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, CK 6800, absence of waxy flexibility or posturing) is neuroleptic malignant syndrome, not catatonia. Lorazepam has an adjunctive role but is not the primary initial intervention. Cooling, aggressive IV hydration, and dantrolene or bromocriptine are the primary directed interventions. (Source: eTG: Psychotropic)

NMS management requires immediate cessation of the antipsychotic, aggressive IV rehydration to prevent acute kidney injury from myoglobinuria, active cooling for hyperthermia, and consideration of dantrolene or bromocriptine for severe rigidity or hyperthermia. This is the highest-yield first bundle. (Source: eTG: Psychotropic)

ECT is a recognised option for NMS that fails to respond to supportive care and pharmacotherapy, or for malignant catatonia, but is not the first intervention. Supportive care and dantrolene precede ECT in the treatment ladder. (Source: RANZCP Professional Practice Guideline)

Rechallenging with any antipsychotic during active NMS worsens the syndrome. Antipsychotics are withheld until at least two weeks after complete resolution, and rechallenge uses a low-potency agent from a different class. (Source: AMH)

Sepsis and CNS infection are important differentials and workup is reasonable, but the constellation of recent antipsychotic exposure, lead-pipe rigidity, CK 6800, and myoglobinuria makes NMS the leading diagnosis requiring directed intervention. Empirical antibiotics do not address the primary pathology. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Catatonia has a broad medical differential including general medical illness (metabolic derangement, infection, autoimmune encephalitis), neurological disease (frontal lobe pathology, non-convulsive status), and drug-induced states, as well as primary psychiatric causes. First-presentation catatonia in later life with no prior psychiatric history should prompt an accelerated organic workup including MRI brain, CSF cell count, protein, glucose, viral PCR, and autoantibody panels (NMDA-R, LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B).
key_points: New catatonia after age 40 without prior psychiatric history is organic until proven otherwise
MRI brain and LP with autoantibody panel are next-tier after unremarkable CT
Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis classically presents with psychiatric prodrome, catatonia, seizures, dysautonomia
Lorazepam challenge remains appropriate as a parallel therapeutic step
explanation.pearls: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is treatable with early first-line immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange) and second-line rituximab or cyclophosphamide; delay to treatment is the strongest predictor of poor neurological outcome.

options.rationale: Urinalysis is negative and there are no urinary symptoms beyond the new incontinence, which is part of the catatonic presentation. Empirical antibiotics are not indicated. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

New-onset catatonia in a 62-year-old with no prior psychiatric history, recent viral illness, and new urinary incontinence warrants exclusion of autoimmune encephalitis (particularly anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis) and infectious encephalitis. MRI brain and CSF studies including autoantibody panels and viral PCR are the next-tier investigation once CT is unremarkable. (Source: RANZCP Professional Practice Guideline)

Wilson disease presents in adolescence and early adulthood with movement disorders and Kayser-Fleischer rings. First presentation at 62 with catatonia is not consistent with Wilson disease. (Source: RANZCP Professional Practice Guideline)

Non-convulsive status is on the differential and EEG is important, but structural and infectious/autoimmune workup (MRI + LP) is higher-yield in this presentation. EEG typically accompanies rather than replaces this workup. (Source: RANZCP Professional Practice Guideline)
Serotonin syndrome features autonomic instability, clonus, hyperreflexia, and often serotonergic combinations. Isolated citalopram at stable dose over two years does not fit. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: ECT is second-line treatment for catatonia after adequate benzodiazepine trial has failed, and it is first-line for malignant catatonia with autonomic instability. Response rates for bilateral ECT in catatonia are 80 to 100 percent, often within the first several sessions. In Australia, ECT for an involuntary patient without capacity requires consent from a substitute decision-maker (or Mental Health Tribunal approval, depending on jurisdiction) and independent psychiatric assessment.
key_points: ECT is second-line for lorazepam-refractory catatonia
ECT is first-line for malignant catatonia with autonomic instability
Response is often rapid and complete with bilateral ECT
State Mental Health Act consent processes apply for involuntary patients
explanation.pearls: Bilateral (bitemporal or bifrontal) electrode placement is preferred over right unilateral for catatonia because response is faster and rates of complete response are higher, typically within 3 to 6 sessions.

options.rationale: ICU-level sedation is not a recognised catatonia treatment and would worsen nutritional status and mobility. It is reserved for airway or haemodynamic failure, neither of which is present. (Source: RANZCP Professional Practice Guideline)

Lorazepam can be titrated to 20 to 30 mg per day in catatonia, but at four days of adequate scheduled dosing with persistent Bush-Francis score of 18 and functional decline, further escalation delays effective treatment. ECT is next-line. (Source: eTG: Psychotropic)

Antipsychotics carry a risk of precipitating malignant catatonia or NMS in untreated catatonia and are typically deferred until catatonia has resolved. There is also no evidence of psychotic features here. (Source: eTG: Psychotropic)

NMDA antagonists (amantadine, memantine) have limited evidence and are third-line options considered when ECT is unavailable or contraindicated. They are not the standard next step. (Source: RANZCP Professional Practice Guideline)

Bilateral ECT is the second-line treatment for benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia and has response rates of 80 to 100 percent. Adequate benzodiazepine trial has been given without full response. Substitute consent under the Mental Health Act is in place. (Source: RANZCP Professional Practice Guideline)

explanation.summary: HEEADSSS is a semi-structured psychosocial interview (Home, Education/Employment, Eating/Exercise, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/depression, Safety) that only works when the adolescent is interviewed alone with confidentiality limits made explicit up front. Australian adolescent-friendly practice normalises time alone as a routine part of every adolescent visit so no single family feels targeted, and frames confidentiality as bounded by mandatory-report triggers (self-harm risk, harm to others, abuse). Building this in from age 12-13 makes the transition easier at 14-16.
key_points: Offer time alone routinely, not just when a concern is suspected
State confidentiality limits before sensitive questioning: self-harm, harm to others, abuse
HEEADSSS domains: Home, Education, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide, Safety
Non-verbal answers and written forms in a parent's presence do not confer privacy
Collateral from parents is valuable but is added AFTER the adolescent-alone interview, not before
explanation.pearls: The three standard confidentiality-limit categories in RACGP/RCH adolescent practice are: intent to harm self, intent to harm others, and disclosed abuse. Naming them explicitly before HEEADSSS starts is protective for both parties. In context: adolescent psychosocial assessment fails without alone-time and explicit confidentiality limits, regardless of how carefully questions are worded (Source: RACGP; RCH).

sources.label: RCH CPG: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

options.rationale: The RACGP and RCH adolescent frameworks recommend routinely offering time alone with the young person, normalising it as standard practice rather than singling this family out, and explicitly setting confidentiality limits (self-harm, harm to others, abuse) before sensitive questioning begins (Source: RACGP Adolescent Health; RCH CPG Engaging with and assessing the adolescent).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

options.rationale: Softening wording does not fix the core problem: a third party in the room will suppress disclosure about substances, sex, mood and abuse regardless of phrasing, and non-verbal answers cannot be safely interpreted (Source: RCH CPG; RACGP Adolescent Health).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

options.rationale: Deferring loses the opportunity today when a psychosocial driver is already suspected; time alone can be created now within the existing appointment and follow-up booked to consolidate (Source: RACGP Adolescent Health; RCH).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

options.rationale: Parents provide useful collateral but the HEEADSSS is a first-person tool: adolescent-reported behaviours (substance use, sexuality, self-harm) are frequently unknown to the parent and will not surface if the parent frames the narrative (Source: RCH CPG; RACGP).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

options.rationale: A written questionnaire in the parent's presence does not confer privacy (the parent can read it) and removes the clinician-led interview that identifies safety issues in real time (Source: RCH CPG; headspace clinical practice guidance).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

explanation.summary: CRAFFT is the validated adolescent substance-use screen; a score of 2 or more identifies young people at risk of a substance-use disorder and prompts brief intervention rather than confirmatory testing or immediate residential referral. Motivational interviewing (explore importance/confidence, roll with resistance, elicit change talk) delivered at first contact has evidence for reducing harm even when the young person is not seeking treatment. Escalation to specialist AoD service is guided by dependence severity, mental-health comorbidity and social safety.
key_points: CRAFFT items: Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Friends, Trouble
CRAFFT >=2 = brief intervention indicated; CRAFFT >=4 = higher probability of DSM-5 SUD
MI at first contact is more effective than deferring to a follow-up visit
Confidentiality is not overridden by substance use alone in a competent adolescent
Escalate if dependence, injecting, polysubstance with sedatives, or psychiatric comorbidity
explanation.pearls: The C item (getting in a Car with a driver, including self, who is under the influence) is the strongest single mortality predictor of the CRAFFT items and is worth a direct safety plan on its own. In context: adolescent AoD screening is designed for brief intervention at the point of care, not for confirmatory laboratory workup (Source: CRAFFT 2.1; RACGP).

options.rationale: Residential rehabilitation is reserved for severe dependence, failed outpatient care, or unsafe home environment. A CRAFFT of 2+ warrants brief intervention, not automatic residential referral (Source: RACGP; headspace clinical practice guidance).

Testing is not required for a self-disclosed adolescent substance history and delays the highest-yield intervention (brief MI at first contact). UDS may be adjunctive but is not the primary step (Source: headspace; RACGP).

Normalising a positive CRAFFT screen misses the intervention window; getting into a car with a substance-using driver (the C item) is itself a mortality-risk marker regardless of frequency (Source: CRAFFT 2.1 manual; RACGP).

Substance use in a competent adolescent without acute danger does not meet mandatory-report criteria; breaching confidentiality here would destroy the therapeutic alliance and is not required (Source: RACGP Adolescent health toolkit; NSW/Vic Children and Young Persons Act guidance).

A CRAFFT score of 2 or more identifies a young person at risk of a substance-use disorder and is an indication for brief intervention using motivational interviewing at the same visit. He is engaged and not intoxicated; the highest-yield step is a same-day MI conversation with structured follow-up (Source: RACGP; headspace; CRAFFT 2.1 manual).

explanation.summary: School refusal splits along an anxiety vs conduct axis. Anxiety-driven refusal presents with distress at separation, somatic complaints that remit on weekends and holidays, staying at or near home rather than seeking peers, and no antisocial behaviour. Conduct-driven truancy presents with peer-group activity away from home, no distress on non-attendance, and often lying or rule-breaking. Anxiety-driven refusal responds to graded exposure via a return-to-school plan plus CBT; certificates sanctioning absence and pharmacotherapy-first approaches worsen outcomes.
key_points: Anxiety-driven pattern: distress + somatic + weekends OK + stays home + no conduct
Conduct-driven pattern: no distress + peer-directed absence + antisocial features
Graded return-to-school plan is first-line, not extended absence
CBT with parent involvement is first-line therapy; SSRI is second-line
Extensive somatic workup without red flags reinforces the illness model
explanation.pearls: The weekend-remitting somatic pattern is the most useful clue against organic disease: true GI or headache pathology does not resolve every weekend. In context: adolescent school refusal is treated by re-exposing the child to school in graded steps, not by removing the exposure (Source: RCH; RANZCP FCAP).

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: Sanctioning prolonged absence reinforces avoidance, which is the maintaining mechanism of anxiety-driven school refusal; the evidence-based approach is graded return with parent and school partnership (Source: RCH CPG School refusal; RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: The pattern is anxiety-driven school refusal (child stays with parent, no conduct features, symptom-free on weekends), not neglect or truancy; child protection is inappropriate here (Source: RCH CPG School refusal).

The clinical pattern (separation-themed worry, weekends symptom-free, no conduct features, family-based safety-seeking) is classic anxiety-driven school refusal. Evidence-based management is coordinated graded return with parent-school partnership, CBT-based psychology (including exposure), and validating rather than investigating somatic complaints (Source: RCH CPG School refusal; RANZCP FCAP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: SSRI treatment is second-line for adolescent anxiety after adequate CBT (with or without parent involvement); first-line is CBT and school engagement, not upfront pharmacotherapy (Source: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: In the absence of red-flag features and with weekend-remitting somatic complaints, extensive GI workup is low-yield and delays the anxiety-focused intervention (Source: RCH CPG Chronic abdominal pain; RCH School refusal).

explanation.summary: Adolescent cyberbullying with passive suicidal ideation is managed at the level of the ideation, not the substrate: passive ideation without plan or means is safety-planned in the community with adult supports and early follow-up. Australia's Online Safety Act 2021 empowers the eSafety Commissioner to require rapid removal of cyberbullying material targeting a minor and image-based abuse; formal reporting is both a therapeutic and a protective act. SSRI treatment is not first-line at this presentation stage and requires established depression plus stepped-care rationale.
key_points: Passive ideation, no plan, no means, no history = community safety plan, not admission
eSafety Commissioner can compel takedown of cyberbullying targeting a minor
Involve a trusted adult with the young person's consent wherever possible
SSRI early treatment carries black-box suicidality monitoring requirements
Escalate to ED only if plan, means, prior serious self-harm, or acute intoxication
explanation.pearls: The Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention has 6 steps: warning signs, internal coping, social distractions, adults who can help, professionals + crisis lines, means restriction. In context: adolescent suicide risk stratification determines the level of care, and cyberbullying requires a parallel regulatory response via eSafety (Source: headspace; eSafety).

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: Passive ideation without plan/means/self-harm history is managed with a same-visit collaborative safety plan (Stanley-Brown-style), adult support activation and early follow-up, not inpatient admission. Cyberbullying image-based abuse of a minor is reportable to the eSafety Commissioner, which can compel takedown under the Online Safety Act 2021 (Source: headspace CPG; eSafety Commissioner; RANZCP FCAP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: Passive ideation without plan, means or prior self-harm does not meet involuntary criteria; unnecessary admission fragments school and family supports and disrupts the therapeutic frame (Source: headspace CPG; state Mental Health Act guidance).

She may develop depression but a formal MDD diagnosis and staged treatment plan cannot be justified today; SSRIs also carry a black-box early-treatment suicidality warning that mandates baseline safety planning and monitoring regardless (Source: AMH; TG Psychotropic; headspace CPG).

Passive ignoring alone does not address image-based abuse, and no safety plan is documented; a passive ideation disclosure requires a same-visit response (Source: headspace CPG; eSafety Commissioner).

Peer-to-parent negotiation is not required before eSafety reporting, can escalate the situation, and delays image takedown; the Online Safety Act provides a rapid formal pathway (Source: eSafety Commissioner).

explanation.summary: Conduct disorder is defined by a persistent pattern (>=3 criteria over 12 months) across four groups: aggression to people/animals, destruction of property, deceit or theft, and serious violations of rules. ODD is a narrower defiance/argumentativeness/vindictiveness pattern without the aggression, destruction and theft. The DSM-5 limited prosocial emotions specifier (lack of remorse, callousness, shallow affect, unconcern about performance) marks a group with higher progression to adult antisocial personality disorder. Evidence-based treatments for conduct disorder are behavioural family interventions and multi-systemic therapy; pharmacotherapy is limited to comorbid ADHD or targeted aggression.
key_points: CD requires >=3 criteria over 12 months across 4 groups
ODD = defiance without aggression/destruction/theft
Limited prosocial emotions specifier predicts adult ASPD risk
Parent management training and MST are first-line
ASPD is not diagnosed before age 18
explanation.pearls: Cruelty to animals is one of the DSM-5 conduct-disorder Group 1 criteria (aggression to people or animals) and is a specific antisocial-trajectory marker rather than an ADHD or ODD sign. In context: adolescent externalising presentations must be sub-typed accurately because the treatment (behavioural family therapy vs medication) and long-term prognosis differ substantially (Source: DSM-5-TR; NICE NG158).

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
NICE NG158 Antisocial behaviour and conduct disorders

options.rationale: ODD is limited to defiance, argumentativeness and vindictiveness towards authority; the presence of aggression to people/animals, destruction of property, deceit/theft and serious rule violation over 12 months meets DSM-5 conduct disorder, not ODD (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP FCAP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: There are no positive symptoms, no attenuated psychotic symptoms, no functional decline of the ultra-high-risk pattern, and mental state is otherwise normal; conduct behaviours are not negative symptoms (Source: EPPIC EIS clinical practice guidance).
There are no core inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms described and no learning-disorder features; the behaviour cluster is rule-violating not attention-based (Source: DSM-5-TR).

The 4 DSM-5 conduct-disorder criteria groups (aggression to people/animals, destruction of property, deceit/theft, serious rule violation) are met over 12 months. Absence of remorse meets the limited prosocial emotions specifier, which predicts higher risk of adult antisocial personality disorder. Evidence-based treatments are parent management training and multi-systemic therapy, not medication (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP FCAP; NICE NG158).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
NICE NG158 Antisocial behaviour and conduct disorders

options.rationale: Antisocial personality disorder cannot be diagnosed before age 18 by DSM-5-TR criteria (though a history of conduct disorder before 15 is required); paediatric labelling of a personality disorder is inappropriate (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: ARFID sits between picky eating (no functional impairment) and anorexia nervosa (fear of weight gain, body-image distortion). DSM-5 requires that restriction produces one of: significant weight loss/failure to grow, nutritional deficiency, dependence on enteral feeds/oral supplements, or marked psychosocial interference - WITHOUT the AN cognitive features. The three ARFID subtypes are sensory sensitivity, low interest in eating, and post-traumatic aversive presentation. AU management is multidisciplinary (paediatrician, dietitian, psychology) with age-appropriate feeding therapy and comorbidity (ASD, anxiety) screening.
key_points: ARFID = restriction with impairment WITHOUT AN cognitive features
Any one of weight loss/deficiency/supplement dependence/psychosocial interference qualifies
3 subtypes: sensory, low interest, post-traumatic aversive
Co-occurs with ASD, ADHD and anxiety disorders
AU pathway: paediatrician + dietitian + eating-disorder psychology
explanation.pearls: In ARFID a full paediatric eating-disorder assessment includes ferritin, vitamin D, B12, folate, zinc and a resting ECG (long QT risk with severe restriction and refeeding). In context: adolescent restrictive-eating presentations must be sub-typed accurately because ARFID and AN diverge in aetiology, therapy content and family-therapy approach (Source: ANZAED; RCH).

options.rationale: Anorexia nervosa and its atypical form require fear of weight gain or body-image disturbance; a texture-driven restriction without weight concern is ARFID, not AN (Source: DSM-5-TR; ANZAED).

Picky eating in typical variants does not cross the failure-to-grow or nutritional-deficiency threshold; falling from 25th to 3rd centile with iron deficiency crosses into diagnosable ARFID (Source: DSM-5-TR; RCH).

ARFID is diagnosed when restriction (sensory, low interest, or aversive experience) produces one or more of: significant weight loss/failure to gain, nutritional deficiency, dependence on supplements/enteral feeds, or psychosocial impairment - WITHOUT fear of weight gain or body-image distortion. This presentation meets both weight-trajectory and deficiency criteria and requires MDT care (Source: DSM-5-TR; ANZAED; RCH).

Sensory food selectivity is common in ASD and can co-occur with ARFID, but a growth-failure and nutritional-deficiency pattern meets the ARFID threshold in its own right and needs eating-disorder-specific input alongside any ASD assessment (Source: DSM-5-TR; ANZAED).

Coeliac serology is reasonable to exclude organic causes but does not explain the texture-driven 6-food repertoire since age 4; ARFID is a positive diagnosis, not a diagnosis of exclusion (Source: DSM-5-TR; GESA).

explanation.summary: First-line pharmacotherapy for adolescent moderate-to-severe major depression in Australia is fluoxetine, the only SSRI with a TGA paediatric depression indication and the strongest RCT evidence (TADS: combined fluoxetine + CBT superior to either alone). Sertraline and escitalopram are reasonable second-line SSRIs. Venlafaxine is avoided (worse risk profile). Every SSRI initiation in a person under 25 carries a black-box early-treatment emergent-suicidality warning: weekly review for 4 weeks then 2-weekly, with a safety plan and means restriction in place. Bipolar screen must be negative before SSRI initiation.
key_points: Fluoxetine is first-line adolescent SSRI in Australia (TGA-approved)
Combined SSRI + CBT beats either alone for moderate-severe MDD
Screen for bipolar before starting any antidepressant
Weekly monitoring x 4 weeks, then 2-weekly, for emergent suicidality
Safety plan + means restriction documented before script
explanation.pearls: Fluoxetine's long half-life (72 h for norfluoxetine metabolite) makes it more forgiving of missed doses and less prone to discontinuation syndrome, which suits adolescent adherence patterns. In context: adolescent depression pharmacotherapy is a stepped decision after adequate psychological therapy trial, not a first-visit reflex (Source: AMH; TG Psychotropic; RANZCP FCAP).

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: Sertraline is a reasonable SSRI in some contexts, but fluoxetine is the only SSRI with a TGA-approved paediatric depression indication in Australia and the strongest RCT evidence base for adolescent MDD (Source: AMH; TG Psychotropic; RANZCP FCAP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: Mirtazapine lacks adolescent-specific efficacy evidence for major depression and is not first-line; using its sedative side-effect profile as the prescribing rationale is a common error (Source: AMH; TG Psychotropic).

Venlafaxine has a poor benefit-risk balance in adolescent depression (increased suicidality signal without efficacy advantage over SSRIs) and is not first-line for this age group (Source: AMH; TG Psychotropic).

Fluoxetine is the SSRI with a TGA-approved paediatric depression indication and the largest evidence base (TADS trial). It is combined with continued CBT for best outcomes and requires close early-treatment monitoring (weekly for 4 weeks then 2-weekly) for the well-documented paediatric emergent suicidality signal (Source: AMH; TG Psychotropic; RANZCP FCAP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: CBT alone has already failed at adequate dose; combined SSRI + CBT is more effective than either alone for moderate-severe adolescent MDD. The black-box warning mandates monitoring, not avoidance (Source: RANZCP FCAP; TG Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

explanation.summary: NSSI (non-suicidal self-injury) is distinguished from a suicide attempt by function (emotion regulation, communication, self-punishment) and by absence of intent to die. Australian and international guidelines (RANZCP FCAP, NICE NG225) treat NSSI in adolescents with emerging BPD features using adolescent-modified DBT (Miller, Rathus and Linehan), which combines individual therapy, multi-family skills groups, phone coaching and therapist consultation over 16-24 weeks. NSSI nonetheless raises prospective suicide risk and demands a safety plan and family support. Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive for specific comorbidities.
key_points: NSSI: no intent to die, function is affect-regulation/communication/self-punishment
NSSI still raises prospective suicide risk despite different intent
DBT-A is the highest-evidence therapy for adolescent NSSI + emerging BPD
Emerging BPD can and should be formulated in adolescence (Chanen et al)
Meds are adjunctive: SSRI for depression, no antipsychotic first-line for NSSI
explanation.pearls: Adolescent-modified DBT (DBT-A) includes a multi-family skills group and a fifth 'walking the middle path' skills module addressing dialectical family conflicts, which is not present in adult DBT. In context: adolescent self-harm must be sub-typed by function and intent because that determines whether the pathway is DBT-A, MDD treatment, or emergency risk management (Source: RANZCP FCAP; NICE NG225).

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
NICE NG225 Self-harm assessment and management

options.rationale: This is non-suicidal self-injury (emotion-regulation function, no intent to die, superficial pattern) not a suicide attempt; involuntary admission mislabels the behaviour and iatrogenically reinforces it in some presentations (Source: RANZCP FCAP; headspace CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: NSSI without suicidal intent nonetheless increases prospective risk of future suicide attempt and warrants targeted therapy; wound-care alone is inadequate (Source: RANZCP FCAP; NICE NG225 Self-harm).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
NICE NG225 Self-harm assessment and management

options.rationale: The behaviour is NSSI (emotion-regulation function, no intent to die, superficial repetitive pattern) in a young person with emerging borderline features. DBT-A (16-24 weeks, individual + skills + family + phone coaching) has the strongest RCT evidence for reducing NSSI and suicidal behaviour in adolescents with these features (Source: RANZCP FCAP; NICE NG225; Miller DBT-A manual).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
NICE NG225 Self-harm assessment and management

options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not first-line for NSSI or adolescent emerging BPD; psychological therapy (DBT-A) is; medication is adjunctive for specific comorbidities like depression or PTSD (Source: RANZCP FCAP; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: Emerging BPD features in adolescents can and should be formulated and treated in adolescence; deferring evidence-based DBT-A to adulthood loses the developmental treatment window (Source: RANZCP FCAP; Chanen Chartsheet).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

explanation.summary: The Gillick or mature minor doctrine (established in the UK, adopted in Australia by the High Court in Marion's Case, 1992) recognises that a young person under 18 with sufficient understanding and intelligence can consent to their own medical treatment. Australian jurisdictions do not impose a blanket age below which parental consent is required for a competent minor's own care. The clinician's duties are: assess and document capacity for the specific decision, explain the fixed confidentiality limits (harm to self, harm to others, disclosure of abuse), actively encourage parental involvement without compelling it, and reassess at every visit. Special protections apply to certain interventions such as gender-affirming care and sterilisation.
key_points: Australia recognises Gillick / mature minor competence via Marion's Case (HCA 1992)
Capacity is decision-specific, not global; reassess each visit
Confidentiality limits: harm to self, harm to others, abuse disclosure
Encourage parental involvement; do not compel unless a limit is met
Coercing disclosure through prescription limits is a breach, not a workaround
explanation.pearls: The four documentation elements of a mature-minor consent are: understanding of the condition, understanding of the proposed treatment (benefits and risks), understanding of alternatives (including no treatment), and ability to weigh and communicate a decision. In context: adolescent mental-health prescribing is legally and ethically permissible in a capable minor, and clinicians who default to parental consent overstep in the other direction (Source: RACGP; AHPRA).

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: NSW does not impose a blanket age or parental-consent rule; a mature minor with capacity can consent to her own treatment under the Gillick / mature minor doctrine adopted in Australia (Marion's Case, HCA 1992) (Source: RACGP Adolescent Health; AHPRA/Medical Board of Australia).

Gillick / mature minor competence (adopted in Australia via Marion's Case) permits a capable adolescent to consent to her own treatment. The clinician's task is to (a) formally assess and document capacity, (b) explain the fixed confidentiality limits (self-harm, harm to others, abuse), (c) actively encourage - but not compel - parental involvement, and (d) reassess at each visit (Source: RACGP; RANZCP FCAP; NSW Health youth consent guidance).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: A capable minor's consent is not overridden by the existence of a black-box warning; unilateral parental disclosure without a mandatory-report trigger breaches confidentiality and the therapeutic frame (Source: RACGP; AHPRA).
There is no such NSW prescribing restriction; GPs can and do initiate fluoxetine in capable adolescents after inadequate psychological therapy trial (Source: AMH; TG Psychotropic; RACGP).
Using medication supply as coercion to force parental disclosure breaches consent principles and is not the correct mechanism to encourage parental involvement (Source: AHPRA; RACGP).

explanation.summary: MARSIPAN-AU (Australian adaptation of the UK MARSIPAN framework) stratifies anorexia nervosa medical risk by anthropometric, cardiovascular, biochemical and behavioural criteria. Very-high-risk features (BMI <13 or <70% median for age, HR <40, systolic BP postural drop >=20 mmHg, K <3.0, PO4 <0.5, QTc >450 ms, temperature <35.5) mandate medical admission for cardiac monitoring and cautious refeeding. Refeeding syndrome (further drops in phosphate, potassium, magnesium, plus thiamine deficiency causing Wernicke's) is the main early risk; therefore start low-calorie (~20 kcal/kg/day) with pre-emptive electrolyte + thiamine, monitor daily, and titrate up. Family-based treatment (FBT) is the outpatient framework after medical stabilisation.
key_points: MARSIPAN-AU very-high-risk = medical admission, not outpatient or psych ward
HR <40, postural systolic drop >=20 mmHg, K <3.0, QTc >450 all trigger admission
Refeeding syndrome: PO4/K/Mg drop, thiamine deficiency, cardiac failure
Start ~20 kcal/kg/day; replace electrolytes and thiamine BEFORE caloric escalation
FBT (Maudsley) is the first-line outpatient therapy for adolescent AN post-stabilisation
explanation.pearls: The QTc >450 ms threshold in MARSIPAN-AU is more conservative than the general cardiology 470/480 cut-off because malnutrition adds electrolyte and cardiac muscle vulnerability. In context: adolescent AN medical management is governed by MARSIPAN-AU, not by BMI alone, and refeeding is always cautious and monitored (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU 2020; RCH).

options.rationale: MARSIPAN-AU very-high-risk criteria are met (bradycardia <40, postural hypotension with 20 mmHg systolic drop, hypokalaemia, QTc >450 ms, hypothermia); outpatient management would be unsafe (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU 2020).

MARSIPAN-AU very-high-risk features (bradycardia <40, postural drop >=20 systolic, K <3.0, QTc >450, hypothermia, phosphate low) mandate medical admission for cardiac monitoring and cautious refeeding. First 48-72 h prioritises electrolyte replacement (K, PO4, Mg) and thiamine BEFORE full caloric load to prevent refeeding syndrome; specialist ED input from day 1 (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU 2020; RCH CPG Eating disorders).

She has multiple MARSIPAN-AU very-high-risk medical features; a psychiatric unit does not have cardiac monitoring or the refeeding syndrome resources. Medical stabilisation precedes psychiatric admission (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU 2020).

Rapid high-caloric refeeding in this biochemistry precipitates refeeding syndrome (further phosphate drop, cardiac failure, Wernicke). MARSIPAN-AU starts cautiously (~20 kcal/kg/day) with pre-emptive electrolyte and thiamine replacement (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU 2020).

Aggressive fluid bolus in refeeding-vulnerable anorexia risks precipitating cardiac failure and worsening electrolyte disturbance; the disposition is already determined by MARSIPAN-AU criteria (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU 2020).

explanation.summary: In adolescent bulimia nervosa the Australian first-line psychological therapy is FBT-BN (family-based treatment for bulimia): three phases in which parents initially take charge of eating and interrupt binge-purge cycles, then progressively hand control back to the adolescent. CBT-E is first-line in adults and second-line in adolescents (when family engagement is unavailable or FBT-BN has failed). Fluoxetine 60 mg daily is the evidence-based SSRI dose for bulimia but is adjunctive in adolescents. Admission is reserved for medical instability or failed intensive outpatient care.
key_points: Adolescent BN first-line psychological therapy = FBT-BN, not CBT-E
CBT-E is first-line for adults and second-line for adolescents
Fluoxetine 60 mg daily is the anti-bulimic dose (adjunctive in adolescents)
Admission is for medical instability or failed intensive outpatient care
Contraindications to FBT: severe trauma, parental psychopathology preventing engagement
explanation.pearls: The FBT phase 1 externalising language (naming the eating disorder as a separate agent) helps parents take charge without turning the adolescent into the problem, mirroring the FBT-AN Maudsley approach. In context: adolescent bulimia therapy choice is family-first when family is available, not individual-first as it is for adults (Source: ANZAED CPG 2020).

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: In adolescents with bulimia nervosa where family is engaged and there is no contraindication (severe trauma, parental psychopathology preventing engagement), FBT-BN is first-line in Australian guidance and has RCT evidence for higher abstinence rates at end of treatment than individual CBT-BN in the adolescent age band (Source: ANZAED CPG Eating disorders 2020; RANZCP FCAP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: CBT-E is first-line in adults and second-line in adolescents with bulimia if FBT-BN is not indicated or has failed. When family engagement is available, FBT-BN comes first (Source: ANZAED CPG 2020).

IPT is a slower-acting alternative to CBT-E in adults with bulimia and is not first-line for adolescents; direct behavioural focus on eating and purge cycles is essential in adolescent presentations (Source: ANZAED CPG 2020).

Fluoxetine 60 mg daily has evidence for adult bulimia but is adjunctive not primary in adolescents; psychological therapy (FBT-BN or CBT-E) is first-line, with SSRI added if inadequate response (Source: ANZAED CPG 2020; AMH).
Admission for bulimia is reserved for medical instability, failed intensive outpatient care, or acute safety issues; this adolescent is medically stable and treatment-naive (Source: ANZAED CPG 2020).

explanation.summary: Australian first-line pharmacotherapy for adolescent ADHD is a stimulant (methylphenidate or dexamfetamine); non-stimulants (atomoxetine, guanfacine) are second-line. Formulation choice is driven by required duration of cover: IR (~3-4 hours), MR/LA (~8 hours), osmotic-release (~10-12 hours). Class switch (dexamfetamine <-> methylphenidate) is standard when one class fails to control symptoms adequately or produces intolerable rebound. Cardiac screening is by personal and family history plus resting ECG; routine echo or Holter is not indicated when these are negative. Treated ADHD reduces motor-vehicle crash risk relative to untreated ADHD.
key_points: Stimulants are first-line; atomoxetine/guanfacine are second-line
Formulation choice matches required duration of cover
Class-switch between methylphenidate and dexamfetamine is standard next step
Cardiac screening: history + resting ECG (no routine echo/Holter)
Treated ADHD REDUCES crash risk versus untreated ADHD (Austroads)
explanation.pearls: In Australia stimulants are Schedule 8 in most states and require an authority-to-prescribe from a paediatrician, child psychiatrist or (in some states) approved GP with training. In context: adolescent ADHD stimulant selection is a formulation-and-class decision guided by duration of cover, rebound pattern and comorbidity, not a stimulant-versus-nothing decision (Source: TG Psychotropic; AMH; Austroads).

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: Atomoxetine is a reasonable non-stimulant option but is second-line to stimulants in adolescent ADHD without contraindication; stimulants IMPROVE (not worsen) driving performance in treated ADHD by reducing inattention-related risk (Source: TG Psychotropic; AMH; RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: Adding a late-afternoon IR dose worsens rebound at the new dose-off time and can impair sleep; a switch to a modified-release formulation is a more coherent solution (Source: TG Psychotropic; AMH).

Switching to a modified-release methylphenidate formulation (osmotic-release, ~10-12 hours) directly addresses both the rebound and the late-day cover issue for a young driver in his final school year with evening work. Modified-release stimulants improve driving performance in treated ADHD compared with untreated ADHD; class-switch from dexamfetamine to methylphenidate is standard when dexamfetamine trial is unsatisfactory (Source: TG Psychotropic; AMH; RANZCP FCAP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: There is no evidence base or Australian guideline recommending stimulant withholding on the basis of a learner permit; treated ADHD lowers crash risk relative to untreated ADHD (Source: RANZCP FCAP; Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.rationale: Routine echo/Holter are not required before adolescent stimulant initiation when personal and family cardiac history are negative and resting ECG is normal; screening is by history and ECG only (Source: TG Psychotropic; AMH; RANZCP FCAP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

explanation.summary: Autism spectrum disorder in adolescent girls is chronically under-recognised because the female phenotype includes social masking, camouflage of stereotypies, one or two close friendships (rather than social isolation), and intense but socially normative interests (horses, animals, celebrities, languages). Presentations often emerge as anxiety, depression, eating disorders or burnout when masking becomes unsustainable in secondary school. The Autism CRC national guideline (endorsed by NDIS since 2018) recommends multidisciplinary assessment using female-sensitive instruments (ADOS-2 module 4 or MIGDAS-2 with clinical formulation). Reframing anxiety as ASD comorbidity changes therapy targets (accommodations, sensory environment, anti-masking, autistic-affirming approaches) rather than repeating standard CBT.
key_points: Girls with ASD often mask, so ASD is missed until secondary school
Female phenotype: 1-2 close friendships, socially normative interests, masking exhaustion
Autism CRC national guideline is the NDIS-endorsed AU standard
Anxiety, depression, eating disorders, burnout are common presenting comorbidities
Standard CBT often fails in autistic girls; autism-adapted CBT or accommodations work better
explanation.pearls: Selective mutism at school but normal speech at home in an adolescent girl is a strong indicator to broaden to an ASD-plus-anxiety formulation rather than treat as isolated selective mutism. In context: adolescent presentations that fail two rounds of standard CBT deserve a neurodevelopmental reformulation, not a third round (Source: Autism CRC national guideline; RANZCP FCAP).

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
Autism CRC national guideline for assessment and diagnosis of autism 2018

options.rationale: The picture (lifelong scripted phrases, narrow interests, sensory sensitivities, masking-driven exhaustion, home-vs-school speech difference) fits underlying ASD masked in a girl; treating anxiety without formulating ASD misses the driver and prior CBT has already failed (Source: RANZCP FCAP; Autism CRC national guideline).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
Autism CRC national guideline for assessment and diagnosis of autism 2018

options.rationale: Autistic burnout is a recognised concept but the correct pathway is assessment-and-formulation-first, not attendance-reduction without diagnosis; a formal ASD assessment enables appropriate accommodations (Source: Autism CRC national guideline).
source_refs: Autism CRC national guideline for assessment and diagnosis of autism 2018

options.rationale: Selective mutism can be a stand-alone diagnosis in younger children but here it is one facet of a broader ASD-plus-anxiety picture in an adolescent; isolated speech-pathology intervention will not address the underlying formulation (Source: DSM-5-TR; Autism CRC national guideline).
source_refs: Autism CRC national guideline for assessment and diagnosis of autism 2018

options.rationale: Social anxiety does not explain lifelong scripted phrases, narrow intense interests or sensory sensitivities; and generic social skills groups may increase distress in an autistic girl trying to mask (Source: Autism CRC national guideline).
source_refs: Autism CRC national guideline for assessment and diagnosis of autism 2018

options.rationale: The clinical pattern (lifelong scripted phrases, narrow intense interests, sensory sensitivities, masking-driven exhaustion, home-vs-school speech asymmetry) fits ASD masked in a girl. The Autism CRC national guideline (endorsed by NDIS) recommends multidisciplinary assessment with female-sensitive instruments; formulating anxiety as an ASD comorbidity changes therapy targeting to accommodations and anti-masking work (Source: RANZCP FCAP; Autism CRC national guideline).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
Autism CRC national guideline for assessment and diagnosis of autism 2018

explanation.summary: In Australian youth suicide the male-to-female ratio for completion is approximately 3:1, rural rates exceed urban rates, and firearms account for a disproportionately high case-fatality ratio in rural presentations. Means restriction has the strongest single-intervention evidence for reducing suicide mortality. When a plan is specific and the means are in the home, restricting access to that specific method saves lives even when substitution to other methods is possible, because most attempts are ambivalent, impulsive at the moment of action, and the transition between one method and another is not automatic. Structured risk tools (C-SSRS, SAD PERSONS) have poor predictive validity for individual suicide; no-suicide contracts are not evidence-based; collaborative safety planning has replaced both.
key_points: Means restriction is the highest-evidence suicide-prevention intervention
Firearms: case-fatality ~85% vs <5% for many other methods
AU rural youth suicide rate > urban; male:female completion ~3:1
Structured risk tools have poor PPV; do not replace clinical formulation
No-suicide contracts are superseded by collaborative safety planning
explanation.pearls: Under Queensland weapons legislation a family member or police can remove a firearm from a licensed owner's home when there is a mental health concern, without requiring the licence-holder's consent for temporary safe storage. In context: adolescent suicide-risk management is means-first, medication-second, therapy-third within the first 24 hours (Source: Black Dog Institute; QPS weapons licensing).

options.rationale: Means restriction is the single highest-evidence-per-hour intervention in suicide prevention.
