options.rationale: Antipsychotics can precipitate malignant catatonia and NMS; they are avoided in acute catatonia until it has resolved and are not first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
Persistent catatonia with food and fluid refusal is life-threatening; discharge is not safe. (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Memorandum: Use of Electroconvulsive Therapy

options.rationale: A positive response to a lorazepam challenge (any partial improvement) confirms catatonia and justifies scheduled benzodiazepine therapy with escalating doses. Australian and international practice (RANZCP, Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic) recommends scheduled lorazepam 6-24 mg/day depending on response, with ECT if catatonia does not resolve within 48-72 hours or if malignant features develop. Supportive care includes hydration, DVT prophylaxis, and skin care (Source: RANZCP ECT memorandum; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Memorandum: Use of Electroconvulsive Therapy

options.rationale: She has no dopamine antagonist exposure, no lead-pipe rigidity, and no hyperthermia; the CK is only mildly elevated from prolonged posturing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness Medicine

options.rationale: A one-off larger dose without scheduled maintenance risks relapse of the catatonia; scheduled dosing (with monitoring for over-sedation) is the standard, not a single larger dose. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Memorandum: Use of Electroconvulsive Therapy

explanation.summary: Baby blues are transient (days 3-14), self-limiting, and managed with psychoeducation and support; repeat EPDS in 2 weeks screens for evolving postnatal depression.
key_points: Baby blues: 50-80% incidence, peak day 3-5, resolve by day 10-14
Postnatal depression: symptoms beyond 2 weeks, EPDS at least 13 on repeat testing
Postpartum psychosis: typically abrupt onset, days 3-14, urgent admission
Always screen for suicidal and infanticidal thoughts and psychotic features
Involve partner and family in support and monitoring
explanation.pearls: Distinguishing baby blues from early postnatal depression is a temporal call as much as a symptom call; the 2-week repeat is a low-cost, high-value intervention. In context: overtreating baby blues risks unnecessary medication exposure, while undertreating early postnatal depression delays effective care (Source: COPE).

sources.label: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.rationale: Postpartum thyroiditis typically presents from 3-6 months, TSH is within normal limits, and the clinical picture fits baby blues; further testing is not indicated (Source: RCPA thyroid function testing guide).
Pharmacotherapy is not indicated for baby blues and would expose an infant to an unnecessary medication. (Source: COPE).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.rationale: There are no risk features (suicidal, infanticidal, psychotic, functional collapse) to justify urgent specialist review; primary care management is appropriate. Would rarely be correct (Source: COPE).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.rationale: Breastfeeding cessation is neither indicated nor supported by evidence for baby blues; sleep support strategies with the partner are preferred. (Source: COPE).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.rationale: Baby blues affect around 50-80% of women, peak on days 3-5, and resolve by day 10-14; they do not require pharmacotherapy. EPDS of 9 (below 10) with transient symptoms fits the pattern. COPE advises psychoeducation, family support, and repeat EPDS in 2 weeks to catch evolving postnatal depression (Source: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

explanation.summary: Neonatal adaptation syndrome after third-trimester SSRI exposure is common, self-limited, and managed with observation and feeding support; maternal SSRI is continued, breastfeeding encouraged, and additional interventions reserved for evolving illness.
key_points: Adaptation features: tremor, jitteriness, hypertonia, mild tachypnoea, feeding difficulty
Onset within hours to days; resolves in about 2-14 days
Sertraline has the lowest relative infant dose in breast milk; continue in most cases
PPHN is rare (absolute risk ~3 per 1000 exposed), presents with sustained severe hypoxaemia
Screen the mother for postnatal depression and monitor infant weight and hydration
explanation.pearls: The lay narrative of "SSRI withdrawal" is misleading because the syndrome is thought to reflect neonatal serotonergic effects rather than a physical dependence. In context: continuity of maternal treatment protects both the mother-infant dyad and long-term infant outcomes (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).

sources.label: MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.rationale: SSRI adaptation is self-limited and does not require pharmacotherapy; phenobarbital is used for opioid neonatal abstinence, not SSRI adaptation. (Source: RCH Neonatal Handbook).

The temporal pattern and typical features (tremor, jitteriness, mild tachypnoea within hours of birth) with no maternal risk factors point to SSRI adaptation, not sepsis; septic workup is not routinely required unless the clinical picture evolves. Would rarely be correct (Source: RCH Neonatal Handbook).

Maternal SSRI cessation in the immediate postpartum period doubles the risk of relapse of depression and does not shorten neonatal adaptation; formula feeding is not indicated for sertraline exposure. (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet

options.rationale: Neonatal adaptation syndrome after third-trimester SSRI exposure is common (up to 30% of exposed infants), typically self-limited over 2-14 days, and managed with observation, feeding support, and glucose monitoring. Maternal sertraline is continued because sertraline has the lowest relative infant dose in breast milk, breastfeeding provides continuity, and abrupt maternal cessation risks postpartum relapse; formula is not indicated (Source: MotherToBaby Australia; RANZCP; RCH Neonatal e-Handbook).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.rationale: PPHN is a rare complication (absolute risk about 3 per 1000 exposed) and typically presents with sustained severe hypoxaemia (SpO2 below about 90% or a pre-post ductal difference), not mild self-limited tachypnoea with normal saturations. Would rarely be correct with SpO2 96% (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet

explanation.summary: Continue an effective SSRI (typically sertraline) through pregnancy and the immediate postpartum period; tapering before delivery does not reliably prevent neonatal adaptation syndrome and increases maternal relapse risk.
key_points: Neonatal adaptation syndrome: common (up to 30%), mild, self-limited (2-14 days)
Late-pregnancy taper: no reliable prevention benefit and higher maternal relapse
Postpartum is the highest-risk period for recurrence of mood disorders
Sertraline preferred in breastfeeding (lowest relative infant dose)
Plan neonatal observation, breastfeeding support, and postpartum mental health follow-up
explanation.pearls: In perinatal psychiatry the counter-factual (untreated maternal illness) is the appropriate comparator, not a hypothetical unexposed pregnancy. In context: continuity of effective treatment usually serves both mother and infant better than well-intentioned tapering (Source: COPE).

sources.label: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)
MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health
RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 23: Timing of elective caesarean

options.rationale: Caesarean is not indicated for SSRI use and adds surgical and obstetric risks with no benefit; the delivery mode is chosen on obstetric grounds. (Source: RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 23: Timing of elective caesarean

options.rationale: Late-pregnancy taper does not reliably prevent neonatal adaptation and raises the risk of maternal relapse. Would rarely be correct (Source: COPE).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.rationale: Fluoxetine has the highest relative infant dose of the SSRIs in breast milk and its long half-life prolongs neonatal exposure; sertraline is preferred. (Source: MotherToBaby Australia; AMH).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet

options.rationale: Reducing to a subtherapeutic dose increases the risk of maternal relapse at the highest risk period without meaningful benefit for the neonate; effective dose is maintained. Would rarely be correct (Source: MotherToBaby Australia).
source_refs: MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet

options.rationale: Late-pregnancy SSRI cessation does not reliably prevent neonatal adaptation syndrome (which is usually mild and self-limited) but substantially increases the risk of maternal relapse in the puerperium (roughly doubling relapse risk), which is worse for the mother-infant dyad than adaptation symptoms. COPE and MotherToBaby Australia advise continuation of a well-tolerated SSRI throughout pregnancy in a woman with recurrent depression, with neonatal observation for adaptation (Source: COPE; MotherToBaby Australia; RANZCP).
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)
MotherToBaby Australia SSRI in pregnancy factsheet
RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: Postpartum prophylactic mood stabilisation (usually lithium) at or shortly after delivery substantially reduces the risk of postpartum psychosis and mania in women with bipolar I disorder; breastfeeding on lithium is acceptable with informed consent and monitoring.
key_points: Recurrence risk in bipolar I postpartum without prophylaxis: about 20-30%; higher with personal or family history of postpartum psychosis
Lithium: strongest evidence for postpartum prophylaxis
Alternatives: olanzapine or quetiapine when lithium is not tolerated or breastfeeding priority
Baseline UEC, TSH before starting lithium; level at day 5 then weekly for 2 weeks
Paediatric monitoring of infant on maternal lithium: serum lithium, UEC, TSH periodically
explanation.pearls: The postpartum period is the highest-risk time for a woman with bipolar I; prevention outperforms rescue. In context: informed shared decision-making about lithium and breastfeeding is a signature perinatal psychiatry conversation (Source: RANZCP).

sources.label: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health
COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar I risks precipitating mania; the priority is mood stabiliser prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Watchful waiting misses the window for prophylaxis in the highest-risk period and does not exploit her strong evidence-based option. Would rarely be correct (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

options.rationale: Valproate is teratogenic and its use in a woman of reproductive potential requires pregnancy prevention program compliance; it is also not the first-line prophylactic for bipolar I; formula feeding is not necessary for lithium. (Source: AMH; RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Women with bipolar I disorder have a postpartum psychosis risk of about 20-30% (much higher with a personal or family history), and prophylactic mood stabilisation started at or shortly after delivery substantially reduces recurrence. Lithium is the most evidence-supported prophylactic agent. Contemporary Australian practice (RANZCP, MotherToBaby Australia) accepts lithium in breastfeeding of a well term infant with informed consent, paediatric involvement, and monitoring (Source: RANZCP; MotherToBaby Australia; COPE).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health
COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (Beyond Blue)

options.rationale: Delaying until symptoms emerge is the strategy that failed her mother and is associated with worse outcomes; prophylaxis is the point. (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement 89: Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: The NHMRC 2013 CPG names DBT, mentalisation-based therapy, schema therapy, and transference-focused psychotherapy as first-line evidence-based treatments for borderline personality disorder. Medications are for comorbidities only.
key_points: First-line is structured evidence-based psychotherapy, not medication
DBT has the strongest local availability and evidence in Australia
Antipsychotics and mood stabilisers should not be prescribed for the core disorder
Prolonged inpatient admission is discouraged; brief crisis admissions only
Longitudinal data show over 80 percent achieve remission within 10 years
explanation.pearls: In context, when a patient with borderline personality disorder asks what will change the pattern itself, the answer is structured psychotherapy, not a medication substitution.

options.rationale: Antipsychotics have no first-line role in the core disorder and carry metabolic risk; they may be considered short-term for acute crisis only. Would only be appropriate if a comorbid indication were present (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

Mood stabilisers do not have robust evidence for the core disorder and the NHMRC guideline recommends against routine pharmacotherapy. Would only be considered if bipolar disorder were confirmed as a comorbidity (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

Structured evidence-based psychotherapy is first-line for the core disorder; DBT has the strongest Australian evidence for reducing self-harm and emergency presentations and is the most widely funded modality in public services (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).
Two adequate SSRI trials have failed and SSRIs do not treat the core disorder; further trials are reserved for a clearly comorbid depressive episode (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

Prolonged inpatient admission tends to reinforce maladaptive coping and is discouraged; brief crisis admissions are used only when safety cannot be managed in the community (Source: Project Air Strategy 2015).

explanation.summary: Regular and PRN benzodiazepines are not recommended in borderline personality disorder due to disinhibition, overdose potential and dependence, and because they interfere with the new-learning process that DBT relies on.
key_points: Benzodiazepine disinhibition can worsen self-harm and aggression
Overdose potential is high in a population with recurrent overdose behaviour
New skill acquisition in DBT is impaired by regular sedatives
Prior alprazolam dependence increases likelihood of recurrence
Reinforcing the crisis plan is the correct clinical move
explanation.pearls: In context, requests for benzodiazepines from a patient in active DBT are best met with skills coaching, not scripts.

options.rationale: PRN benzodiazepine use in this disorder still confers dependence and overdose risk and undermines the extinction learning DBT depends upon. Would only be considered for a short-lived non-personality crisis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic).

The class objection to benzodiazepines in this disorder is disinhibition and dependence rather than pharmacokinetics; oxazepam still carries these risks. Would only be preferred in a hepatic-impairment inpatient sedation scenario (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Antipsychotic use for the core disorder is not supported and adds metabolic risk without addressing the underlying skills gap. Would only be considered short-term in a documented crisis (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

Pregabalin has an established misuse and dependence profile in this population and no evidence base for the core disorder. Would only be considered for concurrent neuropathic pain (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Regular benzodiazepines are contraindicated in this disorder given disinhibition, overdose potential, dependence risk, and interference with new learning central to DBT. The NHMRC guideline advises against benzodiazepines and prefers reinforcement of psychological crisis skills (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

explanation.summary: Bipolar II hypomania requires a discrete episode of at least 4 days with sustained mood elevation or irritability and a change in functioning independent of interpersonal triggers. Borderline mood shifts are typically hour-to-hour and tightly coupled to interpersonal events.
key_points: Duration criterion for hypomania is 4 consecutive days
Bipolar mood episodes are not phasically driven by interpersonal events
A mood chart tracking triggers is the most useful outpatient tool
The two disorders commonly co-occur; correct differentiation still matters for treatment
First-degree family history for bipolar shifts pre-test probability but is not diagnostic
explanation.pearls: In context, hour-scale mood shifts mapped to interpersonal events on a prospective chart is the single most useful outpatient finding for separating these two diagnoses.

options.rationale: Self-harm is more common in the borderline construct but also occurs in mood disorders, including bipolar II. Would not distinguish the two on its own (Source: RANZCP CPG BPD 2012).

Bipolar II hypomania requires a distinct episode of at least 4 consecutive days of persistently elevated or irritable mood with functional change and is not tightly triggered by moment-to-moment interpersonal events; interpersonal-event-linked mood shifts within a day are core to the borderline construct (Source: DSM-5-TR).

A negative family history lowers pre-test probability but does not itself distinguish the two conditions and cannot rule out bipolar II. Would only be supportive alongside phenomenology (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders 2020).
Emptiness features in the borderline construct but is also common in chronic depression and does not discriminate against bipolar II. Would not distinguish the two on its own (Source: DSM-5-TR).
Both diagnoses can begin in adolescence. Would not distinguish the two on its own (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders 2020).

explanation.summary: The core differentiating features are the developmental conduct disorder history, the premeditated instrumental quality of aggression, and the callous absence of remorse. Borderline aggression is reactive, affectively driven, and typically accompanied by guilt.
key_points: Antisocial personality requires childhood conduct disorder features before age 15
Aggression is instrumental and premeditated rather than reactive
Remorse is characteristically absent
Substance use and relationship instability occur in both and do not discriminate
Comorbid antisocial and borderline features can coexist and require both to be addressed
explanation.pearls: In context, ask about pre-15 conduct-disorder features and the quality of aggression - instrumental with absent remorse points to antisocial, reactive with subsequent guilt points to borderline.

options.rationale: Forensic history increases probability but is not diagnostic on its own; people with the borderline construct can also have violence convictions. Would only be supportive alongside the pattern of premeditation and remorselessness (Source: RANZCP CPG BPD 2012).
Substance use disorders are common in both diagnoses and do not discriminate between them. Would only be relevant to treatment sequencing (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic).

Antisocial personality disorder requires evidence of conduct disorder before age 15 plus adult disregard for others; premeditated instrumental aggression with callous absence of remorse is characteristic and differs from the affectively driven reactive aggression seen in the borderline construct (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Relationship instability is common to both; the qualitative pattern differs but the presence of brief relationships alone is not sufficient. Would only support the diagnosis when the reason for ending is instrumental rather than fear of abandonment (Source: DSM-5-TR).
Many people with either diagnosis have never engaged services, so service contact history does not separate them. Would only reflect access patterns (Source: RANZCP CPG BPD 2012).

explanation.summary: Schizotypal personality disorder is characterised by pervasive cognitive and perceptual distortions, magical thinking and ideas of reference short of fixed delusion, odd speech and interpersonal deficits, present from early adulthood without a distinct psychotic episode or functional decline.
key_points: The threshold for delusion is fixed conviction held against contrary evidence
Odd speech in the schizotypal construct is tangential rather than formally disorganised
Long stable course without functional decline is against schizophrenia
Duration of subthreshold symptoms distinguishes this from attenuated psychosis syndrome
Schizoid presentation lacks the odd cognitive-perceptual features
explanation.pearls: In context, decade-long odd beliefs that stop short of fixed delusion, with preserved function, place the patient in the schizotypal construct rather than in the schizophrenia spectrum.

options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires 2 or more active-phase symptoms (with at least one of delusions, hallucinations, or disorganised speech) for a significant portion of one month, plus 6 months of overall disturbance with functional decline; neither is present here (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Delusional disorder requires one or more fixed delusions held with conviction against evidence for at least one month; his beliefs fall short of that threshold and are more magical than frankly delusional (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Longstanding odd beliefs, magical thinking, ideas of reference falling short of frank delusion, mild perceptual distortions, odd speech, and interpersonal deficits without functional decline or a discrete psychotic episode over a decade characterise this construct (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Schizoid presentation is characterised by pervasive detachment and a genuine preference for solitude without odd beliefs or perceptual distortions; the odd cognitive-perceptual features here place him outside that construct (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Attenuated psychosis syndrome describes recent-onset subthreshold psychotic symptoms typically over the past year with progression; his features have been stable for a decade with no functional decline (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: Avoidant personality disorder features an enduring self-view of inadequacy and avoidance of interpersonal contact that extends beyond performance and scrutiny situations. Social anxiety disorder is more circumscribed to feared evaluative contexts and does not require the pervasive negative self-view.
key_points: Enduring negative self-view is characteristic of the avoidant construct
Social anxiety centres on evaluative and performance situations
The schizoid construct includes genuine preference for solitude
Persistent depressive disorder requires vegetative mood features
Autism spectrum diagnosis requires early social communication difference plus restricted repetitive patterns
explanation.pearls: In context, when the wish for closeness is preserved but the self-view of inadequacy pervades every interpersonal setting, the picture goes beyond social anxiety into the avoidant construct.

options.rationale: Social anxiety typically clusters around performance and scrutiny with situational anxiety symptoms; the enduring self-view of inadequacy and avoidance of non-scrutiny interpersonal contact points beyond this diagnosis. Would be considered when the picture is limited to fear of scrutiny (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Persistent depressive disorder requires depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for at least 2 years with vegetative features; this presentation is dominated by longstanding interpersonal avoidance and self-view rather than pervasive low mood. Would be considered if mood features dominated (Source: DSM-5-TR).

The schizoid construct includes genuine preference for solitude and indifference to relationships; this patient wants closeness and is hurt by its absence. Would be considered when detachment is not distressing (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Pervasive since-childhood pattern of feelings of inadequacy, hypersensitivity to negative evaluation, and avoidance extending beyond performance situations into all interpersonal contact, with an enduring self-view of inferiority, characterises this construct rather than social anxiety disorder (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Autism spectrum diagnosis requires early-childhood social communication deficits and restricted repetitive behaviours; the description here is centred on avoidance driven by feared negative evaluation rather than communication difference. Would be considered if reciprocal-communication difficulty and restricted interests were present (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: The vulnerable subtype of the narcissistic construct is easily missed because it lacks overt grandiosity in the room. Recognising the covert grandiosity, envy, shame, and quiet contempt guides engagement strategy and therapy fit.
key_points: Grandiose subtype is overt and boastful
Vulnerable subtype is shy and shame-driven with covert grandiosity and envy
Both are highly sensitive to perceived slights
Recognition affects therapy engagement rather than requiring pharmacotherapy
Mood syndromes commonly overlie the personality picture and can mask it
explanation.pearls: In context, a shy shame-driven presentation with quiet contempt and envy is often the vulnerable narcissistic construct rather than depression alone.

options.rationale: The overt grandiose subtype is characterised by boastfulness, exhibitionism, and open entitlement in the room; his presenting shy manner and prominent shame move the picture toward the vulnerable subtype. Would be preferred when the presenting posture is openly boastful (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Atypical features require mood reactivity, leaden paralysis, increased sleep or appetite, and interpersonal rejection sensitivity dominating the picture; his mood features are secondary to entrenched personality dynamics rather than an episodic mood disorder. Would be preferred if the reactive mood syndrome were primary (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Illness anxiety is diagnosed when preoccupation with having a serious illness is the primary and enduring focus; here the hypochondriacal worries sit within a wider personality picture of grandiosity and shame. Would be preferred if illness preoccupation dominated in isolation (Source: DSM-5-TR).

The vulnerable presentation combines covert grandiosity with hypersensitivity to criticism, shame, envy, hypochondriasis, and quiet contempt for others behind a shy self-effacing exterior; it is often missed when clinicians expect only the overt grandiose type (Source: DSM-5-TR alternative model).

Persistent depressive disorder requires chronic depressed mood for at least 2 years with vegetative features; the presentation is dominated by entrenched personality dynamics rather than sustained low mood. Would be preferred if chronic depressive vegetative features predominated (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: Splitting is diagnostic data about how a patient organises relationships under stress and is best addressed at the team level. Naming it explicitly, agreeing on a unified approach, and sharing responsibility across the team is the first-line intervention.
key_points: Splitting is a systems-level phenomenon requiring a team response
Restricting care to the idealised staff entrenches the split
Medication does not address interpersonal dynamics
Consistent unified responses across the team model containment
Ward-level supervision or reflective practice reduces staff burnout
explanation.pearls: In context, when the team starts to feel split about a patient, that is diagnostic data - the intervention is at the team level, not the patient level.

options.rationale: Restricting care to the idealised subgroup entrenches the splitting rather than resolving it and burdens a small group. Would only be considered if there were a specific safety-of-staff concern (Source: Project Air Strategy 2015).

Pharmacotherapy does not address the team dynamic and antipsychotics have no first-line role in the core disorder. Would only be considered short-term in a documented crisis (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

She is already in a DBT program and premature discharge without addressing the ward dynamic will lead to repetition on the next admission. Would only be considered when medically fit AND the team dynamic is contained (Source: Project Air Strategy 2015).

Naming the splitting dynamic in a structured team meeting and agreeing on a unified consistent approach reduces the polarisation, models containment, and is the first-line management for this specific ward dynamic (Source: Project Air Strategy 2015).

Outpatient DBT therapists do not routinely deliver inpatient skills coaching and this does not address the polarised staff response. Would only be appropriate as an adjunct once the team dynamic is contained (Source: Project Air Strategy 2015).

explanation.summary: MBT is one of four NHMRC-named first-line structured therapies for borderline personality disorder. Its focus on restoring mentalising capacity under arousal is a particular fit for patients who misread others and who find the skills-based DBT format too mechanical.
key_points: MBT is a first-line NHMRC-named therapy alongside DBT, schema therapy, and TFP
It targets loss of mentalising under emotional arousal
Reflective non-skills format suits patients who found DBT mechanical
Repeat trials of a dropped-out modality without addressing dropout are low-yield
The evidence base includes reduced self-harm and improved interpersonal function
explanation.pearls: In context, patients whose core problem is losing the capacity to think about mental states under emotional arousal are the classical MBT indication.

options.rationale: A repeat trial of the same modality that she recently disengaged from is unlikely to succeed and other evidence-based modalities are available. Would only be considered if the reason for dropout were addressable (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

MBT is an evidence-based structured therapy that specifically targets the loss of mentalising capacity under emotional arousal and the tendency to misread others; its reflective non-skills-based format suits patients who found DBT too mechanical (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

CBT for depression targets depressive cognition and behaviour and is not the first-line structured therapy for the core personality disorder. Would only be considered for a comorbid depressive episode (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders 2020).

Interpersonal psychotherapy targets identified interpersonal problems in the context of a depressive episode and is not indicated as first-line therapy for the core personality disorder. Would only be considered for a comorbid depressive episode (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders 2020).

EMDR is indicated when the presenting problem is post-traumatic stress disorder; her presentation is centred on personality-driven misreading rather than reexperiencing of trauma. Would only be considered if PTSD were prominent (Source: NHMRC PTSD Guideline).

explanation.summary: Guideline-based emergency department care of this disorder emphasises brief-contact intervention with written safety planning, means restriction, family support, and continuity with the existing outpatient therapist, avoiding admission where possible.
key_points: Recurrent low-lethality presentations are the norm in this disorder
Prolonged admission tends to reinforce maladaptive coping
Written safety plans, means restriction, and family involvement are core steps
Continuity with the existing outpatient therapist is protective
Involuntary detention is reserved for clearly unmanageable acute risk
explanation.pearls: In context, the guideline default in the emergency department is discharge with structured safety planning and continuity, not admission.

options.rationale: Prolonged admission is not recommended in this disorder as it tends to reinforce maladaptive coping and can disrupt outpatient therapy. Would only be considered when acute risk cannot be managed in the community (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

Involuntary detention requires statutory criteria including risk that cannot otherwise be managed; she is engaged, calm, family supported and has an active outpatient plan. Would only be considered if she declined engagement and met the statutory threshold (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).

Antipsychotics are not first-line and PRN sedation in this population can accumulate harm without addressing the underlying skills gap. Would only be considered short-term in a documented crisis with clear indication (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

She already has an established DBT therapist and duplicating referrals disrupts continuity and consistency, which are protective. Would only be considered if the existing program were confirmed to have ended (Source: Project Air Strategy 2015).

Brief-contact intervention with structured written safety planning, means restriction, family support, and continuity with the existing outpatient therapist is the guideline-recommended approach; inpatient admission is not indicated in the absence of acute risk that cannot be managed in the community (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

explanation.summary: Coordinated perinatal mental health care with infant mental health input is the guideline-recommended step for this disorder in pregnancy, focused on attachment support and continuity of an established therapeutic relationship rather than pharmacotherapy in a well-engaged patient.
key_points: Perinatal mental health services coordinate obstetric and mental health care
Infant mental health input focuses on attachment and parenting
Continuity of DBT through pregnancy is protective
Antidepressant prophylaxis is not indicated without prior severe episode or current syndrome
Mode of birth is decided on obstetric grounds
explanation.pearls: In context, the additive step in a well-engaged pregnant patient with this diagnosis is perinatal mental health service linkage, not new medication.

sources.label: RANZCP Position Statement Perinatal Mental Health

options.rationale: There is no clear indication for antidepressant prophylaxis in the absence of a current depressive episode or a prior severe postpartum illness. Would only be considered for a prior severe episode or current depressive syndrome (Source: RANZCP Position Statement Perinatal Mental Health).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement Perinatal Mental Health

options.rationale: Continuity of an established therapeutic relationship is protective through the perinatal period and reducing engagement risks decompensation. Would only be considered if the patient herself requested reduction with a specific reason (Source: Project Air Strategy 2015).

Guideline-recommended perinatal management for this disorder involves coordinated multidisciplinary planning across obstetrics, mental health, and infant mental health, focused on attachment and parenting support rather than pharmacotherapy in a well-engaged patient (Source: RANZCP Position Statement Perinatal Mental Health).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement Perinatal Mental Health

options.rationale: A personality disorder diagnosis is not in itself a contraindication to breastfeeding and pre-emptive advice against it is stigmatising and unsupported. Would only be considered if a specific psychotropic incompatibility applied (Source: RANZCP Position Statement Perinatal Mental Health).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement Perinatal Mental Health

options.rationale: Mode of birth is decided on obstetric grounds and a personality disorder diagnosis is not itself an indication for elective caesarean. Would only be considered on obstetric grounds (Source: RANZCOG Statement Intrapartum Care).

explanation.summary: The RANZCP position statement and the NHMRC guideline support diagnosing borderline personality disorder in adolescents when full criteria and a pattern of at least 12 months are present, and referring for early intervention with adolescent DBT.
key_points: The diagnosis is valid in adolescents when full criteria and 12-month duration are met
Early intervention improves trajectory and reduces self-harm
Adolescent DBT (DBT-A) is the best-evidenced structured therapy in this age group
SSRIs do not treat the core disorder and are not a substitute for therapy
Family involvement is a key component of adolescent programs
explanation.pearls: In context, deferring the diagnosis until 18 in a case that meets criteria withholds the evidence-based treatment that changes trajectory.

options.rationale: Deferral withholds access to evidence-based structured therapy during a critical developmental window and is contrary to current guideline advice. Would only be considered when criteria are clearly not met (Source: RANZCP Position Statement Personality Disorders).

The RANZCP position and the NHMRC guideline support making the diagnosis in adolescents when full criteria are met with a pattern present for at least 12 months, and early intervention with adolescent DBT reduces self-harm and improves function (Source: RANZCP Position Statement Personality Disorders).

SSRIs are not indicated for the core personality disorder and are not a substitute for structured therapy in this age group. Would only be considered for a clearly comorbid depressive episode (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

Generic supportive counselling does not have the evidence base that structured adolescent DBT does for this presentation. Would only be considered if structured therapy were unavailable (Source: NHMRC CPG BPD 2013).

When full criteria and duration are met the formal diagnosis is appropriate and using a subthreshold label may block access to guideline-based treatment. Would only be considered when criteria fall short of threshold (Source: RANZCP Position Statement Personality Disorders).

explanation.summary: When personality disorder coexists with an eating disorder that has current medical instability, guideline-based sequencing addresses the acute medical risk and the eating disorder first while the personality-focused therapy proceeds in parallel or once available.
key_points: Symptomatic hypokalaemia in bulimia is an acute medical concern
CBT-E is first-line for bulimia and can start immediately
Fluoxetine 60 mg is adjunctive in bulimia but is not therapy replacement
Prolonged admission is discouraged in the borderline construct
Personality-focused therapy proceeds in parallel or once the waitlist opens
explanation.pearls: In context, when comorbid conditions coexist, the one causing current medical risk sets the sequencing priority.

options.rationale: Waiting 3 months while she has symptomatic hypokalaemia and active purging exposes her to avoidable medical risk. Would only be considered if she were medically stable and asymptomatic (Source: RANZCP CPG Eating Disorders 2014).

Prolonged admission is discouraged in the borderline construct and eating disorder guidelines reserve inpatient care for severe medical instability, treatment failure, or high suicide risk. Would only be considered for severe medical instability (Source: RANZCP CPG Eating Disorders 2014).

Bulimia with symptomatic hypokalaemia carries immediate medical risk and requires potassium replacement and eating disorder focused therapy such as CBT-E without delay; personality-focused therapy can proceed in parallel or once the waitlist opens, as the eating disorder is the more urgent life-threatening comorbidity today (Source: RANZCP CPG Eating Disorders 2014).

Fluoxetine 60 mg is evidence-based for bulimia but is an adjunct rather than a substitute for eating disorder focused therapy and does not address medical instability. Would only be considered as an adjunct to therapy (Source: RANZCP CPG Eating Disorders 2014).

MBT does not directly address bulimic behaviour and delaying eating disorder therapy while she is symptomatically hypokalaemic is medically unsafe. Would only be considered when the eating disorder was in stable remission (Source: RANZCP CPG Eating Disorders 2014).

explanation.summary: Progressive mid-life personality change with disinhibition, loss of empathy, compulsive eating, impulsivity and executive impairment, with disproportionate frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, fulfils international criteria for behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia.
key_points: New-onset antisocial personality is not a valid mid-life diagnosis
Behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia typically presents in the 50s to 60s
Episodic memory is often relatively preserved early
Social cognition and verbal fluency subtests are disproportionately affected
Imaging shows bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy
explanation.pearls: In context, mid-life personality change with preserved memory, executive impairment and frontal atrophy is behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia until proven otherwise.

options.rationale: The antisocial construct requires evidence of conduct disorder before age 15 and is not a valid new-onset diagnosis in mid-life; personality change from a medical or neurological cause must be excluded first. Would only be considered when a lifelong pattern was established (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Late-onset bipolar disorder is uncommon and typically causes episodic distinct mood elevation with reduced sleep need; progressive personality change with executive impairment and structural atrophy is not the picture. Would only be considered with an episodic mood course and no imaging change (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Progressive personality change in mid-life with disinhibition, loss of empathy, compulsive dietary change, impulsivity, executive dysfunction and disproportionately preserved episodic memory alongside frontal and anterior temporal atrophy fulfils the international consensus criteria for behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia (Source: Rascovsky international consensus criteria 2011).

Alzheimer disease characteristically begins with episodic memory impairment; a leading picture of personality change with preserved memory and frontal atrophy points elsewhere. Would only be considered with an amnestic-first presentation (Source: RANZCP CPG Dementia 2016).

Persistent depressive disorder is characterised by sustained depressed mood and does not produce disinhibition, compulsive dietary change, or frontal atrophy. Would only be considered if the picture were dominated by depressed mood (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: The histrionic construct is a declining diagnosis but remains in DSM-5-TR. Its features are excessive attention-seeking, dramatic and vague speech, suggestibility and perceived closeness in shallow relationships, without the volatility and self-harm of the borderline construct.
key_points: Histrionic diagnosis persists in DSM-5-TR though its use is declining
Attention-seeking without self-harm, abandonment fear or volatile idealisation distinguishes it from the borderline construct
Overlap with the borderline construct exists but the two are distinguishable on core features
The grandiose narcissistic construct requires entitlement and exploitation
Comorbidity with mood disorders is common and can mask the personality picture
explanation.pearls: In context, attention-seeking dramaticism without self-harm and without volatile idealisation-devaluation points to the histrionic rather than the borderline construct.

options.rationale: The borderline construct requires features including chronic emptiness, recurrent self-harm or suicide behaviour, fears of abandonment, and volatile idealisation-devaluation, which are absent here. Would only be diagnosed when 5 of 9 criteria are met (Source: DSM-5-TR).

The grandiose narcissistic construct centres on entitlement, exploitation, and inflated self-appraisal; attention-seeking without these core features falls outside it. Would only be diagnosed if grandiosity and exploitation were prominent (Source: DSM-5-TR).

A pervasive pattern from early adulthood of excessive attention-seeking, dramatic and vague speech, provocative appearance, suggestibility, and considering relationships as more intimate than they are, without the self-harm, abandonment fears, and volatile idealisation-devaluation of the borderline construct, characterises this diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Persistent depressive disorder requires sustained depressed mood for at least 2 years with vegetative features, which are not described. Would only be diagnosed with sustained low mood (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Bipolar II requires discrete hypomanic episodes of at least 4 days with a change in functioning; enduring attention-seeking without episodic mood elevation does not meet criteria. Would only be diagnosed with a discrete hypomanic episode (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: OCPD is an ego-syntonic personality pattern characterised by perfectionism, orderliness, workaholism and rigidity, without the intrusive obsessions and neutralising compulsions of obsessive-compulsive disorder.
key_points: OCPD is ego-syntonic and lifelong
OCD is ego-dystonic with intrusive thoughts and neutralising compulsions
Miserliness and hoarding of worn-out items are OCPD features
Generalised anxiety requires pervasive worry across domains
Comorbidity between OCPD and OCD is possible but not the same diagnosis
explanation.pearls: In context, ego-syntonic lifelong perfectionism without intrusive obsessions and rituals is the OCPD construct rather than obsessive-compulsive disorder.

options.rationale: The disorder requires ego-dystonic intrusive obsessions and compulsive behaviours performed to reduce anxiety, which he does not describe. Would only be diagnosed with obsessions and compulsions (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Generalised anxiety requires excessive worry across multiple domains for at least 6 months with physical anxiety symptoms; enduring perfectionism without worry does not meet criteria. Would only be diagnosed with pervasive worry (Source: DSM-5-TR).

A lifelong ego-syntonic pattern of preoccupation with order, perfectionism impairing task completion, workaholism, rigidity, miserliness and stubbornness, without unwanted intrusive obsessions or compulsions performed to neutralise anxiety, characterises this diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Autism spectrum diagnosis requires early-childhood social communication difference and restricted repetitive behaviours; work-related perfectionism alone does not meet the framework. Would only be diagnosed with early social communication difference and restricted interests (Source: DSM-5-TR).

Hoarding disorder requires persistent difficulty discarding due to a perceived need to save and resulting clutter compromising living space; his hoarding is a single trait within a broader personality picture. Would only be diagnosed when hoarding dominates (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: This is chronic lithium toxicity precipitated by ACE inhibitor commencement plus volume depletion from gastroenteritis. The level (3.1) is between 2.5 and 4.0, but AKI and neurotoxicity together are stand-alone dialysis triggers under EXTRIP guidance. Delaying dialysis to give more saline risks Syndrome of Irreversible Lithium-Effectuated Neurotoxicity (SILENT).
key_points: EXTRIP: dialyse if lithium >4.0, or >2.5 with reduced consciousness, seizures, life-threatening arrhythmia, or impaired renal function
ACEi/ARB, NSAIDs, thiazides and dehydration all reduce lithium clearance
Charcoal does not bind lithium; alkaline diuresis is not indicated
Continuous venovenous haemodiafiltration is acceptable when intermittent HD is unavailable
explanation.pearls: In context: any lithium level above 2.5 mmol/L with neurology or AKI is a dialysis conversation; do not wait for the level to climb past 4.

options.rationale: Saline is core supportive care but is inadequate as sole management given level >2.5 mmol/L with neurological features and acute kidney injury; delaying dialysis risks progression to seizures, coma and permanent cerebellar injury (SILENT). (Source: TG Psychotropic: Lithium toxicity)

Charcoal does not bind lithium (a monovalent cation) and there is no role for gut decontamination in chronic toxicity; a ward bed underestimates the required level of care for a patient with GCS 13 and progressive neurotoxicity. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

EXTRIP consensus and Australian toxicology practice recommend extracorporeal treatment when lithium is >4.0 mmol/L in any patient, or >2.5 mmol/L with impaired kidney function or significant neurological features (reduced consciousness, seizures, life-threatening dysrhythmia). This patient meets both the level and the AKI-plus-neurology criteria. (Source: EXTRIP lithium recommendations; PIC 13 11 26)

Urinary alkalinisation is used in salicylate toxicity, not lithium; it does not accelerate lithium excretion and adds a sodium and volume burden that is not indicated here. (Source: TG Toxicology; PIC 13 11 26)

Benzodiazepines are only indicated if seizures occur; they do not address the underlying lithium burden and mask deteriorating consciousness. Spontaneous renal clearance is too slow in AKI. (Source: PIC 13 11 26)

explanation.summary: NSAIDs (including COX-2 selective), ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides and dehydration all reduce renal lithium clearance and are the commonest causes of chronic toxicity in stable outpatients. Paracetamol is the safe first line.
key_points: NSAIDs can raise lithium levels 20-40%
COX-2 selective agents interact the same way
Thiazides reduce clearance; loop diuretics have less effect but still monitor
If NSAID unavoidable, monitor level within 5-7 days and adjust dose
explanation.pearls: In context: any new NSAID, ACEi/ARB, thiazide or GI illness in a lithium patient is a level-check trigger.

options.rationale: NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance by up to 40% via reduced prostaglandin-mediated GFR; even short courses can push levels into the toxic range. Not appropriate to initiate ibuprofen. (Source: AMH: Lithium interactions)

COX-2 selective agents interact with lithium via the same mechanism as non-selective NSAIDs and are not a workaround; AMH lists the interaction for the whole class. (Source: AMH: Lithium interactions)

Paracetamol has no lithium interaction and is first line for mechanical back pain; NSAIDs (including COX-2 selective) are relatively contraindicated as they raise lithium levels unpredictably. (Source: AMH: Lithium; TG Psychotropic)
Thiazides reduce lithium clearance and are a well-documented cause of toxicity; deliberately combining them to reduce dose is unsafe and not a recognised strategy. (Source: AMH: Lithium interactions)

Corticosteroids are not first line for mechanical back pain and carry mood-destabilising risk in bipolar disorder; not an appropriate substitute for simple analgesia. (Source: TG Rheumatology; RANZCP Mood CPG)

explanation.summary: Chronic lithium nephropathy is a slowly progressive tubulointerstitial injury. Continued use is often justified when the psychiatric benefit is clear, but the target level should be lowered, monitoring intensified, and a multidisciplinary discussion held about long-term trajectory.
key_points: Target 0.4-0.6 mmol/L in older adults or CKD
3-monthly levels once monitoring becomes intensive
Abrupt cessation carries a 50% relapse risk within 6 months
Switch requires slow cross-titration under psychiatry review
explanation.pearls: In context: never stop lithium at a single GP visit; adjust and involve the treating team.

options.rationale: Falling eGFR with a level at the upper end of target requires action, not routine annual review; RANZCP recommends 3-monthly levels once monitoring becomes more intensive. (Source: RANZCP Mood CPG)

In older adults and those with reduced eGFR, aim for a lower maintenance target (often 0.4-0.6) with more frequent monitoring; involve psychiatry regarding balance between mood stability and long-term nephrotoxicity, but abrupt cessation risks relapse. (Source: RANZCP Mood CPG; TG Psychotropic)

Abrupt lithium cessation carries a high relapse risk (up to 50% within 6 months) and rebound mania; any switch requires slow cross-titration and shared decision-making, not a same-visit change. (Source: RANZCP Mood CPG)

Biopsy is not routinely indicated for typical lithium nephropathy (chronic tubulointerstitial pattern); nephrology referral is appropriate for co-management but does not obviate the need to adjust lithium now. (Source: KHA-CARI; Australian Prescriber)

ACEi may be a contributor but stopping it does not address cumulative lithium tubulointerstitial injury; the primary issue is lithium exposure, not the antihypertensive class. (Source: KHA-CARI; TG Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Australian clozapine monitoring (CPMS or ClopineCentral) uses a traffic-light system based on ANC. Green (>=2.0) is routine, amber (1.0-1.9 depending on protocol) requires increased monitoring, red (<1.0) requires cessation.
key_points: Green ANC >=2.0: routine monitoring
Amber ANC 1.0-1.9: increase to twice-weekly, continue clozapine
Red ANC <1.0: cease clozapine, notify haematology
G-CSF is used in some rechallenge or persistent red-range cases with haematology guidance
explanation.pearls: In context: know the traffic-light thresholds cold; ANC 1.2 is amber, not red.

options.rationale: This is amber-range (not red), and cessation is not required at ANC 1.2; premature stopping risks psychiatric relapse and rechallenge is often refused. Empirical antibiotics and G-CSF are for febrile neutropenia or ANC <0.5. (Source: TGA clozapine PI; CPMS)

An ANC of 1.2 shifts him from green to amber under the Australian CPMS/ClopineCentral protocol; monitoring must escalate to at least twice-weekly FBCs, not remain at the routine interval. (Source: CPMS/ClopineCentral)

Olanzapine is not equivalent for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (clozapine is uniquely effective); switching at amber range is premature and loses the only agent with demonstrated benefit in this indication. (Source: RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

Under the Australian clozapine monitoring protocol, ANC 1.0-1.5 is amber: continue clozapine but escalate to twice-weekly FBCs until ANC returns to >=2.0. Cessation is only required at red-range (ANC <1.0). Patient education on infection is essential. (Source: CPMS/ClopineCentral protocol; TGA clozapine PI)
Clozapine-induced neutropenia is idiosyncratic, not dose-dependent; dose reduction does not resolve it and may destabilise psychiatric state. (Source: TGA clozapine PI)

explanation.summary: Clozapine myocarditis peaks between weeks 2 and 4 of initiation. Australian practice is baseline troponin/CRP/ECG/echo, then weekly troponin and CRP for the first 4 (some centres 6-8) weeks. Any rise triggers cessation and cardiology review.
key_points: Peak incidence weeks 2-4 of clozapine initiation
Weekly troponin and CRP for at least 4 weeks (many centres 6-8 weeks)
Cease clozapine if troponin or CRP rise with symptoms
Rechallenge only under specialist cardiology and psychiatry co-supervision
explanation.pearls: In context: fever, tachycardia and dyspnoea in the first 8 weeks of clozapine is myocarditis until proven otherwise.

options.rationale: Rising troponin plus CRP with tachycardia and dyspnoea 3 weeks into clozapine is myocarditis until proven otherwise; TGA PI and RANZCP guidance require cessation, cardiology involvement and echo. Rechallenge is possible in selected cases but only under specialist care. (Source: TGA clozapine PI; RANZCP)

Continuing clozapine with clear biochemical and clinical signs of myocarditis risks fulminant progression; delay in cessation is associated with worse outcome including death. (Source: TGA clozapine PI)

Empirical antibiotics without infective focus do not address clozapine myocarditis and the antibiotic choice does not treat the underlying cardiac process; myocarditis mortality is highest in the first 6-8 weeks. (Source: TG Antibiotic; TGA PI)
Dose reduction does not adequately mitigate the risk of established myocarditis and outpatient management is unsafe with an elevated troponin and tachycardia. (Source: TGA clozapine PI)

A 4-week wait for MRI while continuing clozapine risks progression to fulminant myocarditis; cessation and urgent echo are required now, with MRI as an adjunct if diagnosis remains uncertain. (Source: Australian Prescriber; TGA PI)

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility (CIGH) is the highest-mortality clozapine adverse effect, exceeding agranulocytosis. All patients on clozapine should be on scheduled aperient prophylaxis (typically macrogol +/- stimulant), and any established constipation is a medical emergency.
key_points: CIGH mortality up to 15-27% once complicated
Prophylactic aperient (macrogol +/- senna) for all clozapine patients
Established ileus: admit, IV fluids, surgical review, cease clozapine
Avoid opioids and additional anticholinergic drugs on clozapine
explanation.pearls: In context: constipation on clozapine is not a nuisance, it is the biggest killer.

options.rationale: Discharge is unsafe given tympanic distension, tachycardia, elevated lactate and early small bowel dilatation; clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility (CIGH) has a mortality up to 15-27% once complications develop. (Source: Australian Prescriber; TG Psychotropic)

Metoclopramide primarily accelerates upper GI transit and adds extrapyramidal and tardive dyskinesia risk on top of clozapine; it does not reliably resolve colonic hypomotility. (Source: AMH: Metoclopramide)

Disimpaction alone is inadequate for whole-colon faecal loading with proximal dilatation; same-day colonoscopy carries perforation risk in a distended obstructed bowel. Surgical review and admission are required. (Source: Australian Prescriber)

Established clozapine ileus needs admission, fluid resuscitation, surgical involvement (risk of ischaemia or perforation), temporary cessation of clozapine and multi-agent aperient regimen (osmotic plus stimulant). This is the highest-mortality clozapine adverse effect, exceeding agranulocytosis. (Source: Australian Prescriber; TGA PI)
Aggressive bowel prep in a distended, dilated colon risks perforation; outpatient investigation delays management of a potentially fatal complication. (Source: Australian Prescriber)

explanation.summary: Tobacco (not nicotine) induces CYP1A2. Any smoking cessation, hospital admission with enforced abstinence, or planned quit attempt is a trigger for pre-emptive clozapine dose review. Levels can rise substantially within days to weeks.
key_points: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco induce CYP1A2, not nicotine
Cessation can raise clozapine levels 50-100% within 2-4 weeks
Consider 25% dose reduction on planned or enforced cessation
Restart smoking during admission is not the answer; adjust dose
explanation.pearls: In context: any clozapine patient who stops smoking needs a dose plan, not just a patch.

sources.label: Australian Prescriber: Smoking and drug interactions

options.rationale: Tobacco smoke (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, not nicotine) induces CYP1A2, the principal enzyme metabolising clozapine. Cessation removes induction and levels can rise 50-100% within 2-4 weeks (faster on inpatient wards). Dose reduction of ~25% is often required within days. (Source: TG Psychotropic; AMH)
source_refs: Australian Prescriber: Smoking and drug interactions

options.rationale: Nicotine itself does not induce CYP1A2; the inducers are polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke, so NRT does not maintain enzyme induction after cessation. This is a common misconception. (Source: Australian Prescriber)
source_refs: Australian Prescriber: Smoking and drug interactions

options.rationale: Flucloxacillin has no clinically significant effect on CYP1A2 or clozapine levels; the mechanism here is loss of tobacco induction, not antibiotic inhibition. (Source: AMH interactions)
A near-doubling of level with new toxic symptoms cannot be explained by sampling timing alone; the pattern is classic for smoking cessation. (Source: TG Psychotropic)

Acute inflammation can raise clozapine levels somewhat but the dominant driver here is smoking cessation; withholding dose action for another 48 hours risks clinical deterioration when the patient is already toxic. (Source: Australian Prescriber)
source_refs: Australian Prescriber: Smoking and drug interactions

explanation.summary: Valproate carries the highest teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental risk of any commonly used mood stabiliser (up to 30-40% neurodevelopmental disorders, ~10% major malformations). The TGA-mandated Australian pregnancy prevention program requires effective contraception, annual specialist review and documented risk acknowledgement.
key_points: Neurodevelopmental disorder risk 30-40%, malformation risk ~10%
Pregnancy prevention program mandatory in women of childbearing potential
Folate does not mitigate valproate teratogenicity
No safe threshold dose in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: In context: never plan pregnancy on valproate; switch first, then attempt.

options.rationale: Folate does not mitigate the specific teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks of valproate; TGA prescribing information requires pregnancy prevention while on valproate in women of childbearing potential unless there is no alternative and the program is followed. (Source: TGA valproate PI)

TGA/AMH mandate valproate is not used in women of childbearing potential unless there is no effective alternative, and only under the pregnancy prevention program (annual specialist review, effective contraception, acknowledgement of risks). Alternatives must be actively considered before pregnancy planning. (Source: TGA; AMH; RANZCP)

Dose reduction below a threshold does not remove teratogenic risk (dose-response is present but no safe threshold); also risks psychiatric relapse. Not a substitute for switching. (Source: TGA valproate PI)

Abrupt cessation of valproate risks relapse; any switch requires cross-titration under psychiatry, and pregnancy planning should follow stability on the new agent, not commence immediately. (Source: RANZCP; TG Psychotropic)

Valproate-associated malformations and neurodevelopmental problems are not detectable by preimplantation genetic testing; this is not an appropriate substitute for medication review. (Source: TGA valproate PI)

explanation.summary: HLA-B*15:02 is strongly associated with carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN in Han Chinese, Thai, Malay, Filipino, Indian, Vietnamese and some other Asian populations. TGA now recommends screening before initiation.
key_points: HLA-B*15:02 -> carbamazepine SJS/TEN in Asian populations
HLA-A*31:01 -> broader hypersensitivity reactions
Oxcarbazepine also carries the HLA-B*15:02 association at lower risk
Screening and avoidance in positives is standard of care
explanation.pearls: In context: never start carbamazepine in an at-risk ancestry without checking HLA-B*15:02.

options.rationale: TGA product information and eviQ pharmacogenomic guidance recommend HLA-B*15:02 testing before carbamazepine (and oxcarbazepine) in individuals of Han Chinese, Thai, Malay, Filipino, Indian and some other Asian ancestries due to strong association with SJS/TEN. Positive result is a contraindication. (Source: TGA carbamazepine PI; eviQ)

Rash counselling alone is insufficient when a validated screening test with high negative predictive value is available; testing is now standard of care in populations with high HLA-B*15:02 prevalence. (Source: TGA; eviQ)
Oxcarbazepine shares the HLA-B*15:02 association with SJS/TEN, though at lower absolute risk; substitution does not remove the need for screening. (Source: TGA oxcarbazepine PI)

HLA-B*57:01 is the abacavir hypersensitivity marker, not carbamazepine SJS/TEN. The relevant allele is HLA-B*15:02 for carbamazepine SJS/TEN in Asian populations and HLA-A*31:01 for other reactions. (Source: eviQ)

Hepatotoxicity and haematological effects require monitoring but the highest-consequence pharmacogenomic risk in this ancestry group is SJS/TEN; screening is the appropriate first step, not routine LFT surveillance alone. (Source: TGA carbamazepine PI)

explanation.summary: Lamotrigine SJS/TEN risk is highest with rapid titration or overshoot dosing. Valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation (levels roughly double), so halve the starting dose and slow the titration. COC induces lamotrigine glucuronidation, so dose adjustment is required when COC is started or stopped.
key_points: Valproate co-therapy: start 25 mg alternate days, halve steady state dose
COC: induces lamotrigine glucuronidation; adjust dose on starting/stopping
Any rash within first 8 weeks: cease and reassess
No loading doses at any indication
explanation.pearls: In context: lamotrigine + valproate = slow titration; lamotrigine + COC = watch for level changes.

options.rationale: Standard titration is too fast when valproate (a potent lamotrigine metabolism inhibitor) is co-prescribed; risk of SJS/TEN rises with rapid escalation. COC induces lamotrigine glucuronidation and reduces levels. (Source: AMH: Lamotrigine)
Loading doses are contraindicated for lamotrigine at any indication because of SJS/TEN risk; slow titration is essential regardless of urgency. (Source: TGA lamotrigine PI)

Combination of lamotrigine and valproate is a recognised strategy; abrupt cessation of valproate risks relapse and is not required, provided titration is appropriately slow. (Source: RANZCP; TG Psychotropic)

Valproate roughly doubles lamotrigine levels via UGT inhibition, so start at 25 mg on alternate days for weeks 1-2, 25 mg daily weeks 3-4, then increase by 25-50 mg every 2 weeks. Standard titration risks SJS/TEN. COC induces lamotrigine metabolism and dose review is needed when COC starts or stops. (Source: AMH; TG Psychotropic)

COC and lamotrigine can be co-prescribed but the interaction (COC induces lamotrigine metabolism) requires dose review when COC starts or stops; they are not contraindicated together. (Source: AMH: Lamotrigine)

explanation.summary: Irreversible MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) require a 14-day washout before starting any serotonergic drug (SSRI, SNRI, TCA, opioids like tramadol/pethidine, triptans). Fluoxetine to MAOI switch requires a 5-week washout due to fluoxetine's long half-life.
key_points: 14-day washout after phenelzine or tranylcypromine before SSRI
5-week washout after fluoxetine before MAOI
Continue tyramine restriction throughout MAOI washout
Never cross-titrate irreversible MAOI with serotonergic agent
explanation.pearls: In context: 14 days off MAOI, 5 weeks off fluoxetine, always.

options.rationale: TGA product information and TG Psychotropic require at least 14 days off an irreversible non-selective MAOI (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) before commencing an SSRI, SNRI or other serotonergic drug, to allow regeneration of monoamine oxidase enzyme. Tyramine dietary restriction should continue for the full washout. (Source: TG Psychotropic; TGA phenelzine PI)
Cross-titration of an irreversible MAOI and an SSRI is contraindicated because of the risk of fatal serotonin syndrome; overlap must be avoided. (Source: TG Psychotropic; TGA)
Phenelzine is an irreversible MAOI; despite short plasma half-life, MAO enzyme regeneration requires ~14 days. Elimination half-life is not the relevant kinetic parameter. (Source: TG Psychotropic)
Switching one MAOI class to another does not remove the SSRI overlap risk; the required 14-day washout applies before any SSRI regardless of intermediate agents. (Source: TG Psychotropic)
48 hours is grossly insufficient for irreversible MAOI enzyme regeneration; risk of serotonin syndrome remains high. (Source: TGA phenelzine PI)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome and NMS both cause hyperthermia and autonomic instability, but neuromuscular signs distinguish them: hyperreflexia and clonus (SS) vs rigidity and bradyreflexia (NMS). Anticholinergic toxidrome is dry and flushed. Linezolid is a reversible MAOI and a common precipitant of SS when combined with serotonergic antidepressants.
key_points: Hunter criteria: clonus + serotonergic exposure + one of agitation, hyperreflexia, autonomic instability
Linezolid is a reversible MAOI - avoid or cease serotonergic agents
Cease drug, benzodiazepines, active cooling; cyproheptadine for severe cases
NMS: rigidity, bradyreflexia, high CK; anticholinergic: dry, flushed, absent bowel sounds
explanation.pearls: In context: hyperreflexia and clonus with autonomic storm = serotonin syndrome; rigidity + antipsychotic exposure = NMS.

options.rationale: NMS features bradyreflexia and lead-pipe rigidity, not hyperreflexia and clonus; also requires antipsychotic exposure. Clinical pattern here is serotonin syndrome. (Source: TG Psychotropic; Australian Prescriber)

Anticholinergic toxidrome has flushed dry skin, absent bowel sounds and urinary retention, without hyperreflexia or clonus. Sweating in this patient argues against anticholinergic aetiology. (Source: TG Toxicology)

Linezolid is a reversible weak MAOI and combined with venlafaxine (SNRI) can precipitate serotonin syndrome. Hyperreflexia, sustained clonus (particularly lower limb), mydriasis, sweating, agitation and hyperthermia meet Hunter criteria. Cease serotonergic drugs, aggressive supportive care, IV benzodiazepines. Cyproheptadine (5HT2A antagonist) for severe/refractory cases. (Source: TG Psychotropic; PIC 13 11 26)

Malignant hyperthermia requires exposure to a triggering anaesthetic (volatile agent or succinylcholine); the patient has had no such exposure. Presentation is otherwise consistent with serotonin syndrome. (Source: ANZCA)
Sepsis does not cause sustained clonus and hyperreflexia; the pattern here is serotonergic toxicity, not sepsis progression, and steroids are not indicated. (Source: TG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: TCA cardiotoxicity is fast-sodium-channel-blockade-driven. QRS >100 ms predicts seizures, QRS >160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia. Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg IV bolus is first-line, repeated to narrow QRS <100 ms and support blood pressure.
key_points: QRS >100 ms: give sodium bicarbonate
Terminal R wave aVR >3 mm is a supportive marker
Avoid flumazenil, class Ia/Ic antiarrhythmics, physostigmine
Intralipid is rescue for refractory cardiotoxicity
explanation.pearls: In context: any TCA overdose with QRS >100 ms gets bicarbonate.

options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in TCA overdose (may lower seizure threshold and unmask arrhythmia); it does not address sodium channel blockade. (Source: PIC 13 11 26)

Class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics are contraindicated (worsen sodium channel blockade); lidocaine (class Ib) is second line if bicarbonate fails but not first line. Bicarbonate is the primary intervention. (Source: TG Toxicology)
Magnesium has a role for TCA-associated arrhythmias but is not the first-line therapy for QRS widening; sodium bicarbonate is. (Source: PIC 13 11 26)
Intralipid is a rescue therapy for severe cardiotoxicity unresponsive to sodium bicarbonate; not first-line for TCA overdose. (Source: PIC 13 11 26)

TCA cardiotoxicity is driven by fast sodium channel blockade; sodium bicarbonate (1-2 mmol/kg IV bolus) reverses the block by both sodium loading and alkalinisation, aiming to narrow QRS below 100 ms. Also indicated for TCA-associated hypotension and ventricular arrhythmia. (Source: TG Toxicology; PIC 13 11 26)

explanation.summary: Discontinuation syndrome is most marked with short half-life antidepressants (paroxetine, venlafaxine). Symptoms include flu-like features, dizziness, electric shock sensations, insomnia and irritability, typically within days of dose reduction, and are self-limiting.
key_points: Paroxetine and venlafaxine have the strongest discontinuation profile
Distinguish discontinuation (days, self-limiting, flu-like) from relapse (weeks, sustained low mood)
Fluoxetine cross-taper is a rescue strategy for difficult tapers
Slow taper over at least 4 weeks (often longer) is standard
explanation.pearls: In context: never stop paroxetine abruptly; taper over weeks.

options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of paroxetine (a short half-life SSRI with strong discontinuation profile) commonly causes distressing discontinuation symptoms; gradual taper is standard. (Source: TG Psychotropic; AMH)
Cross-taper via fluoxetine can be used for difficult cases but is not first line; a paroxetine taper is usually sufficient and simpler for the patient. (Source: TG Psychotropic)
Discontinuation symptoms on missed doses are pharmacological, not evidence of dependence or need for continued treatment; recurrence risk is a separate consideration. (Source: Australian Prescriber)
A 2-week rapid taper is often too fast for paroxetine and provokes marked discontinuation symptoms; a longer taper (typically 4+ weeks) is standard. (Source: TG Psychotropic)

Paroxetine has a short half-life (~24 h) and strong discontinuation syndrome; gradual taper over weeks reduces symptoms. Discontinuation vs relapse can be distinguished by timing (discontinuation within days, self-limiting) and symptom pattern (flu-like, dizziness, electric shock sensations). (Source: TG Psychotropic; AMH)

explanation.summary: Risperidone, amisulpride and paliperidone are the most prolactin-elevating antipsychotics. Aripiprazole (partial D2 agonist) is the reliable low-prolactin choice and can be used as switch or adjunct to lower prolactin. Cabergoline risks psychiatric destabilisation in schizophrenia.
key_points: High-prolactin: risperidone, paliperidone, amisulpride, haloperidol
Low-prolactin: aripiprazole, quetiapine
Symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia: switch to aripiprazole preferred
Avoid dopamine agonists in schizophrenia unless specialist-guided
explanation.pearls: In context: symptomatic prolactin rise on risperidone -> aripiprazole switch.

options.rationale: Dopamine agonists can precipitate psychotic relapse in schizophrenia and are not first line for antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia; switching antipsychotic is preferred. (Source: RANZCP; TG Psychotropic)
Sustained hyperprolactinaemia is associated with hypogonadism, reduced bone mineral density and infertility; it warrants intervention when symptomatic. (Source: Australian Prescriber)

Olanzapine causes mild-moderate prolactin elevation (less than risperidone but not neutral); abrupt switch risks psychiatric destabilisation. Aripiprazole is the more reliable prolactin-lowering choice. (Source: TG Psychotropic; RANZCP)

Aripiprazole is a partial D2 agonist and consistently lowers prolactin; it is the preferred switch or adjunct in antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia with clinical impact. Cross-titration under psychiatric supervision preserves efficacy while addressing prolactin. (Source: RANZCP; TG Psychotropic)
Dose reduction may modestly reduce prolactin but risks loss of efficacy and does not reliably resolve symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia; switch to aripiprazole is preferred. (Source: RANZCP)

explanation.summary: Depot antipsychotic initiation varies by agent. Paliperidone palmitate 1-monthly uses a loading regimen (150 mg day 1, 100 mg day 8, both deltoid) that removes the need for oral overlap. Most other depots (risperidone LAI, flupentixol decanoate, zuclopenthixol decanoate) require oral overlap of 3-4 weeks. Aripiprazole LAI requires 14 days of oral aripiprazole overlap.
key_points: Paliperidone palmitate 1-monthly: 150 mg deltoid day 1, 100 mg deltoid day 8, no oral overlap needed
Risperidone LAI: 3-week oral overlap while depot levels establish
Aripiprazole LAI: 14 days oral aripiprazole overlap
3-monthly paliperidone palmitate only after 4 months stable on 1-monthly product
explanation.pearls: In context: check the specific depot's oral overlap requirement; paliperidone palmitate is a rare no-overlap exception because of its loading regimen.

options.rationale: Standard paliperidone palmitate initiation uses deltoid (not gluteal) loading with the specific 150/100 mg two-dose regimen; oral overlap is not required if the loading is followed. Also, monthly monotherapy without loading gives sub-therapeutic levels initially. (Source: TGA paliperidone palmitate PI)

Switching agents when the patient has been well controlled on paliperidone loses drug continuity; haloperidol decanoate carries higher EPS risk. Not the best approach when a matched depot exists. (Source: RANZCP; AMH)
Single-dose loading is not the approved paliperidone palmitate 1-monthly regimen; two-dose loading (150 mg day 1, 100 mg day 8) is required. (Source: TGA paliperidone palmitate PI)
The 3-monthly formulation is only used after at least 4 months of stable dosing on 1-monthly paliperidone palmitate, not as an initial depot start. (Source: TGA paliperidone palmitate PI)

TGA-approved initiation for paliperidone palmitate 1-monthly uses a two-injection loading regimen (150 mg IM deltoid day 1, 100 mg IM deltoid day 8) which achieves therapeutic levels quickly enough that oral overlap is not required. This is a distinguishing feature versus most other depot antipsychotics which do require oral overlap. (Source: TGA paliperidone palmitate PI; TG Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: In alcohol withdrawal complicated by significant hepatic impairment, glucuronidated benzodiazepines without active metabolites (oxazepam, lorazepam) are chosen; symptom-triggered CIWA-Ar-guided dosing is standard.
key_points: Child-Pugh B/C -> oxazepam or lorazepam (glucuronidation)
Preserved hepatic function -> diazepam loading is preferred
Symptom-triggered dosing beats fixed dosing on cumulative dose
Parenteral thiamine before glucose to prevent Wernicke
Target CIWA-Ar under 10
explanation.pearls: In context: the mnemonic LOT (Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam) marks the glucuronidated benzodiazepines safest in liver failure.

sources.label: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Diazepam has active metabolites cleared by hepatic CYP oxidation; in Child-Pugh B cirrhosis this drives oversedation and hepatic encephalopathy. Oxazepam or lorazepam (glucuronidated) is preferred (Source: eTG Addiction).
Chlordiazepoxide is long-acting and oxidatively metabolised; accumulation in cirrhosis is problematic and it is not on the AU first-line list (Source: AMH).

In significant hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B/C) the recommended benzodiazepines are those metabolised by phase II glucuronidation and lacking active metabolites - oxazepam (or lorazepam). Symptom-triggered dosing to CIWA-Ar is preferred over fixed schedules to reduce cumulative dose.
