Oxazepam 15-30 mg 2-hourly to a CIWA-Ar target of under 10 is standard (Source: NSW Health D and A Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines; eTG Addiction).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: IV midazolam is short-acting with active hydroxymetabolites; reserved for ICU-level severe withdrawal or delirium tremens, not ward CIWA-guided care (Source: eTG Addiction).
Clonazepam is long half-life and hepatically oxidised without a specific role in AU withdrawal protocols; risks accumulation in Child-Pugh B (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Delirium tremens emerges 48-96 hours from last drink with autonomic hyperactivity, confusion, hallucinations. Management is aggressive symptom-triggered diazepam loading plus Wernicke-treatment-dose parenteral thiamine and magnesium correction.
key_points: Withdrawal seizure peaks 12-48 h, DTs 48-96 h, Wernicke any time in malnourished
DTs mortality untreated up to 15 percent, treated under 5 percent
Wernicke treatment dose thiamine = 500 mg IV TDS for 2-3 days
Magnesium is required for benzodiazepine and thiamine action
Antipsychotics adjunctive only, never first-line in DTs
explanation.pearls: In context: any at-risk patient with confusion, ataxia or ophthalmoplegia gets Wernicke-treatment-dose thiamine (500 mg IV TDS) - the prophylactic dose (300 mg IV daily) is inadequate for suspected active Wernicke.

sources.label: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Fixed-dose escalation is too slow for established delirium tremens with CIWA-Ar 26 and haemodynamic instability; symptom-triggered loading with larger diazepam boluses is required (Source: eTG Addiction).

Antipsychotics do not treat GABAergic withdrawal, lower seizure threshold, and delay definitive benzodiazepine loading; may be added later for persistent agitation once benzodiazepine loaded (Source: eTG Addiction).

This is established delirium tremens (timing 48-96 hours, confusion, hallucinations, autonomic hyperactivity, CIWA-Ar >=20). AU management is aggressive diazepam loading titrated to a CIWA target under 10, with parenteral thiamine at Wernicke-treatment dose 500 mg IV TDS for 2-3 days given the pancreatitis-driven malnutrition risk and hypomagnesaemia correction because magnesium is a cofactor for thiamine-dependent enzymes and benzodiazepine efficacy (Source: eTG Addiction; NSW Health D and A Withdrawal Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Timing (day 3, last drink 68 hours), CIWA-Ar 26, autonomic hyperactivity and normal CT plus absence of meningism make CNS infection unlikely; treat withdrawal first (Source: eTG Neurology).
Phenytoin does not prevent alcohol withdrawal seizures - benzodiazepines do. Phenytoin has a specific indication only if a coexisting seizure disorder is being covered (Source: eTG Neurology).

explanation.summary: Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy needs high-dose parenteral thiamine (500 mg IV TDS for 2-3 days), given before any carbohydrate load. Magnesium is a required cofactor and should be corrected.
key_points: Classical triad: confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia (all three in only 10 percent)
Treatment dose: 500 mg IV TDS x 2-3 days
Prophylactic dose (300 mg IV daily) is not enough for active Wernicke
Thiamine before glucose (glucose-first can precipitate Wernicke)
Magnesium is a thiamine-enzyme cofactor - correct alongside
explanation.pearls: In context: any at-risk patient with even one Wernicke feature earns treatment-dose thiamine; the diagnosis is clinical and treatment cannot wait for MRI.

options.rationale: 100 mg IM is a prophylactic-only dose; a patient with the Wernicke triad requires the Wernicke-treatment dose (500 mg IV TDS x 2-3 days) which produces substantially higher CSF concentrations (Source: eTG Neurology).

The triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia (nystagmus counts) and ataxia is presumed Wernicke encephalopathy until proven otherwise. AU guidance is high-dose parenteral thiamine 500 mg IV TDS for 2-3 days, then step-down to 300 mg IV daily for a further 3-5 days, then oral 100 mg TDS. Magnesium is a cofactor and should be corrected. Any carbohydrate load must follow, not precede, thiamine (Source: eTG Neurology; RANZCP Wernicke position statement).
Administering carbohydrate before parenteral thiamine in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy; thiamine must precede glucose (Source: eTG Neurology).
Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed in this population and inadequate for suspected acute Wernicke; parenteral route is required initially (Source: eTG Neurology).
The clinical picture is not a seizure; benzodiazepines do not treat Wernicke and delay definitive thiamine (Source: eTG Neurology).

explanation.summary: In treatment-naive opioid use disorder without contraindications, buprenorphine-naloxone is first-line where early take-aways are needed and where children in the home make diversion prevention important. Methadone is favoured when higher potency, sedation, or full-agonist coverage is needed (severe dependence, existing methadone tolerance, pregnancy is a nuanced discussion).
key_points: Buprenorphine-naloxone: safer overdose profile, faster take-away schedule
Methadone: full agonist, longer supervised phase, QT and interaction risk
Mono-buprenorphine indications: pregnancy, naloxone hypersensitivity
Depot buprenorphine (Buvidal) after SL stabilisation typically
Confirm objective withdrawal (COWS >=12) before first buprenorphine dose
explanation.pearls: In context: PBS Section 100 lists methadone syrup, sublingual buprenorphine, buprenorphine-naloxone, and depot buprenorphine for OUD; the choice hinges on lifestyle, safety-critical work, home environment, and drug-drug interactions.

options.rationale: Methadone requires prolonged supervised dosing (typically 3+ months of stability) before take-aways, and QT-prolonging risk profile is less favourable here. Buprenorphine-naloxone has a better take-away trajectory in a young worker with children in the home (Source: RACGP MATOD; National Guidelines for MATOD).

Mono-product buprenorphine is reserved for pregnancy or documented naloxone hypersensitivity; naloxone-combined product is preferred to reduce injection diversion, especially with children in the home (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD).

Buprenorphine-naloxone is preferred first-line in the setting of a young worker who wants early take-aways, has children in the home (naloxone reduces IV diversion risk), and has no contraindication. The National Guidelines for MATOD support quicker take-away schedules on buprenorphine-naloxone than on methadone. Start day 1 dose 4 mg after objective withdrawal has begun (COWS >=12) to reduce precipitated-withdrawal risk (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD; RACGP).
Oral naltrexone has poor adherence and high overdose-on-relapse risk after detox; not first-line in daily heroin dependence per AU guidelines (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD).

Depot buprenorphine is a reasonable option but AU practice usually stabilises on sublingual buprenorphine-naloxone first before conversion to depot; loading straight to depot in a treatment-naive patient risks precipitated withdrawal management complexity (Source: RACGP MATOD).

explanation.summary: Micro-induction (Bernese method) allows transition from methadone to buprenorphine without a symptomatic withdrawal window by starting very-low-dose buprenorphine alongside continued full agonist and titrating up over days.
key_points: Standard induction: stop full agonist, wait COWS >=12 (72-96 h)
Micro-induction: overlap tiny buprenorphine doses with full agonist, double every 1-2 days
Rationale: buprenorphine slow off-rate at mu allows gradual displacement
Stop full agonist once buprenorphine ~8-12 mg
Depot buprenorphine requires prior SL stabilisation from full agonist
explanation.pearls: In context: micro-induction protocols are increasingly the AU standard for methadone-to-buprenorphine switching in patients who cannot afford a withdrawal window (parenting, working, chronic pain).

sources.label: AChAM Australasian Chapter of Addiction Medicine

options.rationale: Standard induction from methadone requires 72-96 h wait and produces a substantial withdrawal window, which she cannot accommodate as sole carer. Micro-induction is the alternative (Source: RACGP MATOD).

Simple methadone dose reduction does not lower the mu-agonist ceiling enough to avoid precipitated withdrawal at a buprenorphine 8 mg dose; risks the exact adverse event the patient wants to avoid (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD).
Precipitating a full antagonist reversal to shorten the switch is dangerous and not endorsed by any Australian guideline; it causes severe iatrogenic withdrawal (Source: AMH).

Depot induction from methadone requires prior sublingual stabilisation or a micro-induction protocol; direct depot induction from a full agonist risks precipitated withdrawal and cannot be reversed until the depot dissipates (Source: RACGP MATOD).

The Bernese-style micro-induction (increasing sub-therapeutic buprenorphine while the full agonist remains on board) exploits buprenorphine's slow off-rate at the mu-opioid receptor to displace methadone gradually without a precipitated-withdrawal spike. AU addiction services increasingly offer this to patients who cannot tolerate a standard washout window. Once buprenorphine reaches approximately 8-12 mg daily, methadone can be stopped (Source: RACGP MATOD; AChAM position statement).
source_refs: AChAM Australasian Chapter of Addiction Medicine

explanation.summary: Naltrexone (mu-antagonist) suits reward-driven cravings; acamprosate (glutamatergic) suits maintenance abstinence with protracted withdrawal; disulfiram is aversive and requires supervision and adherence.
key_points: Naltrexone: reward-craving phenotype, no opioid use, no severe liver disease
Acamprosate: negative-reinforcement drinking, maintain abstinence
Disulfiram: aversive; requires supervision and adherence
Baclofen: reserved for severe liver disease or first-line failures
All AU AUD pharmacotherapies are PBS authority-required
explanation.pearls: In context: "first drink is the best drink" is a mnemonic for reward-craving that flags naltrexone; "drinking to feel normal" flags acamprosate.

options.rationale: Acamprosate is a glutamatergic modulator best suited to sustaining abstinence where protracted withdrawal and negative-reinforcement drinking predominate; would also be a reasonable second-line here but naltrexone matches her reward-craving phenotype better (Source: RACGP AUD).
Disulfiram produces an aversive reaction on drinking - she has expressly ruled this out; requires supervised administration and high adherence, less effective in unselected settings (Source: NHMRC).
Baclofen is a second- or third-line option in AUD, considered mainly when first-line agents are contraindicated (e.g. significant liver disease); not first-line here (Source: NHMRC).

Naltrexone is a mu-opioid antagonist that reduces the reward-response to alcohol; it is first-line where craving and reward drive drinking ("first drink is the best drink"). No opioid contraindication, no significant liver disease, and no aversive-reaction concern make it the best fit. AU listing on PBS is authority-required for AUD (Source: RACGP AUD guideline; AMH; NHMRC).
Topiramate is off-label in AUD in AU and reserved as later-line; cognitive side effects can affect a client-facing role (Source: NHMRC).

explanation.summary: AU acute severe behavioural disturbance guidelines recommend IM droperidol 10 mg as the first-line sedating agent for stimulant intoxication when IV access is not feasible.
key_points: Droperidol 10 mg IM first-line in AU for severe agitation
Olanzapine IM alternative, but avoid IM benzo within 60 min
Midazolam IM alternative but shorter and more respiratory depression
Ketamine reserved for refractory extreme cases
Physical monitoring: SpO2, HR, BP, temp every 15 min post-sedation
explanation.pearls: In context: rehydration, active cooling, and workup for rhabdomyolysis and hyponatraemia sit alongside sedation - agitation is only the presenting problem.

sources.label: NSW Health Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance guideline

options.rationale: Olanzapine IM is a reasonable alternative but not first-line in AU stimulant intoxication guidelines; must not be combined with parenteral benzodiazepines within 60 min because of respiratory depression risk (Source: eTG Psychotropic).
Midazolam alone is an alternative but has shorter duration and more respiratory depression risk; droperidol is preferred first-line in AU stimulant agitation (Source: NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance guideline

options.rationale: Haloperidol-promethazine combination is a NICE regimen; AU practice favours droperidol monotherapy for stimulant agitation (Source: NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance guideline

options.rationale: AU acute behavioural disturbance guidelines (NSW MoH, Queensland Health) endorse droperidol 10 mg IM as first-line for severe stimulant-related agitation where IV access is not possible. Onset is 10-15 minutes and safety profile (including QT concerns) is well-characterised at this dose (Source: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance).
source_refs: NSW Health Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance guideline

options.rationale: Ketamine is reserved for extreme agitation refractory to first-line droperidol/midazolam or where retrieval-medicine protocols apply; not first-line ward-ED practice (Source: NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance guideline

explanation.summary: Methamphetamine-induced psychosis that resolves rapidly with abstinence is managed with 3-6 months of antipsychotic cover then staged taper, plus AOD relapse-prevention work; lifelong therapy is not indicated unless recurrence off substances occurs.
key_points: Substance-induced psychosis resolves within days-weeks of abstinence
Primary schizophrenia symptoms persist despite documented abstinence
3-6 months antipsychotic cover then staged taper is standard
AOD referral is core, not adjunctive
Recurrence off substances suggests primary psychotic disorder emerging
explanation.pearls: In context: 20-30 percent of meth-induced psychosis eventually converts to a primary psychotic disorder, so continued monitoring post-taper is essential.

sources.label: RANZCP Australian and New Zealand clinical practice guideline for schizophrenia

options.rationale: Lifelong antipsychotic and mood stabiliser are not indicated for a clearly substance-induced psychotic episode with rapid resolution on abstinence (Source: RANZCP guidelines).
source_refs: RANZCP Australian and New Zealand clinical practice guideline for schizophrenia

options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after only 7 days risks relapse of positive symptoms during the vulnerable abstinence window; a staged taper over months is preferred (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

AU practice (RANZCP addiction faculty, eTG Psychotropic) for substance-induced psychosis that clearly resolves with abstinence is to continue the antipsychotic for 3-6 months while symptoms stabilise, then taper against ongoing abstinence, coupled with AOD engagement for relapse prevention. Prolonged empiric antipsychotic risks metabolic burden without benefit; premature cessation risks relapse and evolution to primary psychotic disorder (Source: RANZCP; eTG Psychotropic; RANZCP Addiction Faculty).
Clozapine requires two documented antipsychotic failures at adequate dose/duration; the picture here is responsive substance-induced psychosis, not treatment resistance (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Australian and New Zealand clinical practice guideline for schizophrenia

options.rationale: LAI is reserved for confirmed primary psychotic disorders with poor oral adherence; premature use in likely substance-induced psychosis is not supported (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Australian and New Zealand clinical practice guideline for schizophrenia

explanation.summary: GHB overdose has no reversal agent; management is supportive with airway monitoring and observation for spontaneous emergence, typically within 2-4 hours. Intubate only if apnoea or loss of protective reflexes.
key_points: No reversal agent for GHB (GABA-B and specific GHB receptors)
Typical duration 2-4 hours
Airway attendance and capnography, not automatic intubation
Naloxone and flumazenil have no role and risk confounding
Screen for co-ingestants (ethanol, stimulants, benzos)
explanation.pearls: In context: patients often emerge suddenly and combatively from GHB coma - staff and equipment must be prepared for that transition.

options.rationale: GHB overdose has no reversal agent. The mainstay is intensive supportive care in a monitored resuscitation bay with continuous SpO2 and capnography, airway attendance ready to intubate if apnoea or loss of gag develops, and observation until sedation resolves (typically within 2-4 hours). Do NOT give naloxone or flumazenil (no benefit, risk of confounding). Consider intubation only if apnoea, aspiration, or loss of airway reflexes (Source: eTG Toxicology; NSW Poisons Information Centre).
Naloxone does not reverse GHB (which acts via GABA-B and endogenous GHB receptors, not mu-opioid); no reversal agent exists (Source: eTG Toxicology).
Flumazenil reverses only benzodiazepines and carries seizure risk in undifferentiated overdose; not indicated for GHB (Source: eTG Toxicology).

RSI is not automatically required at GCS 9 with a preserved gag and stable vitals; GHB coma typically resolves within 2-4 hours and premature intubation adds ventilator-associated risks (Source: eTG Toxicology).
Charcoal in a patient with reduced GCS and no protected airway risks aspiration; GHB is also rapidly absorbed and decontamination is not effective 45 minutes post-ingestion (Source: eTG Toxicology).

explanation.summary: MDMA-induced severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (Na 118, seizure) from SIADH plus water loading is treated with 3 percent saline boluses aiming to raise Na 4-6 mmol/L in the first hour, capped at 10 mmol/L over 24 h. Serotonin syndrome requires neuromuscular hyperactivity that is absent here.
key_points: MDMA -> SIADH + intentional water loading -> hyponatraemia
Hypertonic saline for symptomatic severe hyponatraemia (Na <125 with seizure/coma)
Raise Na 4-6 mmol/L in first hour, cap at 10 mmol/L over 24 h
Serotonin syndrome triad: mental state, autonomic, neuromuscular
Isotonic saline worsens SIADH-driven hyponatraemia
explanation.pearls: In context: young women are disproportionately affected because of smaller total body water and the SIADH effect of MDMA compounded by well-meaning water loading.

options.rationale: This is symptomatic severe hyponatraemia (Na 118, seizure) caused by MDMA-induced SIADH plus large free-water intake. AU acute severe symptomatic hyponatraemia guidance is 100-150 mL 3 percent saline IV over 10 min, repeated once if needed, aiming to raise Na by 4-6 mmol/L in the first hour to control seizure; total 24-hour rise capped at 10 mmol/L to avoid osmotic demyelination. Fluid restriction alone is inadequate when seizing (Source: eTG Endocrinology; eTG Toxicology).

Serotonin syndrome requires the triad of altered mental state, autonomic hyperactivity, and neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia, rigidity). She has none of the neuromuscular features - this is MDMA-induced hyponatraemia (SIADH), not serotonin syndrome (Source: eTG Toxicology).

In SIADH, isotonic saline can paradoxically worsen hyponatraemia because free water is retained while sodium is excreted; hypertonic saline is required for symptomatic severe hyponatraemia (Source: eTG Endocrinology).
Fluid restriction is chronic-SIADH management but is inadequate for acute symptomatic severe hyponatraemia with a seizure - hypertonic saline is required first (Source: eTG Endocrinology).
Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia and severe NMS with hyperthermia and rigidity - neither is present here (Source: eTG Toxicology).

explanation.summary: Cannabis use disorder in AU is managed first-line with CBT and motivational interviewing; there is no PBS-listed pharmacotherapy.
key_points: CBT + MI is first-line
No PBS-listed pharmacotherapy for CUD in AU
Withdrawal peaks day 2-6, resolves ~2 weeks
Sleep advice and time-limited non-benzo sleep support if needed
Screen for co-occurring depression, anxiety, psychosis
explanation.pearls: In context: chronic high-potency THC use is a modifiable risk factor for psychotic illness in young adults - psychoeducation is part of care.

sources.label: RACGP guidance on cannabis use disorder

options.rationale: Naltrexone has no established indication for cannabis use disorder (Source: AMH).
N-acetylcysteine has mixed evidence in cannabis use disorder in adolescents; not first-line and not PBS-listed for this indication in AU (Source: AMH).
Substitution therapy for cannabis is not an AU-approved treatment for cannabis use disorder outside research settings (Source: RACGP).
source_refs: RACGP guidance on cannabis use disorder

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not indicated for cannabis withdrawal, carry dependence risk, and do not address the disorder (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

Australian guidance (RACGP, National Cannabis Prevention and Information Centre, eTG) endorses CBT and motivational interviewing as first-line for cannabis use disorder. No pharmacotherapy is PBS-listed for cannabis use disorder; adjunctive short-term sleep advice and monitoring for withdrawal is standard (Source: RACGP; eTG Psychotropic).
source_refs: RACGP guidance on cannabis use disorder

explanation.summary: Long-term benzodiazepine deprescribing uses equivalent-dose diazepam substitution and slow taper (5-10 percent every 1-2 weeks) alongside CBT-I; abrupt cessation risks seizures.
key_points: Temazepam 20 mg ~= diazepam 10 mg
Reduce by 5-10 percent every 1-2 weeks, slower at the end
Diazepam long half-life smooths withdrawal
CBT-I is core alongside pharmacological taper
Never abrupt-stop after prolonged use - seizure risk
explanation.pearls: In context: elderly women on long-term benzodiazepines are a common deprescribing cohort; falls, cognitive impairment and MVA risk make sustained withdrawal worthwhile.

options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after 12 years risks severe withdrawal (anxiety, insomnia rebound, seizures); tapering is required (Source: AMH; RACGP).
Zopiclone is not a taper-friendly substitute; it has its own dependence potential and swapping does not enable a smooth withdrawal (Source: AMH).
Flumazenil infusions for accelerated benzodiazepine detox are experimental, not AU standard, and carry seizure risk (Source: eTG Toxicology).
Pregabalin carries its own dependence and misuse risk in older adults; not routinely used to cover benzodiazepine withdrawal in AU (Source: AMH).

AU deprescribing guidance (RACGP; NSW Health) is to substitute the short/intermediate-acting benzodiazepine (temazepam 20 mg ~= diazepam 10 mg) with equivalent diazepam and reduce by 5-10 percent of the starting dose every 1-2 weeks, slower toward the end. Diazepam's long half-life smooths withdrawal. Non-pharmacological insomnia strategies (CBT-I) are co-delivered (Source: RACGP; NSW Health).

explanation.summary: Lie/Bet is the recommended 2-item brief screen for problem gambling in AU primary care; a positive answer to either question prompts full assessment (e.g. PGSI, DSM-5-TR criteria).
key_points: Lie/Bet: 2 items, positive on either -> full assessment
PGSI (9 items) for severity classification
Naltrexone has some evidence in gambling disorder (off-label)
First-line management is psychological therapy (CBT)
Screen for depression, alcohol use disorder, suicidality co-occurrence
explanation.pearls: In context: gambling disorder is a DSM-5-TR behavioural addiction that clusters with substance use disorders, depression, and suicide - screening the cluster together is efficient.

options.rationale: PHQ-9 screens for depression, not gambling; useful adjunct but not the primary tool here (Source: RACGP).

The Lie/Bet screen is a validated 2-item screen for problem gambling that AU primary care resources (RACGP, Gambling Help Online) recommend as the first-pass tool: (1) Have you ever lied to people important to you about how much you gambled? (2) Have you ever felt the need to bet more and more money? A yes to either warrants full assessment (e.g. PGSI) (Source: RACGP; Gambling Help Online).
AUDIT-C is an alcohol tool; useful comorbidity screen, not primary here (Source: RACGP).
K10 measures nonspecific psychological distress; complements but does not replace a gambling-specific screen (Source: RACGP).
GAD-7 measures anxiety severity; will not identify gambling disorder (Source: RACGP).

explanation.summary: Alcohol and benzodiazepine (both GABA-A) detoxes are managed in parallel with a single diazepam-based regimen; meth needs psychosocial support, not pharmacological detox.
key_points: Alcohol + benzo = single GABAergic detox with diazepam
Meth has no pharmacological detox pathway (dopaminergic, not GABA)
CIWA-Ar covers alcohol component; scheduled diazepam covers benzo taper
Rehab handoff post-detox is core, not optional
Splitting cross-tolerant detoxes across admissions is unsafe
explanation.pearls: In context: identifying which of a patient's substances actually have physiological withdrawal (alcohol, benzos, opioids, GHB) versus psychological withdrawal (cocaine, methamphetamine, cannabis) drives the sequencing.

sources.label: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Meth has no physiological withdrawal syndrome requiring pharmacological detox; sequencing alcohol/benzodiazepine after "meth detox" wastes time and delays the highest-risk withdrawal (Source: eTG Addiction).
Splitting cross-tolerant GABAergic detox across admissions risks rebound and undermines the planned rehab pathway; parallel management is preferred (Source: NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Ongoing heavy alcohol use during a 6-month outpatient benzo taper is high risk and does not accomplish the goal of a single supervised withdrawal (Source: NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Alcohol and benzodiazepine both act at GABA-A; they are managed in parallel with a single diazepam-based taper that first covers alcohol withdrawal symptoms (CIWA-Ar) and then transitions to a scheduled diazepam taper for the benzodiazepine component. Methamphetamine does not have a physiological withdrawal syndrome needing pharmacotherapy; psychosocial support (motivational interviewing, sleep hygiene) is the mainstay. Prior withdrawal seizure raises the priority for effective GABAergic cover (Source: NSW Health D and A Withdrawal; eTG Addiction).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Requiring pre-abstinence to access a supervised withdrawal service is not AU practice and creates unnecessary access barriers (Source: eTG Addiction).

explanation.summary: Stable opioid substitution in pregnancy is continued (not tapered), with dose adjustment as pregnancy metabolism accelerates and neonatal team involvement for NAS at delivery. Switching stable methadone antenatally is not routine.
key_points: Continue stable methadone through pregnancy; anticipate 3rd trimester dose increase or split dosing
Buprenorphine mono-product preferred over combo in pregnancy
Do NOT taper off maintenance antenatally - relapse and overdose risk
NAS prepared for at delivery, not prevented by ceasing maintenance
Breastfeeding compatible with methadone and buprenorphine
explanation.pearls: In context: benzodiazepine co-use in pregnancy is separately deprescribed via slow diazepam taper, alcohol is abstinence, and stimulant co-use is managed psychosocially - each substance in a polysubstance-using pregnant woman needs its own plan.

options.rationale: AU guidance (National Guidelines for MATOD, RANZCOG) is that stable methadone is continued at the effective dose during pregnancy, with dose adjustments (often split-dosing or dose increases in the third trimester) as metabolism accelerates. Switching stable methadone to buprenorphine-naloxone antenatally is not routinely done because of switching-related destabilisation risk. Buprenorphine (mono-product) is preferred over buprenorphine-naloxone in pregnancy where a NEW start is planned. NAS is managed at delivery with the neonatal team (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD; RANZCOG).

Tapering opioid substitution off during pregnancy is not recommended - it carries relapse and overdose risk that far exceeds any theoretical benefit of avoiding neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS). Continue maintenance (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD; RANZCOG).

Switching a stable pregnant patient off methadone risks destabilisation; if a switch is chosen, mono-buprenorphine (not the naloxone-combined product) is the AU-preferred pregnancy product (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD).
Late-pregnancy cessation is associated with relapse and preterm delivery risk; maintenance continued to delivery with neonatal team preparation is standard (Source: RANZCOG).
Naltrexone maintenance in pregnancy is not AU-standard and detoxification during pregnancy is high-risk; maintenance is preferred (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD).

explanation.summary: NHMRC 2020 alcohol guidelines: healthy adults no more than 10 standard drinks per week AND no more than 4 on any one day; pregnancy and under-18 = zero.
key_points: 10 SD/week AND 4 SD/session for healthy adults
Pregnancy: no alcohol
Under 18: no alcohol
1 AU standard drink = 10 g ethanol
Guidelines are population risk-reduction, not safe-use thresholds
explanation.pearls: In context: brief interventions in general practice for above-guideline drinkers deliver measurable reductions and are AU-funded via the mental health care plan / chronic disease framework.

options.rationale: Weekly total of 10 SD sits at the cap, not above it; only per-session limit is breached (Source: NHMRC 2020).

The NHMRC 2020 Australian guidelines to reduce health risks from drinking alcohol recommend healthy adults drink no more than 10 standard drinks per week AND no more than 4 standard drinks on any one day. Her weekly total (10) sits at the cap, but 5 drinks in one session breaches the single-session limit (Source: NHMRC 2020).
Per-session limit is 4 SD; 5 SD per session exceeds it (Source: NHMRC 2020).
Weekly limit is 10 SD; her total sits at the cap; per-session is the breach (Source: NHMRC 2020).
The NHMRC guideline is expressed in Australian standard drinks (10 g ethanol per standard drink), not grams (Source: NHMRC 2020).

explanation.summary: TCA overdose causes an anticholinergic toxidrome plus fast-sodium channel blockade producing QRS widening, aVR terminal R wave over 3 mm, seizure, hypotension and ventricular arrhythmia. Sodium bicarbonate is the antidote because it narrows QRS by increasing extracellular sodium and pH-dependent unbinding from the sodium channel. Target pH 7.50 to 7.55 titrated to QRS narrowing.
key_points: QRS over 100 ms or aVR terminal R over 3 mm predicts seizure and VT
Bicarbonate 1-2 mmol per kg IV bolus then infusion to pH 7.50 to 7.55
Physostigmine and class I/III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated
Charcoal within 1-2 hours only after airway protection; not a substitute for bicarbonate
explanation.pearls: The aVR terminal R wave over 3 mm is the QRS-independent marker that flips the case to bicarbonate before the QRS reaches 100 ms.

options.rationale: Charcoal is used within 1 to 2 hours of a potentially toxic ingestion if the airway is protected, but it is an adjunct - it does not treat the sodium channel blockade already causing QRS widening. Bicarbonate is the immediate life-saving intervention. (Source: eTG complete: TCA poisoning)

Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate seizure, bradyarrhythmia and asystole in the context of sodium channel blockade. It is used in pure anticholinergic toxidrome without cardiac conduction disturbance. (Source: eTG complete: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning)

QRS over 100 ms and terminal R wave in aVR over 3 mm are markers of TCA sodium channel blockade with risk of ventricular arrhythmia and seizure. Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol per kg IV bolus (roughly 100 mL of 8.4 percent) is antidotal and repeated to a target pH 7.50 to 7.55, with QRS narrowing as the endpoint. (Source: eTG complete: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning)

Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist and is not indicated in TCA overdose - it would not treat toxicity and risks precipitating seizure in mixed overdoses. (Source: eTG complete: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning)

Class III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated because they prolong QT and worsen conduction; class Ia and Ic are also contraindicated. Sodium bicarbonate is both antidotal and the correct rhythm treatment for TCA-induced wide complex tachycardia. (Source: eTG complete: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning)

explanation.summary: For a heavily dependent smoker (FTND 7 of 10) with stable schizophrenia, varenicline is first-line per RACGP because it has the highest cessation rate. EAGLES supports its safety in stable psychiatric illness. Behavioural support runs in parallel. Second-line agents are combination NRT and bupropion; nicotine vaping is reserved for those who fail approved pharmacotherapy.
key_points: Varenicline first-line for heavy dependence per RACGP
EAGLES trial reassures neuropsychiatric safety in stable psychiatric illness
Combination NRT (patch + short-acting) beats patch monotherapy at high dependence
Nicotine vaping is second-line, prescription only in AU
explanation.pearls: Stable schizophrenia is not a contraindication to varenicline - the historical black-box concern was diluted by EAGLES.

options.rationale: Varenicline is first-line for heavy smokers with high nicotine dependence per the RACGP guideline; it has the strongest quit rate at 12 weeks compared with NRT and bupropion. Prior concerns about neuropsychiatric adverse effects have been largely reassured by the EAGLES trial including in patients with stable psychiatric illness. Titration and early review are standard. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation guideline 2019)

Bupropion is second-line and is contraindicated or requires caution in patients with seizure risk, eating disorders, and MAOI use; olanzapine is not a contraindication but bupropion is less effective than varenicline as first-line in heavy dependence. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation guideline 2019)

Combination NRT (patch plus short-acting oral form) is more effective than monotherapy for heavy smokers; patch alone is inadequate at FTND 7. Varenicline still has the strongest evidence at this level of dependence. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation guideline 2019)

Nicotine vaping is second-line in the RACGP guideline reserved for patients who have failed or cannot tolerate approved pharmacotherapy (varenicline, NRT, bupropion). Regulatory access under prescription applies since 2024. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation guideline 2019)

Behavioural intervention combined with pharmacotherapy has superior quit rates versus behavioural alone. Stable schizophrenia is not a contraindication to varenicline; withholding pharmacotherapy on that basis is under-treatment. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation guideline 2019)

explanation.summary: For medically stable adolescents with anorexia nervosa, FBT (Maudsley model) is the first-line psychological intervention in AU per RANZCP and NEDC. FBT has three phases: parents take control of refeeding, staged handover of control, and adolescent development. CBT-E is the adult first-line and an adolescent alternative when FBT is not feasible. Medication has no first-line role in anorexia.
key_points: Adolescent anorexia first-line psychological therapy is FBT
Adult anorexia first-line is CBT-E, MANTRA, or SSCM
SSRIs do not restore weight in acute anorexia - reserve for persistent post-restoration depression
Refeeding syndrome risk requires phosphate, magnesium, potassium and thiamine monitoring
explanation.pearls: FBT is the AU first-line for adolescent anorexia when the parents are able to take charge of refeeding - do not default to individual CBT in this age group.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023
NEDC National Eating Disorders Collaboration guidelines

options.rationale: For adolescents with anorexia nervosa who are medically stable enough for outpatient care, FBT (Maudsley model) is the first-line psychological therapy per RANZCP Australian and NEDC guidelines. Parents take control of refeeding in phase 1, with staged transfer of control back to the adolescent through phases 2 and 3. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023

options.rationale: CBT-E is first-line for adults with eating disorders and is an alternative for adolescents where FBT is unavailable or unsuitable; in adolescents FBT has stronger evidence and is first-line per RANZCP. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023

options.rationale: IPT has some evidence in bulimia nervosa and MDD but is not first-line for anorexia in adolescents; FBT has the strongest evidence base in this age group. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023

options.rationale: SSRIs do not improve weight restoration or core anorexia symptoms in the acutely underweight state; they are considered only for persistent comorbid depression or anxiety after weight restoration. Fluoxetine is first-line for bulimia, not anorexia. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023

options.rationale: Olanzapine has modest evidence for weight gain in adults with severe anorexia but is not first-line psychological or pharmacological therapy in adolescents. It is not recommended by RANZCP as a first-line intervention. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Eating Disorders 2023

explanation.summary: MDMA plus SSRI creates a mixed picture: serotonin syndrome (hyperreflexia, clonus, hyperthermia, agitation, diaphoresis, hyperactive bowel sounds), plus SIADH with excess water intake causing dilutional hyponatraemia. In festival goers this hyponatraemia with encephalopathy is the leading cause of death and must be corrected first with hypertonic saline. Cooling, benzodiazepines and supportive care follow.
key_points: MDMA hyponatraemia is dilutional plus SIADH plus water intake - encephalopathy is the killer
Symptomatic hyponatraemia: 3 percent saline 150 mL IV over 15 min, repeatable to Na rise 4-6 mmol/L
Serotonin syndrome features - hyperreflexia, clonus, autonomic instability - present but not the immediate lethal issue here
Cyproheptadine and dantrolene are adjuncts, not first-line rescue
explanation.pearls: In an MDMA festival collapse, always check the sodium before you chase serotonin syndrome - dilutional hyponatraemia kills faster than clonus.

options.rationale: The most urgent life threat is severe hyponatraemia (Na 122 mmol/L) with encephalopathy from MDMA-induced SIADH and free water excess, at risk of cerebral oedema and seizure. eTG poisoning guidance for symptomatic hyponatraemia after MDMA is 3 percent saline 150 mL IV over 15 min, repeatable to a total sodium rise of 4-6 mmol/L in the first hour. Cyproheptadine and dantrolene address serotonin syndrome and hyperthermia but the sodium is the immediate killer. (Source: eTG complete: Amphetamine toxicity)

Cyproheptadine is an adjunct in serotonin syndrome but does not address the acute cerebral oedema from severe hyponatraemia which is the immediate life threat here. It also cannot be given orally to a confused patient safely. (Source: eTG complete: Serotonin syndrome)

Dantrolene is used in malignant hyperthermia and severe MDMA-related hyperthermia (over 39.5 C refractory to cooling); active external cooling, benzodiazepines and paralysis-plus-intubation are first-line and the hyponatraemia takes priority. (Source: eTG complete: Amphetamine toxicity)

Charcoal is not indicated 3 hours after MDMA ingestion in a confused patient without airway protection; adsorbent decontamination will not fix the sodium of 122 mmol/L. (Source: eTG complete: Amphetamine toxicity)

This is not NMS - the trigger is a serotonergic drug (MDMA plus SSRI), not a dopamine antagonist. Bromocriptine has no evidence in serotonin syndrome and is not the immediate life-saving intervention. (Source: eTG complete: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome)

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder is diagnosed when psychotic symptoms develop during or shortly after cannabis use, exceed intoxication effects, and cannot be better explained by a primary psychotic disorder. About 40-50 percent of cannabis-induced psychosis progresses to schizophrenia within 8 years, so structured follow up is critical, but the initial label should be substance-induced when the pattern fits. Short course low-dose antipsychotic plus cessation is the current standard.
key_points: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder: temporal link, exceeds intoxication, not better explained by primary
Schizophrenia requires 6 months of active plus prodromal features
40-50 percent conversion to schizophrenia within 8 years - structured follow up mandatory
Short course low-dose antipsychotic plus cessation is the standard first step
explanation.pearls: Do not label schizophrenia at 5 weeks with a temporally linked substance and prior self-resolving episode - the diagnosis matters for prognosis and prescribing years ahead.

sources.label: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders
DSM-5-TR criteria for substance-induced psychotic disorder

options.rationale: Schizophreniform requires 1 to 6 months of characteristic symptoms without full schizophrenia criteria. It is a possible differential but the temporal link to cannabis and prior resolution with cessation make cannabis-induced disorder the primary formulation now. (Source: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Schizophrenia diagnosis requires 6 months of active plus prodromal symptoms per DSM-5. His duration is 5 weeks with a temporally linked substance use and a prior episode that resolved with cessation. Premature schizophrenia labelling exposes him to indefinite antipsychotic treatment. (Source: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: DSM-5 cannabis-induced psychotic disorder is diagnosed when psychotic symptoms develop during or shortly after intoxication, exceed the expected effects of intoxication, and are not better explained by a primary psychotic disorder. Weekly progression across substance use, prior self-resolving episode with cessation, and negative family history support this over primary schizophrenia. Short course low-dose antipsychotic plus cessation support is standard; a diagnosis of schizophrenia requires 6 months of active plus prodromal features per DSM-5. (Source: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder requires less than 1 month duration; he is at 5 weeks so it does not fit. Observing without treatment for actively delusional symptoms with hallucinations is under-treatment; his agitation and delusions warrant a brief antipsychotic course. (Source: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires non-bizarre delusions without prominent hallucinations for at least 1 month, and functioning is largely preserved. His third-person auditory hallucinations and cannabis link do not fit. Pimozide is rarely used in AU practice. (Source: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG for schizophrenia and related disorders

explanation.summary: Treatment resistance has a definition that has to be met before it is declared: failure of at least two antipsychotics, each given at an adequate dose for at least six weeks, with adherence established rather than assumed. Checking adherence, substance use and the accuracy of the diagnosis comes first, because each is a commoner explanation of non-response than true resistance. Once resistance is established, clozapine is the treatment, and the evidence extends to schizoaffective disorder as well as schizophrenia. Australian practice starts it with slow titration, baseline and regular full blood counts for neutropenia, and monitoring for myocarditis in the first weeks, constipation, sedation and metabolic effects. In context: about a third of people with a schizophrenia-spectrum illness respond poorly to standard antipsychotics, and long delays before clozapine are associated with worse outcomes, so recognising the threshold promptly is the clinically useful skill.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Two adequate trials of different antipsychotics at therapeutic dose and duration with confirmed adherence define treatment resistance, and clozapine is the only agent with established superiority in that setting.
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.rationale: A third conventional antipsychotic trial adds little once two have failed, and delays clozapine. Switching agents is appropriate earlier in the sequence or when the problem is tolerability.
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.rationale: Combining antipsychotics increases adverse effects without convincing benefit and is considered only after an adequate clozapine trial has failed or clozapine is not tolerated.
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.rationale: Pushing beyond the effective dose range mainly adds sedation and metabolic burden. Dose escalation is reasonable only when the current dose is subtherapeutic.
An antidepressant is added for a depressive episode in schizoaffective disorder under mood stabiliser cover. Her mood is stable and the unresolved problem is psychosis.
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

explanation.summary: GHB overdose is characterised by rapid-onset coma from a small volume of clear liquid, bradycardia and hypothermia, preserved airway reflexes, and rapid spontaneous emergence within 20 to 40 minutes. There is no antidote; supportive care with airway protection and cardiac monitoring is standard. Do not use naloxone or flumazenil - both waste time and flumazenil can be harmful in mixed overdose.
key_points: GHB coma is typically rapid onset and offset within 20 to 40 minutes
Bradycardia and hypothermia are typical; pupils remain reactive
No antidote - supportive care with airway protection
Naloxone and flumazenil are not indicated; flumazenil may be harmful
explanation.pearls: The GHB fingerprint is rapid coma to rapid recovery from a small volume clear liquid, with reactive pupils and bradycardia - naloxone tempts you but is the wrong reflex.

options.rationale: His ethanol level is only 0.02 percent which cannot account for GCS 8; ethanol toxicity at this level does not cause coma. The rapid onset and offset pattern is inconsistent with ethanol. (Source: eTG complete: Alcohol intoxication)

Opioids typically cause pinpoint pupils (not 3 mm reactive), respiratory depression rather than bradycardia as the earliest finding, and do not spontaneously resolve within 20 to 40 minutes. Naloxone will fail to reverse GHB and would waste time. (Source: eTG complete: Opioid poisoning)

Flumazenil is contraindicated in overdose of unknown ingestion because it can precipitate seizures in mixed overdoses (particularly TCA or chronic benzo use). Benzodiazepine coma also does not typically cause this degree of rapid emergence. (Source: eTG complete: Benzodiazepine poisoning)

The GHB pattern is rapid-onset coma from a clear liquid drink 40 minutes prior, bradycardia (typical of GHB), preserved airway reflexes with pupillary reactivity and minimal ethanol, and characteristic rapid emergence in 20 to 40 minutes. There is no specific antidote; supportive care with airway protection and monitoring is standard; naloxone and flumazenil are ineffective. (Source: eTG complete: GHB toxicity)

Ketamine typically produces dissociative agitation, nystagmus, hypersalivation, tachycardia and hypertension, not bradycardia and unresponsiveness. His clinical pattern does not fit ketamine. (Source: eTG complete: Ketamine)

explanation.summary: Clozapine myocarditis characteristically occurs in the first 4-6 weeks of initiation with fever, tachycardia, raised troponin, raised BNP, ECG changes, and reduced left ventricular function on echocardiogram. Australian protocols mandate baseline and weekly troponin, BNP, and CRP for the first 4 weeks. Suspected myocarditis requires immediate clozapine cessation, cardiology review, echocardiogram, and cardiac MRI. Rechallenge is contraindicated in confirmed myocarditis. Dose reduction, continuing therapy, or empirical antibiotics all miss the diagnosis and delay definitive management.
key_points: Clozapine myocarditis window: first 4-6 weeks of initiation
Screen with troponin, BNP, CRP weekly for first 4 weeks in AU protocols
Confirmed or suspected myocarditis: immediate cessation, cardiology review
Rechallenge is contraindicated after myocarditis
explanation.pearls: Fever plus tachycardia plus raised troponin in weeks 2-4 of clozapine is myocarditis until proved otherwise; stop it immediately and never rechallenge.

options.rationale: The clinical picture (initiation window at 2-4 weeks, fever, tachycardia, raised troponin and BNP, ECG changes) is clozapine-induced myocarditis. Australian clozapine protocols mandate immediate cessation, cardiology review, echocardiogram, and cardiac MRI. Rechallenge is contraindicated. (Source: RANZCP clozapine safety guidelines)

Empirical antibiotics without evidence of infection miss the diagnosis of myocarditis and expose the patient to unnecessary antibiotics; continuing clozapine in confirmed or suspected myocarditis worsens outcomes. (Source: RANZCP clozapine safety guidelines)

Dose reduction is not adequate management of clozapine myocarditis; immediate cessation is required. Continuing at any dose risks progression to cardiogenic shock or death. (Source: RANZCP clozapine safety guidelines)

This is not acute coronary syndrome (young, no chest pain, widespread T-wave changes and initiation timing point to myocarditis). ACS pathway does not address clozapine cessation which is the priority. (Source: RANZCP clozapine safety guidelines)

Even brief re-exposure risks recurrence; the rule after suspected clozapine myocarditis is permanent cessation and formal cardiology assessment, not empirical rechallenge. (Source: RANZCP clozapine safety guidelines)

explanation.summary: This is acute-on-chronic lithium toxicity precipitated by gastroenteritis, ACE inhibitor introduction, and resulting acute kidney injury. EXTRIP criteria for haemodialysis: lithium above 4 mmol/L OR 2.5-4 mmol/L with severe neurological symptoms (impaired consciousness, seizures, life-threatening arrhythmia) OR acute kidney injury reducing clearance. This patient meets multiple criteria. Cease lithium and all nephrotoxins (including ACE inhibitor), commence isotonic fluid resuscitation, and arrange urgent haemodialysis with toxicology and renal input.
key_points: EXTRIP HD in lithium tox: level >4 OR 2.5-4 with severe symptoms OR AKI
Cease all nephrotoxins including ACE inhibitors and diuretics
Activated charcoal does NOT bind lithium
Chronic on acute toxicity has higher risk than pure acute at same level
explanation.pearls: Any lithium level above 2.5 mmol/L with AKI and neurotoxicity is a dialysis case; do not chase levels with fluid alone.

options.rationale: Lithium 3.6 mmol/L with acute-on-chronic toxicity, severe neurological symptoms, and acute kidney injury meets Extracorporeal Treatments in Poisoning workgroup (EXTRIP) criteria for haemodialysis. Fluid alone is insufficient with reduced clearance and continuing neurotoxicity. (Source: EXTRIP lithium recommendations)

EXTRIP criteria for haemodialysis in lithium toxicity: level above 4 mmol/L OR level 2.5-4 mmol/L with severe symptoms (impaired consciousness, seizures, life-threatening arrhythmia) OR acute kidney injury reducing lithium clearance. This patient meets all three qualifying features. Cease all nephrotoxins including ACE inhibitor. (Source: EXTRIP lithium recommendations)

Continuing lithium at any dose in the setting of acute toxicity with neurotoxicity and AKI is inappropriate. Dextrose is not the appropriate fluid and delaying dialysis in the face of neurological symptoms and reduced clearance risks preventable disability. (Source: EXTRIP lithium recommendations)
Activated charcoal does NOT bind lithium and has no role in lithium toxicity; using it delays definitive treatment. (Source: EXTRIP lithium recommendations)

Sodium polystyrene sulfonate has been trialled as gut binding but is inferior to dialysis in severe toxicity and carries GI necrosis risk. It is not standard first-line management. (Source: EXTRIP lithium recommendations)

explanation.summary: This is serotonin syndrome (SNRI plus tramadol, hyperreflexia with clonus greater in lower limbs, dilated pupils, agitation, diaphoresis, hyperthermia, tremor within days of adding the second serotonergic agent). NMS is distinguished by dopamine antagonist exposure, lead-pipe rigidity, marked CK rise, and pupil size usually normal. Management of serotonin syndrome is withdrawal of serotonergic agents, aggressive benzodiazepine sedation, cooling, and cyproheptadine 12 mg orally then 2 mg every 2 hours. Bromocriptine and dantrolene treat NMS not serotonin syndrome. Haloperidol can precipitate NMS.
key_points: Serotonin syndrome: clonus greater in lower limbs, dilated pupils, agitation, within days of new serotonergic drug
NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, marked CK rise, dopamine antagonist exposure, over days-weeks
Serotonin syndrome treatment: benzodiazepines plus cyproheptadine
NMS treatment: bromocriptine and dantrolene
explanation.pearls: Clonus that is greater in the lower limbs than upper limbs, plus dilated pupils, plus a recent serotonergic drug, is serotonin syndrome; give benzodiazepines and cyproheptadine, not bromocriptine.

options.rationale: Paracetamol does not treat serotonin syndrome or NMS; the temperature is centrally driven. Continuing serotonergic drugs is dangerous. Cooling is a supportive adjunct but must be paired with drug withdrawal and pharmacological treatment. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)

Bromocriptine and dantrolene are the NMS treatment. This patient has no antipsychotic exposure, has clonus and hyperreflexia (typical of serotonin syndrome), and lacks the lead-pipe rigidity and marked CK elevation typical of NMS. The clinical picture is serotonin syndrome, not NMS. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)

This is serotonin syndrome (Sternbach and Hunter criteria: recent addition of a second serotonergic agent, hyperreflexia with clonus greater in lower limbs, agitation, diaphoresis, hyperthermia, dilated pupils). Management is withdrawal of serotonergic agents, aggressive benzodiazepine sedation, cooling, and cyproheptadine 12 mg orally then 2 mg every 2 hours as an antihistamine and 5-HT2A antagonist. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)

Haloperidol can precipitate NMS in someone already unstable, worsening the picture, and blocks dopamine which is unhelpful here. There is no clinical evidence of sepsis; the picture is serotonergic toxidrome. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)

Naloxone treats opioid toxicity (miosis and respiratory depression); this picture is mydriatic, hyperreflexic and hyperadrenergic. Physostigmine treats anticholinergic toxidrome (dry, warm, red) not this presentation. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)

explanation.summary: Stimulants (methylphenidate, dexamfetamine, lisdexamfetamine) are relatively contraindicated in structural heart disease including hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due to risk of arrhythmia, outflow tract obstruction, and sudden death. Atomoxetine is the preferred non-stimulant first-line for adult ADHD in this scenario with a favourable cardiovascular risk profile. Blood pressure and heart rate monitoring is still needed as atomoxetine can raise both. Bupropion and modafinil are not first-line for ADHD in Australia.
key_points: Structural heart disease is a relative contraindication to stimulants for ADHD
Atomoxetine (selective NRI) is preferred non-stimulant first-line in this scenario
Atomoxetine still needs BP and HR monitoring
Bupropion and modafinil are not first-line for ADHD in Australia
explanation.pearls: In adult ADHD with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or a structural cardiac lesion, atomoxetine beats stimulants; the ICD does not make it safe to start a stimulant.

options.rationale: Stimulants (methylphenidate and dexamfetamine) are relatively contraindicated in structural heart disease including hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due to arrhythmia and outflow tract obstruction risks. Even ECG monitoring does not mitigate the underlying risk in a patient with an ICD. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guidelines)

Dexamfetamine carries the same stimulant-mediated cardiovascular risks as methylphenidate and is relatively contraindicated in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Cardiology liaison does not overcome the structural risk. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guidelines)

Atomoxetine is a non-stimulant selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor and is preferred first-line for adult ADHD when stimulants are contraindicated (structural heart disease, substance-use risk, tics). It still requires BP and HR monitoring but has a favourable risk profile in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy compared with stimulants. RANZCP guidance endorses atomoxetine in this scenario. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guidelines)

Bupropion has weak evidence for adult ADHD, lowers seizure threshold, and is not first-line non-stimulant in Australia. Atomoxetine is the preferred non-stimulant when stimulants are contraindicated. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guidelines)

Modafinil is used for narcolepsy in Australia; it is off-label for ADHD and has arrhythmogenic risks that make it unsuitable in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Atomoxetine is the RANZCP-preferred non-stimulant. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guidelines)

explanation.summary: This is catatonia (Bush-Francis features: mutism, staring, waxy flexibility, echopraxia, negativism) without autonomic instability or rigidity to suggest malignant catatonia. The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV, observed over 20-30 min) is both diagnostic and initial therapy; a positive response is dramatic. Responders continue on regular lorazepam 6-24 mg/day, tapered as symptoms resolve. ECT is second-line if lorazepam fails or if malignant catatonia develops (autonomic instability, hyperthermia, rigidity, raised CK). Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and NMS.
key_points: Bush-Francis features: mutism, staring, waxy flexibility, echopraxia, negativism, posturing
First-line: lorazepam challenge 1-2 mg IV, observe 20-30 min
Second-line: ECT if lorazepam fails or malignant catatonia
Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and NMS
explanation.pearls: Give 1-2 mg IV lorazepam as your first move in a new catatonia; do NOT reach for olanzapine, which can precipitate malignant catatonia or NMS.

options.rationale: Bromocriptine and dantrolene treat NMS, not catatonia. This patient has no rigidity, autonomic instability, or raised CK; the picture is pure catatonia without NMS overlap. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guidance)

Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and increase the risk of NMS in a patient who is already catatonic. First-line is a lorazepam challenge, and antipsychotics are added only after catatonia is controlled. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guidance)

There is no fever, altered vitals, focal neurology, or CSF or imaging evidence of encephalitis. Empirical aciclovir is not indicated in an afebrile patient with classic Bush-Francis catatonic signs. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guidance)

ECT is highly effective in catatonia but is second-line in AU practice after a lorazepam challenge has been tried. It is escalated to when lorazepam is ineffective or in the presence of malignant catatonia (which requires autonomic instability, not present here). (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guidance)

Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale features (mutism, staring, waxy flexibility, echopraxia, negativism) meet catatonia diagnostic criteria in DSM-5. The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV, observe for symptom improvement over 20-30 min) is the standard diagnostic and initial therapeutic step. Responders continue on regular lorazepam 6-24 mg/day. ECT is second-line if lorazepam fails. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guidance)

explanation.summary: The RANZCP and NHMRC-endorsed Australian PTSD guidelines recommend an SSRI (sertraline or paroxetine) as first-line pharmacotherapy for PTSD in adults, ideally as an adjunct to trauma-focused psychotherapy. Sertraline is typically started at 50 mg daily and titrated to 100 to 200 mg over 4 to 6 weeks. Benzodiazepines are contraindicated because they impair extinction learning; antipsychotics are augmentation agents only.
key_points: SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) are first-line pharmacotherapy for PTSD
Benzodiazepines should be avoided in PTSD
Antipsychotics are augmentation, not first line
Prazosin is specifically for trauma-related nightmares
explanation.pearls: For trauma-related nightmares refractory to SSRI, add prazosin starting at 1 mg at night with blood pressure monitoring; titrate weekly by 1 mg to a maximum of about 15 mg at night.

options.rationale: Second-generation antipsychotics are not first line for PTSD; quetiapine is considered only as an augmentation agent and its metabolic risks argue against routine use in this setting.
AU RANZCP guidance recommends an SSRI (sertraline or paroxetine) as first-line pharmacotherapy for PTSD in adults, starting at 50 mg daily and titrating to a therapeutic dose over 4 to 6 weeks.
Benzodiazepines are contraindicated as first line in PTSD; they worsen extinction of trauma memories and carry dependence risk in a chronic condition like this.
Prazosin has a specific role for trauma-related nightmares but does not address the full PTSD symptom cluster; SSRIs remain first line by RCT evidence.
Mirtazapine has limited evidence in PTSD and is a second- or third-line option; SSRIs remain first line based on stronger RCT evidence in this population.

explanation.summary: Chronic self-harm in borderline personality disorder is best managed in the emergency department by medical wound care, collaborative safety planning with the patient, and communication with the treating DBT team. Discharge is structured with crisis contacts and clear plans for follow-up. Involuntary admission is avoided unless a superimposed acute major mental illness or an escalating atypical presentation raises acute risk. Intramuscular sedation of a cooperative patient reinforces sedation as a coping strategy and is not indicated.
key_points: Involuntary admission for chronic self-harm in BPD is usually counter-therapeutic
ED management: wound care, collaborative safety plan, treating team contact
Sedation for a cooperative patient is not indicated
Limit medication quantities to reduce overdose risk
explanation.pearls: Reserve inpatient admission for BPD when there is superimposed major mental illness, an atypical or escalating pattern, or when brief admission is planned for a specific goal with an agreed discharge date.

options.rationale: Involuntary admission for chronic self-harm in BPD is generally counter-therapeutic, reinforcing crisis behaviours and worsening long-term outcomes for the patient over time.
IM olanzapine is not indicated in a coherent cooperative patient without acute agitation, psychosis or mania and would reinforce sedation as a coping strategy long term.

Best-practice ED management of chronic BPD self-harm is wound care, collaborative safety planning, communication with the treating team and structured discharge; hospital admission is avoided unless acute major mental illness risk is present.
There is no strong evidence for SSRIs specifically for chronic self-harm in BPD, and prescribing 3 months of an antidepressant to a patient with chronic suicidality raises overdose risk.
Medical admission for uncomplicated superficial cutting is not indicated and delays discharge planning without adding clinical benefit for a patient engaged with DBT.

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia is most reliably managed by switching to a prolactin-sparing agent. Aripiprazole (partial dopamine agonist) is first choice; olanzapine and quetiapine are lower-risk alternatives compared with risperidone and paliperidone. Cross-titration should be done over 4 weeks with monitoring for symptom recurrence. Adding a dopamine agonist to the current antipsychotic risks psychotic relapse and is generally avoided.
key_points: Switch to aripiprazole is preferred over adding a dopamine agonist
Prolactin elevation is weakly dose-related for risperidone at therapeutic doses
Cross-titrate over 4 weeks and monitor for psychotic relapse
Persistent hyperprolactinaemia risks bone loss and amenorrhoea
explanation.pearls: For patients where a switch is not tolerated, low-dose adjunctive aripiprazole 5 to 10 mg added to the existing antipsychotic has emerging evidence for lowering prolactin without triggering psychosis relapse.

options.rationale: Adding a dopamine agonist to an antipsychotic risks triggering relapse of psychosis; the guideline-preferred approach is to switch to a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic rather than add a dopamine agonist.
Prolactin elevation is only weakly dose-related for risperidone at therapeutic doses; halving the dose may destabilise psychosis without normalising the prolactin level in this patient.
Haloperidol raises prolactin at least as much as risperidone; it is not a prolactin-sparing option and would not resolve the endocrine adverse effect she is experiencing.

Aripiprazole is prolactin-sparing as a partial dopamine agonist and is the AU-preferred switch strategy for antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia; olanzapine and quetiapine are also lower-risk options for switching.
An untreated prolactin above 2000 mIU/L over months increases the risk of bone mineral density loss and persistent amenorrhoea; specific action from psychiatry is needed now.

explanation.summary: For a new prescription in pregnancy, sertraline is the AU-preferred SSRI due to the largest safety database, minimal placental transfer, and lowest breast milk concentrations for future breastfeeding. Paroxetine is avoided in pregnancy because of a small increased risk of fetal cardiac malformations. Fluoxetine and venlafaxine are reasonable if already effective for the woman but are not first-choice new prescriptions.
key_points: Sertraline is first-choice SSRI for a new prescription in pregnancy
Paroxetine avoided due to small VSD risk
Fluoxetine acceptable if already effective, longer half-life
Venlafaxine risks maternal hypertension and neonatal adaptation syndrome
explanation.pearls: Neonatal adaptation syndrome (jitteriness, feeding difficulty, transient tachypnoea) affects 10 to 30 percent of SSRI-exposed neonates; it is short-lived and stopping SSRIs in the third trimester is not recommended because relapse risk exceeds neonatal risk.

options.rationale: Paroxetine is associated with a small increased risk of fetal cardiac malformations (ventricular septal defect) and is generally avoided as a new prescription in pregnancy.
Fluoxetine is reasonable but has a longer half-life and higher milk-plasma ratio than sertraline; sertraline is preferred as a new prescription in pregnancy for these reasons.
Venlafaxine is associated with increased risk of maternal hypertension and neonatal adaptation syndrome; SSRIs are preferred as first line in pregnancy over SNRIs like venlafaxine.
Mirtazapine has a smaller safety database than SSRIs in pregnancy and is not first line; SSRIs remain the preferred first choice for treating depression in the perinatal period.
Sertraline is the AU-preferred SSRI for depression in pregnancy due to the largest safety database, minimal placental transfer, and low breast milk concentrations for future breastfeeding.

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome presents within hours of a serotonergic combination with the triad of neuromuscular hyperactivity (lower limb hyperreflexia, clonus, tremor), autonomic instability (hyperthermia, tachycardia, mydriasis, diaphoresis, diarrhoea) and altered mental status. It is distinguished from NMS by rapid onset, lower limb dominance, clonus and lower CK. Management is cease serotonergic agents, benzodiazepines, active cooling and cyproheptadine if refractory.
key_points: Serotonin syndrome: clonus, lower limb dominant, autonomic instability, rapid onset
NMS: rigidity, upper motor tone increase, days-long onset, very high CK
Treat serotonin syndrome with benzodiazepines, cooling, cyproheptadine
Avoid haloperidol; it worsens NMS if misdiagnosed
explanation.pearls: Tramadol, linezolid, MAOIs and MDMA are potent serotonergic agents commonly overlooked; a careful drug and supplement history including St John's wort is essential when serotonin syndrome is suspected.

options.rationale: Serotonin syndrome from a serotonergic combination is treated by ceasing offending agents, benzodiazepines for agitation, active cooling for hyperthermia, and cyproheptadine 12 mg PO stat as an antidote in refractory cases.

Dantrolene is used for NMS or malignant hyperthermia, not serotonin syndrome; the clinical picture here with inducible clonus and diaphoresis 6 hours after adding a serotonergic is serotonin syndrome.
Bromocriptine is for NMS, not serotonin syndrome; paracetamol does not treat centrally driven hyperthermia; sertraline must also be ceased as it is the primary serotonergic driver.
Haloperidol is an antidopaminergic that can precipitate or worsen NMS and dystonia and should be avoided; continuing serotonergic agents in serotonin syndrome is inappropriate.
Therapeutic hypothermia to 33 C is used post cardiac arrest, not for serotonin syndrome; simple external cooling to below 38.5 C is sufficient unless the case is refractory.

explanation.summary: High-risk alcohol withdrawal (heavy chronic intake, GGT elevated, MCV raised) is managed with parenteral thiamine 300 mg IV three times daily for at least 3 to 5 days to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, plus symptom-triggered benzodiazepines (oral diazepam) guided by CIWA-Ar. Glucose must not precede thiamine in a chronic heavy drinker. Antipsychotics are contraindicated as they lower seizure threshold, and elective surgery should be deferred until withdrawal is managed.
key_points: IV thiamine 300 mg TDS for at least 3 to 5 days in high-risk drinkers
Thiamine must precede glucose in chronic heavy drinkers
Symptom-triggered diazepam by CIWA-Ar is preferred to fixed-dose
Avoid antipsychotics (lower seizure threshold) and defer elective surgery
explanation.pearls: Wernicke encephalopathy is under-recognised: only 10 percent have the classical triad of ataxia, ophthalmoplegia and confusion at presentation; treat empirically in any at-risk patient with any one of these features.

options.rationale: Oral thiamine 100 mg is inadequate for a high-risk drinker facing surgery; parenteral thiamine at 300 mg IV is preferred to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy in this scenario.
AU eTG advises IV thiamine 300 mg three times daily for at least 3 to 5 days in high-risk drinkers to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, plus symptom-triggered oral diazepam guided by CIWA-Ar.
Giving glucose before parenteral thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in a chronic heavy drinker; parenteral thiamine must be given first before any glucose infusion.
Withholding thiamine entirely in a chronic heavy drinker risks Wernicke encephalopathy and proceeding to elective surgery risks unmanaged withdrawal intra- and postoperatively; defer surgery.
Haloperidol lowers seizure threshold and is contraindicated in alcohol withdrawal; benzodiazepines are the definitive treatment for prevention of alcohol withdrawal seizures.

explanation.summary: Delirium superimposed on dementia is diagnosed by acute onset, fluctuating attention, altered arousal and disorientation. The precipitant here (likely urinary sepsis) is identified and treated. Non-pharmacological measures are first line: hydration, quiet environment, family involvement, orientation cues, and avoiding restraints. Antipsychotics are last resort at low doses (risperidone 0.25 to 0.5 mg) for severe distress or safety risk.
key_points: Identify and treat the precipitant of delirium (infection, medication, metabolic)
Non-pharmacological measures first line
If antipsychotic needed, low dose (risperidone 0.25 to 0.5 mg), short-term, daily review
CT and LP only if focal signs, trauma, anticoagulation or no clear cause
explanation.pearls: Cholinesterase inhibitors used for dementia do not treat delirium and should not be started acutely for confusion; there is evidence they may worsen delirium duration and outcomes.

options.rationale: Antipsychotics for delirium should be short-term, low-dose (risperidone 0.25 to 0.5 mg), reserved for severe distress or safety risk, and reviewed daily; 2 mg twice daily for 4 weeks is inappropriate.

CT head is warranted if there is focal neurology, recent trauma or anticoagulation, or if no clear precipitant is found; LP if CNS infection is suspected. Neither is a routine first step with a clear UTI.

Delirium superimposed on dementia is managed by identifying and treating the precipitant (here likely UTI), maintaining hydration, avoiding restraints, providing quiet single-room care and involving family.
Steroids can worsen delirium and are not indicated. Cholinesterase inhibitors may help dementia symptoms and should not be stopped abruptly during an acute confusional episode.
Discharge home with acute delirium and safety concerns without treating the precipitant is unsafe; admission for management of the delirium and its cause is warranted here today.

explanation.summary: AU RANZCP metabolic monitoring on antipsychotics includes baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months and then 6-monthly weight, BMI, waist, BP; fasting glucose, HbA1c and lipids at baseline, 3 months then annually (more frequently if abnormal or rapid weight gain). Rapid weight gain (over 5 kg in 3 months) mandates repeat panel and consideration of metformin, exercise referral and antipsychotic switch to a lower metabolic-risk agent such as aripiprazole.
key_points: Metabolic panel at baseline, 3 months, then annually
Weight, BMI, waist, BP at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months, then 6-monthly
Rapid weight gain triggers earlier panel and intervention
Consider switch to aripiprazole or add metformin
explanation.pearls: Aripiprazole, ziprasidone and lurasidone have the lowest metabolic risk among second-generation antipsychotics; olanzapine and clozapine have the highest, and quetiapine, risperidone and paliperidone sit in between - factor this into first-choice selection at initiation.

options.rationale: 6 kg weight gain in 3 months on olanzapine is rapid; deferring bloods to 6 months misses the early metabolic syndrome window where intervention prevents diabetes.
Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after 2 failed trials; and clozapine has similar or worse metabolic profile than olanzapine, not a rational switch here.
Prescribing metformin before repeat fasting glucose or HbA1c is empirical without indication; AU guidance is to reassess metabolic panel first before adding metformin.
Lifestyle alone is not sufficient given rapid weight gain and BP change; monitoring bloods are the AU standard at 3 months, especially with early metabolic signals.

RANZCP AU metabolic monitoring on olanzapine requires 3 month bloods (fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids) with earlier repeat if rapid weight gain; a 6 kg gain and rising BP warrant same-visit bloods and follow up.

explanation.summary: TCA overdose causes sodium channel blockade with QRS widening, terminal R in aVR, hypotension and seizures. QRS >100 ms is the trigger for IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus with target arterial pH 7.5. Airway protection is required for falling GCS. Class I and III antiarrhythmics, flumazenil and physostigmine are contraindicated. Charcoal only within 1 to 2 hours in an awake and protected airway.
key_points: QRS >100 ms triggers IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg
Target arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55 by titrated bicarbonate
Contraindicated: class I/III antiarrhythmics, flumazenil, physostigmine
Charcoal only if airway protected and within 1 to 2 hours
explanation.pearls: In refractory hypotension despite bicarbonate and adrenaline, intravenous 20 percent lipid emulsion (1.5 mL/kg bolus then 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion) is considered under Poisons Information advice; TCA is lipid-soluble and lipid rescue targets the free drug fraction.

options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated after TCA overdose because it can precipitate seizures; and it treats benzodiazepines, not TCA; the priority is sodium bicarbonate for the cardiotoxicity.
Class III antiarrhythmics worsen sodium channel blockade in TCA overdose; sodium bicarbonate is the specific treatment, not amiodarone.

QRS above 100 ms with terminal R in aVR after significant TCA ingestion mandates sodium bicarbonate to overcome sodium channel blockade and prevent VT; airway protection given falling GCS is standard.
Charcoal is only effective within 1 to 2 hours of ingestion in awake protected airways; at 90 minutes with falling GCS, aspiration risk is high and the priority is bicarbonate plus airway.
Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate bradyarrhythmias, asystole and seizures.

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome presents rapidly (within 24 hours) after a serotonergic drug interaction with a triad of autonomic instability, neuromuscular excitation (lower limb-predominant clonus, hyperreflexia) and altered mental state.
