Serotonin-noradrenergic antidepressants carry higher switching risk in bipolar and are not appropriate when the presentation is antidepressant-driven mixed features. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

Lamotrigine is useful for bipolar depression maintenance but not for acute mixed features and does not address the destabilising antidepressant; the slow titration also delays therapeutic effect. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

Benzodiazepines are adjunctive symptom control at best; the driver is antidepressant-induced destabilisation and continuing sertraline perpetuates the mixed episode. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

explanation.summary: Established PTSD (symptoms persisting more than a month with functional impairment) is best treated with trauma-focused psychological therapy: TF-CBT with prolonged exposure or cognitive processing, or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR). Around 8-12 sessions are typical. SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) or SNRI (venlafaxine) are second-line, particularly for comorbid depression or when TF therapy is refused or unavailable. Benzodiazepines are contraindicated because they impair fear-extinction learning. Prazosin is adjunctive for PTSD-associated nightmares. Single-session debriefing after trauma has no benefit and may harm.
key_points: First-line PTSD: TF-CBT or EMDR, 8-12 sessions
SSRI/SNRI second-line or adjunct for depression/anxiety
Benzodiazepines contraindicated in PTSD
Prazosin adjunct for nightmares
explanation.pearls: Prolonged exposure therapy uses in-vivo and imaginal exposure to trauma cues to habituate the fear response; cognitive processing therapy targets stuck-point beliefs; both have around 60-70 percent response rate with sustained benefit at 12 months.

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines worsen PTSD outcomes and interfere with fear-extinction learning underpinning trauma-focused therapy; they are contraindicated as PTSD treatment. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) are second-line for PTSD when trauma-focused therapy is unavailable or refused, or when comorbid depression drives; TF therapy has larger effect sizes. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

Trauma-focused psychological therapy (TF-CBT or EMDR) is first-line in adult PTSD per Phoenix Australia and NICE; pharmacotherapy is added if TF therapy is refused or unavailable, or if severe comorbid depression complicates. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)
Prazosin has role for PTSD-associated nightmares but is adjunctive; first-line for the overall disorder is trauma-focused psychological therapy. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

Single-session psychological debriefing after trauma is not recommended and can worsen outcomes; established PTSD needs structured trauma-focused therapy over 8-12 sessions. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: First episode psychosis carries a favourable response rate to low-dose second-generation antipsychotics; RANZCP recommends risperidone or aripiprazole first-line because of the metabolic profile relative to olanzapine and clozapine. Start low and titrate slowly (risperidone 1 mg BD to 2-4 mg total; aripiprazole 10 mg to 15 mg daily) with monitoring for EPS. Substance use co-management (cannabis in particular) is essential as continued use predicts poorer response and relapse. Family psychoeducation and vocational support are cornerstones. Metabolic baseline and 3-monthly monitoring (weight, waist, glucose, lipids, BP) is required.
key_points: Risperidone or aripiprazole first-line in first episode
Low starting dose, slow titration, EPS monitoring
Cannabis co-management essential
Metabolic baseline and 3-monthly monitoring
explanation.pearls: Around 60-80 percent of first episode psychosis responds within 6 weeks to adequate dose; treatment for at least 12 to 24 months after remission is standard, with individualised discussion around continuation, given up to 80 percent relapse rate if stopped after single episode remission.

options.rationale: Olanzapine has substantial metabolic burden (weight gain 5-12 kg in first year) and is not recommended first-line in first episode psychosis per RANZCP; risperidone or aripiprazole are preferred for their metabolic profile and dopaminergic effect. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)
Typical antipsychotics carry high EPS risk and are not first-line in first episode psychosis; second-generation agents (risperidone or aripiprazole) are standard. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of 2 antipsychotics at adequate dose and duration); it is not first-line in first episode psychosis. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

Risperidone or aripiprazole are first-line in first episode psychosis per RANZCP CPG because of the more favourable metabolic profile; low starting dose with weekly titration to 2-4 mg is standard, with EPS monitoring. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

Quetiapine is used but has weaker antipsychotic effect at low doses and is often subtherapeutic; risperidone or aripiprazole are preferred first-line per RANZCP with better response in first episode psychosis. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

explanation.summary: Postnatal depression affects around 10-15 percent of new mothers and warrants active treatment given impact on infant attachment, cognitive and emotional development. Sertraline has the strongest breastfeeding safety data of the SSRIs, with negligible infant serum levels and no reported adverse effects at therapeutic maternal doses. Start 50 mg daily (25 mg for the first 3 days if anxious features) and review at 2 weeks. Psychological therapy (interpersonal therapy or CBT) is offered concurrently. Postpartum psychosis or severe depression with active suicidal or infanticidal ideation warrants urgent psychiatric admission with mother-baby unit consideration.
key_points: Sertraline first-line SSRI in breastfeeding (low RID)
Paroxetine also acceptable in breastfeeding
Fluoxetine higher infant serum levels (long half-life)
IPT or CBT concurrent psychological therapy
explanation.pearls: The relative infant dose (RID) for sertraline is around 0.5-2 percent of maternal weight-adjusted dose; the general threshold of concern is 10 percent; monitor infant for sedation, feeding, weight gain, and irritability.

options.rationale: Sertraline has the strongest safety data in breastfeeding, with negligible infant serum levels and low relative infant dose (<2 percent); it is first-line SSRI in perinatal depression per Beyond Blue and LactMed. (Source: LactMed Sertraline)

Fluoxetine and its active metabolite norfluoxetine have long half-lives (2-4 days and 7-15 days respectively), leading to higher infant serum levels compared to sertraline; sertraline or paroxetine are preferred in breastfeeding. (Source: LactMed Sertraline)
Escitalopram is second-line in breastfeeding; sertraline has more robust safety data and lower relative infant dose in the perinatal literature. (Source: LactMed Sertraline)

Venlafaxine has less breastfeeding safety data than sertraline and is not first-line perinatally; SSRIs (sertraline preferred) are first-line for depression with mixed anxiety features in breastfeeding mothers. (Source: LactMed Sertraline)

St John's wort is not recommended in breastfeeding due to inconsistent standardisation, drug interactions (CYP3A4 inducer), and infant safety uncertainty; sertraline is first-line. (Source: LactMed Sertraline)

explanation.summary: Depressive pseudodementia is late-life depression presenting with prominent cognitive complaints. Distinguishing features from Alzheimer's disease include prominent affective symptoms, insight into cognitive change (complaining rather than concealing), global rather than domain-specific cognitive reduction, recall improving with cueing, poor effort on testing, and preserved autobiographical memory. Treat depression with an SSRI at reduced starting dose (elderly) and reassess cognition 8-12 weeks after mood remission. Persistent cognitive deficits after mood remission warrant further neurodegenerative workup including MRI and neuropsychology.
key_points: Pseudodementia: prominent depression, insight preserved
Recall improves with cueing (not seen in Alzheimer's)
SSRI first-line, reduced starting dose in elderly
Reassess cognition 8-12 weeks after mood remission
explanation.pearls: Up to 40 percent of pseudodementia patients develop true dementia within 5 years; ongoing cognitive monitoring is warranted even after mood remission; consider MRI, neuropsychology, and possible CSF biomarkers if cognition does not fully recover.

options.rationale: Cognitive picture with intact recall on cueing, global (not domain-specific) reduction, and depressive symptoms fits pseudodementia rather than Alzheimer's; treating depression first clarifies the diagnosis and avoids inappropriate cholinesterase inhibitor exposure. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

CSF biomarkers are not first-line in this scenario where depression is a strong alternative explanation; treat depression first, then reassess cognition and consider structural imaging or biomarker referral if deficits persist. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

Depressive pseudodementia is common in late-life depression; recall improving with cueing, global cognitive reduction, and prominent depressive features support depression as primary; treat with an SSRI at reduced starting dose (elderly), then reassess cognition 8-12 weeks after mood remission. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

MRI is useful when structural cause is suspected but should not delay treatment of clearly identified depression; treat first and image if cognitive deficits persist after mood remission. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

Memantine is for moderate to severe Alzheimer's, not a diagnostic trial; and the clinical picture supports pseudodementia rather than established dementia at this point. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

explanation.summary: Escalating self-injurious behaviour and aggression in an autistic adolescent with intellectual disability warrants a structured medical (rule out pain, constipation, dental, otitis) and behavioural (functional analysis, visual schedules, sensory adaptations) assessment first. When these are optimised and injury risk remains, risperidone or aripiprazole are the two agents with the strongest evidence and TGA indication in Australia for irritability associated with autism. Titrate slowly from a low starting dose (risperidone 0.25 mg nocte) with metabolic baseline (weight, waist, glucose, lipids, prolactin, BP) and monitoring every 3 months. Reassess indication regularly and taper when clinically stable.
key_points: Rule out pain, constipation, dental, otitis before pharmacotherapy
Risperidone or aripiprazole first-line for autism irritability
Metabolic baseline and 3-monthly monitoring
Reassess indication and taper when stable
explanation.pearls: Aripiprazole tends to cause less weight gain and hyperprolactinaemia than risperidone but higher akathisia; both have TGA approval for autism-associated irritability; typical response emerges within 2-4 weeks.

options.rationale: Melatonin may help sleep initiation but does not treat established self-injurious behaviour or aggression; when behavioural measures have failed and injury risk is present, targeted pharmacotherapy is indicated. (Source: RCH Melbourne Autism Behaviour Guideline)

Clonidine is used for ADHD-symptom overlap and sleep in autism but has weaker evidence than risperidone or aripiprazole for irritability and self injurious behaviour of the severity described. (Source: RCH Melbourne Autism Behaviour Guideline)

Benzodiazepines cause paradoxical disinhibition in autism and intellectual disability and are not first-line; risperidone or aripiprazole is preferred with better evidence. (Source: RCH Melbourne Autism Behaviour Guideline)

SSRIs have limited evidence for irritability and aggression in autism and may worsen agitation, particularly in intellectual disability; risperidone or aripiprazole is preferred for irritability with SIB. (Source: RCH Melbourne Autism Behaviour Guideline)

Risperidone (or aripiprazole) is TGA-indicated for irritability and aggression in autism when behavioural interventions have failed; slow titration and metabolic baseline plus 3-monthly monitoring are required to minimise weight gain, hyperprolactinaemia, and metabolic burden. (Source: RCH Melbourne Autism Behaviour Guideline)

explanation.summary: TCA toxicity produces anticholinergic, alpha-blocking, sodium channel blocking and CNS depressant effects. Cardiovascular toxicity is the leading cause of death: QRS widening beyond 100 ms predicts seizures, above 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia. Management is airway (intubate if GCS deterioration), IV access, cardiac monitoring, IV sodium bicarbonate boluses (1-2 mmol/kg) titrated to QRS <100 ms and arterial pH 7.45-7.55, and correction of hypokalaemia (which worsens QT). Benzodiazepines for seizures. Lipid emulsion 20 percent 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus is considered in cardiac arrest or refractory shock. Avoid class Ia, Ic, and III antiarrhythmics; avoid flumazenil.
key_points: QRS >100 ms = give NaHCO3 1-2 mmol/kg IV, titrate to QRS <100 ms
Target pH 7.45-7.55 (alkalinisation dissociates drug from sodium channels)
Correct hypokalaemia (QT prolongation)
Avoid flumazenil, class Ia/Ic/III antiarrhythmics
Lipid emulsion for refractory cardiac arrest
explanation.pearls: The terminal R wave in aVR >3 mm and R/S ratio in aVR >0.7 predict severe TCA toxicity independently of QRS width and should trigger empirical alkalinisation even when QRS is <100 ms.

options.rationale: QRS widening beyond 100 ms in TCA overdose reflects sodium channel blockade and predicts VT/VF. The intervention is IV sodium bicarbonate boluses (1-2 mmol/kg, i.e. 100 mmol here) titrated to narrow QRS below 100 ms and to alkalinise pH to 7.45-7.55. Alkalinisation shifts drug away from cardiac sodium channels via protein binding and reduces free drug. This is a class I recommendation in the AU Toxicology & Toxinology Poisons Information text. (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook)

Flumazenil is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate seizures in a patient at risk of pro-convulsant drug effects; TCAs lower seizure threshold and flumazenil unmasks epileptogenic drug effects. It also does not reverse TCA toxicity. (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook)

Class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics (procainamide, flecainide) and class III agents that prolong QT (amiodarone, sotalol) worsen TCA cardiotoxicity by further blocking sodium channels or prolonging repolarisation. Sodium bicarbonate is the specific antidote. (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook)

Activated charcoal is considered within one hour of ingestion in patients with intact airway; at 90 minutes with reduced GCS the risk of aspiration outweighs the benefit unless the airway is secured. Sodium bicarbonate takes priority for the cardiotoxic manifestation. (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook)

Hypertonic saline does not have the same sodium-channel-shifting effect as bicarbonate because it does not alkalinise, and the therapeutic effect is combined sodium load AND alkalinisation. Bicarbonate is the specific treatment. (Source: Australian Toxicology Handbook)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is highly teratogenic (major malformations in 10 percent, neurodevelopmental disability in 30-40 percent of exposed pregnancies). Since 2019 the TGA has required a pregnancy prevention program for reproductive-age women, mirroring the UK MHRA Valproate PPP. Requirements are documented counselling about specific risks, highly effective contraception (LARC or dual method), annual specialist review, and signed acknowledgment. Prescribers should actively avoid valproate in reproductive-age women unless alternatives (lamotrigine, atypical antipsychotic, lithium) have been considered and rejected on clinical grounds. Folate supplementation does not mitigate valproate teratogenicity. Women already stable on valproate who become pregnant need urgent specialist review, not abrupt cessation which risks relapse.
key_points: 10% major malformations, 30-40% neurodevelopmental disability in exposed pregnancies
TGA pregnancy prevention program mandatory for reproductive-age women
LARC (implant or IUD) preferred; document counselling and acknowledgment
Folate does NOT mitigate valproate teratogenicity
Never abruptly cease in established pregnancy - urgent specialist review
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine is the preferred first-line mood stabiliser in reproductive-age women wishing to conceive because its bipolar depression prophylaxis is strongest and the malformation risk (~2 percent) is close to background; it needs 4-8 week uptitration to avoid Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

options.rationale: Valproate carries a 10 percent congenital malformation risk and 30-40 percent neurodevelopmental disability risk in exposed pregnancies. The TGA and RANZCP guidance mandates that valproate is not initiated in a woman of reproductive potential unless highly effective contraception (LARC or dual method) is in place and a pregnancy prevention program is documented. A negative pregnancy test alone is not sufficient. (Source: TGA valproate pregnancy prevention)

Folate supplementation does not mitigate valproate teratogenicity - valproate causes major malformations across multiple systems (neural tube, cardiac, craniofacial, limb) and neurodevelopmental disability by mechanisms beyond folate antagonism. Folate is used with all AEDs but is not a substitute for contraception. (Source: TGA valproate pregnancy prevention)

The TGA pregnancy prevention program for valproate requires that reproductive-age women initiating or continuing valproate have documented (a) counselling about teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks, (b) highly effective contraception in place, (c) annual specialist review, and (d) signed acknowledgment of understanding. LARC (etonogestrel implant or copper/hormonal IUD) is preferred. If she declines LARC, the recommendation is to use an alternative mood stabiliser (e.g. lamotrigine, atypical antipsychotic, remain on lithium with dose optimisation). (Source: TGA valproate pregnancy prevention)

Combination therapy does not remove valproate's teratogenic risk and adds side effect burden. The valproate pregnancy prevention program applies regardless of dose or combination status. (Source: TGA valproate pregnancy prevention)

Menstruation does not confirm the absence of an ongoing pregnancy or prevent future pregnancy. The requirement is for documented ongoing highly effective contraception, not menstrual timing. (Source: TGA valproate pregnancy prevention)

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced myocarditis occurs in around 3 percent of Australian initiations and clusters between days 14 and 28 of titration. Presentation is non-specific: fever, tachycardia disproportionate to fever, malaise, dyspnoea, chest discomfort, sometimes eosinophilia. Australian clozapine protocols mandate baseline troponin and CRP, then weekly for 4 weeks, then as clinically indicated. Any of the following triggers immediate cessation and cardiac evaluation: troponin more than double the upper limit, CRP >100 mg/L, tachycardia >120 sustained, unexplained fever, chest pain, or heart failure signs. Management is drug cessation, echocardiogram, cardiology involvement, and heart failure therapy if LV dysfunction develops. Re-challenge is only in specialist settings after full recovery and multidisciplinary discussion.
key_points: Days 14-28 of titration is the peak window
Fever, tachycardia disproportionate to fever, malaise, eosinophilia, troponin/CRP rise
Cease clozapine, urgent echocardiogram, cardiology, cardiac monitoring
Weekly troponin/CRP for the first 4 weeks per AU protocols
Re-challenge only in specialist setting after MDT discussion
explanation.pearls: Clozapine cardiomyopathy is a separate later complication (months to years after initiation) presenting with progressive heart failure symptoms; annual echocardiography is recommended for long-term clozapine-treated patients under AU protocols.

options.rationale: Empirical high-dose steroids for clozapine myocarditis without confirmed left ventricular dysfunction is not standard care - management is drug cessation, supportive care, cardiology review and consideration of heart failure therapy if reduced ejection fraction. Steroid use is contested. (Source: RANZCP clozapine)

Missing early clozapine-induced myocarditis is fatal (mortality up to 30 percent if unrecognised). Attributing fever to viral illness in the myocarditis window without troponin testing is negligent; the raised troponin and eosinophilia here rule this out. (Source: RANZCP clozapine)

Dose reduction is not appropriate management of clozapine myocarditis - the drug must be ceased. Structural cardiac assessment (echocardiogram) is required immediately, not deferred. (Source: RANZCP clozapine)

Clozapine-induced myocarditis typically presents in weeks 2-4 of titration with fever, tachycardia, dyspnoea, malaise, elevated CRP, elevated troponin and often eosinophilia. Any suspicion mandates immediate cessation, urgent echocardiogram, cardiology involvement, and cardiac monitoring. Even with normal ECG the raised troponin and eosinophilia are consistent with the AU Clozapine Monitoring Protocol (Northwick Park style adopted by state HHS clozapine services) and cessation is time-critical - continued exposure kills. (Source: RANZCP clozapine)

Isolated benign clozapine fever without cardiac or infective source is a diagnosis of exclusion made after cardiac and infective workup. Raised troponin excludes benign fever - the diagnosis here is myocarditis. (Source: RANZCP clozapine)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome, not a diagnosis - it complicates severe affective disorders (most commonly bipolar depression and mania), psychotic disorders, medical illness (autoimmune encephalitis, metabolic derangement), and drug effects (steroids, dopamine antagonists). Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale scores three or more of 12 signs. The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV or IM) is diagnostic and therapeutic - 60-80 percent respond within 30 minutes. Failure to respond does not exclude catatonia; escalate to ECT which is highly effective. Antipsychotics risk precipitating malignant catatonia/NMS and are avoided until catatonia is treated. Underlying cause (medical, psychiatric) is investigated and treated in parallel.
key_points: Bush-Francis: 3+ of 12 features (mutism, stupor, waxy flexibility, etc.)
Lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV) diagnostic + therapeutic
60-80% respond in 30 min; escalate scheduled lorazepam then ECT if refractory
Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia is treated (NMS risk)
Investigate underlying medical, autoimmune, and psychiatric cause
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (catatonia plus autonomic instability, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis) has mortality up to 30 percent and is a psychiatric emergency requiring ECT within 24 hours; benzodiazepines are a bridge but ECT is the definitive intervention.

options.rationale: Catatonia is clinically diagnosed with three or more of 12 Bush-Francis features (mutism, stupor, waxy flexibility, echolalia, negativism, staring, posturing, grimacing, immobility, mannerisms, echopraxia, stereotypy - this patient has seven). The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV) is both diagnostic and therapeutic: 60-80 percent respond within 30 minutes with reduction in Bush-Francis score, confirming catatonia. First-line ongoing management is scheduled lorazepam (usually 8-24 mg/day). ECT is indicated if lorazepam fails or in malignant catatonia. (Source: RANZCP catatonia)

Antipsychotics in undiagnosed catatonia risk precipitating neuroleptic malignant syndrome and worsening the catatonic state. Lorazepam is first-line before any dopamine antagonist is considered. (Source: RANZCP catatonia)

Autoimmune encephalitis is a differential but is not the initial move without more directive clinical or CSF findings. Lorazepam challenge is safe and diagnostic in typical catatonia; autoantibody workup runs in parallel if there are red flags (focal neurology, seizures, autonomic instability). (Source: RANZCP catatonia)

There are no signs of encephalitis (no fever spike, no seizures, no focal neurology, no CSF concerns). Lorazepam challenge is the appropriate first-line diagnostic. LP may follow if features evolve. (Source: RANZCP catatonia)

Lithium acts too slowly (weeks) to treat catatonia, and dose escalation in a patient with reduced oral intake risks toxicity. Lorazepam is the specific first-line intervention. (Source: RANZCP catatonia)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome is a clinical diagnosis based on Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria: in a patient exposed to a serotonergic agent, one of - spontaneous clonus, inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, tremor with hyperreflexia, or hypertonia with temperature >38 and clonus. Onset is within hours of drug addition; features include neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor), autonomic instability (fever, tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis, diaphoresis, hyperactive bowel sounds), and altered mental state. NMS by contrast develops over days to weeks after dopamine antagonist exposure with lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, fever, autonomic instability. Management of serotonin syndrome: cease serotonergic drugs, benzodiazepine sedation, aggressive cooling and IV fluids, cyproheptadine for severe cases.
key_points: Hunter criteria: clonus + hyperreflexia + agitation/diaphoresis in serotonergic patient
Onset over hours (SS) vs days-weeks (NMS)
Clonus + hyperreflexia (SS) vs lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia (NMS)
Cease serotonergic drugs, benzodiazepines, cooling, IV fluids; cyproheptadine for severe
Mydriasis in SS; pupils typically normal in NMS
explanation.pearls: Tramadol and pethidine both have serotonergic activity and are frequently overlooked culprits when added to SSRIs; fentanyl is a safer opioid choice in patients on SSRIs when acute analgesia is needed.

options.rationale: Bromocriptine treats NMS by reversing dopamine blockade; it is not indicated in serotonin syndrome and could worsen it. The temporal pattern (hours, not days after antipsychotic) and clonus (not rigidity) point to serotonin toxicity. (Source: eTG Complete Toxicology)

Continuing the serotonergic drugs is the opposite of what is needed. Dantrolene is used in malignant hyperthermia and adjunctive in severe NMS, not first-line in serotonin syndrome. Rigidity here is clonic, not the lead-pipe rigidity of NMS. (Source: eTG Complete Toxicology)

The features (rapid onset over hours after adding tramadol and olanzapine to sertraline plus St John's wort, tremor, hyperreflexia with sustained lower limb clonus greater than upper limb, mydriasis, hyperactive bowel sounds if elicited, autonomic instability) fit the Hunter serotonin toxicity criteria. Management is cessation of serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, tramadol, St John's wort), aggressive benzodiazepine sedation for autonomic instability and muscle activity, active cooling, IV fluids, and cyproheptadine (5HT2A antagonist) for refractory cases. NMS presents more slowly (days to weeks after antipsychotic exposure) with rigidity (not clonus), hyporeflexia, normal pupils. (Source: eTG Complete Toxicology)

Acute dystonia presents with focal muscle spasm (oculogyric crisis, torticollis, trismus), not autonomic instability, clonus and fever. Benzatropine has no role in serotonin syndrome. (Source: eTG Complete Toxicology)

The clinical picture (drug additions, hyperreflexia and clonus, mydriasis, no headache/neck stiffness/rash) is drug toxicity, not CNS infection. Empirical antibiotics delay specific management. (Source: eTG Complete Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is the acute biochemical decompensation (severe hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, thiamine deficiency, glucose intolerance, cardiac failure) that occurs when carbohydrate is reintroduced to a starved patient. Insulin surge drives intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium; thiamine is consumed in glucose metabolism. Deaths occur within days of refeeding when this is not anticipated. Australian ANZAED/ABC-2020 guidance for severe malnutrition: start 10-20 kcal/kg/day, give IV thiamine 300 mg daily before feed, prophylactic phosphate and multivitamin, daily K/PO4/Mg/Ca/glucose for 5 days, continuous cardiac monitoring for 5 days, specialist eating disorder team, gradual increase over 5-7 days to full requirement, weight gain target 0.5-1 kg/week. Involuntary admission under the state mental health act may be required if capacity is lost.
key_points: Start 10-20 kcal/kg/day, escalate over 5-7 days
IV thiamine 300 mg daily BEFORE feeds (Wernicke prevention)
Prophylactic phosphate + multivitamin; K/Mg replaced to mid-range
Daily electrolytes for 5 days, continuous cardiac monitoring 5 days
Specialist eating disorder team; consider Mental Health Act if capacity lost
explanation.pearls: A prolonged QTc in severe anorexia nervosa is more often multifactorial (hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, low T3) than structural; replacement of electrolytes and thyroid stabilisation with refeeding typically normalises the QTc without cardiology intervention.

options.rationale: Rapid refeeding in severe malnutrition (BMI under 13, recent rapid weight loss, minimal recent intake) causes refeeding syndrome (hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, cardiac failure, arrhythmia, neurological complications, death). Australian guidance is to start at 10-20 kcal/kg/day with gradual escalation, close electrolyte monitoring, and prophylactic phosphate and thiamine. (Source: ANZAED refeeding guidelines)

TPN is reserved for patients who cannot use the GI tract (obstruction, malabsorption). Enteral feeding is preferred where the gut works. TPN is associated with catheter sepsis and biochemical instability and is not first-line for anorexia nervosa refeeding. (Source: ANZAED refeeding guidelines)

Delaying feeding entirely in a critically malnourished patient worsens outcomes because ongoing starvation depletes reserves further. The correct approach is careful low-rate refeeding with intensive electrolyte support, not fasting. (Source: ANZAED refeeding guidelines)

40 mL/hour of 1 kcal/mL = 960 kcal/day, exceeding the 10-20 kcal/kg/day (340-680 kcal/day at 34 kg) initial target. Weekly bloods are inadequate - daily electrolytes are needed for at least 5 days in high-risk patients. (Source: ANZAED refeeding guidelines)

Australian guidance (ANZAED, ABC-2020 update from MARSIPAN) for severe malnutrition (BMI <13 or rapid loss >15 percent, low intake, biochemistry already at low reference range) recommends starting at 10-20 kcal/kg/day, giving IV thiamine 300 mg daily before feeds start (Wernicke prophylaxis), prophylactic phosphate (Phosphate Sandoz orally or IV Addiphos), K/Mg replacement to keep levels mid-range, daily electrolytes for 5 days then alternate days, continuous cardiac monitoring for at least 5 days, and specialist eating disorder consultation. (Source: ANZAED refeeding guidelines)

explanation.summary: Emergency management of self-injury in BPD focuses on medical care of the wound, brief structured risk assessment, collaborative safety planning, warm handover to community mental health services, and reinforcement of existing therapeutic work. Admission is reserved for acute suicidal intent not manageable in the community, severe comorbidity, or protective needs during a specific crisis. Routine admission of chronic self-injury worsens outcomes by reinforcing dependency, disrupting DBT skills work, and exposing the patient to iatrogenic harms. Safety planning is a specific intervention (Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention) - written, personalised, collaborative, identifying warning signs, coping strategies, contacts, and means restriction.
key_points: Structured safety plan + rapid community follow-up outperforms admission for chronic BPD self-injury
Admission reserved for acute intent not manageable in the community
Avoid routine benzodiazepines and PRN sedation in BPD
Reinforce existing DBT skills; do not disrupt outpatient work
Involuntary treatment threshold applies same as other conditions
explanation.pearls: The Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention (SPI) is a six-step written plan (warning signs, internal coping, social contacts and settings, people to help, professional agencies, means restriction) shown in AU cohorts to reduce re-presentation over the following 6 months when combined with rapid follow-up.

options.rationale: Structured discharge with a personalised written safety plan (identifying triggers, coping strategies, distraction techniques, contacts and 24-hour crisis lines), confirmed rapid community mental health follow-up (within 24-48 hours), and reinforcement of her existing DBT skills is the evidence-based response for chronic self-injury in BPD without acute suicidal intent. Admission increases dependency, disrupts DBT progress and does not reduce longer-term risk. (Source: RANZCP borderline personality disorder)

Involuntary admission requires evidence of severely disordered decision-making capacity or imminent risk not manageable in the community. Chronic self-injury without acute intent does not meet criteria. Repeated admissions worsen BPD outcomes and undermine therapeutic work. (Source: RANZCP borderline personality disorder)

Pharmacological sedation of a non-agitated distressed patient with BPD is not therapeutic and can medicalise emotional dysregulation. Guidelines advise against routine pharmacotherapy for the core features of BPD; only comorbid conditions and short-term distress are targets. (Source: RANZCP borderline personality disorder)

DBT is delivered in structured weekly group and individual outpatient sessions over months to years; an inpatient DBT intensive is not the standard AU care model for chronic self-injury without acute crisis. Rapid outpatient follow-up with her existing DBT team is optimal. (Source: RANZCP borderline personality disorder)

Benzodiazepines in BPD carry disinhibition, dependency and overdose risks. RANZCP guidance advises against routine PRN benzodiazepine prescribing for distress in BPD; skills-based crisis planning is safer and more effective. (Source: RANZCP borderline personality disorder)
